#7954. Frost Coming Your Way? What to Do With Veggies in the Garden

Updated Oct 28, 2026 4:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

While some people welcome the cooling that accompanies autumn, gardeners know they have work to do before the coming frost kills off the literal fruits (and veggies) of their labor.

First, find out the typical frost dates for your USDA hardiness zone and learn what temperatures cause frost damage. Then, watch local weather forecasts. Understand the difference between frost and light freeze, and which plants are more susceptible to frost damage.

Start with healthy plants and the right soil. Next, you’ll need to know which plants are tender and which can withstand a light frost and which delicious homegrown fruits and vegetables you’ll need to harvest before it’s too late.

Tender plants are easily damaged by frost or cold weather, requiring protection to survive. Common tender fruits and vegetables include watermelon, squash, pumpkin, cantaloupe and muskmelon, eggplant, cucumber, okra, pepper, beans, tomatoes, and most herbs.

Frost-tolerant plants can withstand brief periods of cold or frost, but beyond very limited periods, would require protection. Examples of frost-tolerant plants include lettuce, cauliflower, endive, peas, carrots, Chinese cabbage, celery, chard, and chicory.

Hardy plants generally have higher levels of sugar in their leaves, which enables them to tolerate lower temperatures. Cool-season crops that can survive a frost or even an early freeze include asparagus, cabbage, kale, spinach, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, collards, potatoes, and onions.

Many crops can be saved from an early frost. Even cool-season crops like lettuce and other leafy greens, carrots, and radishes can benefit from overnight covering to protect the plants from frost and extend the growing season. You can use old sheets or drop cloths (using supports to keep the cover from touching the plants), burlap, row covers made of non-woven polyester, or cloches.

Whichever type of plant cover you choose, make sure it is breathable. Do not use plastic. Ensure air circulation and be sure to remove the covers during the heat of the day, and put them back on in the early evening.If you have a greenhouse, move as many plants as you can inside.

Bio Green’s heater has a digital thermostat, sturdy stainless steel build, and is intended for spaces up to 130 square feet. Read the review.

Adding a 2- to 4-inch layer of mulch, particularly in the afternoon while the soil is warm, can help protect roots from overnight dips in temperature. Material choices to minimize frost damage include wood chips, bark, pine needles, straw, and even shredded leaves (including if they’re moldy). Dark mulch absorbs more of the sun’s warmth, which it releases into the soil around the plants at night.

Mulching the garden also preserves much-needed moisture. In addition, a layer of mulch will prevent perennials from putting out new growth at the end of the season, allowing them to go dormant for the winter.

Moist soil actually holds up to four times more heat than dry soil, and conducts that heat to the soil surface faster, creating a microclimate in which the air above it is 5 degrees warmer. In addition to providing an insulating effect, water helps plants withstand temperature changes better.

For best results, water late in the day because the water vapor creates a microclimate that will help plants stay warm and resist freezing.

When all else fails, harvest what you can. Beans, peas, corn, melons, cucumbers, eggplant, and most greens should be harvested early, since they don’t handle frost well. Be sure to pick tender herbs such as basil and oregano.

Tomatoes and peppers can ripen indoors after harvest. In fact, many fruits, including apples, peaches, pears, grapes, cantaloupe, and persimmon, ripen after picking. Store pumpkins and squash in a dry location for later use.

It can be tough to eat all of the last harvest right away, but there are plenty of ways to preserve your bounty: dry herbs, and can, dry, or freeze fruits and vegetables.

Many fruits can ripen indoors more quickly if they’re kept in a paper bag that is loosely closed at the top. Storing them this way traps ethylene gas that helps ripen fruit. Because rice also traps ethylene gas, fruits can be placed in containers of rice, although this is not recommended for tender fruits such as peaches that can suffer bruising. Taking these steps can typically help fruit ripen within a few days.

Plastic bags are not advised for ripening fruit because they don’t allow for ventilation.

Not all produce has to be harvested at the first sign of frost. Many root vegetables, like beets, carrots, onions, turnips, parsnips, and potatoes can easily survive a light frost. So can kale, artichokes, broccoli, cabbage, radishes, leeks, spinach, Brussels sprouts, and chard. In fact, cold temperatures improve the flavor of crops such as carrots and kale.

Several of these can even survive a hard frost, including broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, collards, kale, kohlrabi, mustard, onions, parsley, peas, radishes, spinach, turnips, leeks, and sorrel.

If frost gets your fruits and vegetables, they may not be edible. Tender plants like peppers, tomatoes, and many fruits may be mushy. Lettuces and other greens often turn dark and limp. Beans, eggplant, and potatoes are also susceptible to frost, and may exhibit crystalized moisture in their cells. Even carrots can become rubbery or limp after a hard frost.

If the produce is past its prime, dispose of it in your compost pile or bin, where it can benefit next year’s garden.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

Hidden in plain sight in the posters and trailers, these 12 plants could reveal more than you think about The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's something about Suzanne Collins' iconic dystopian series that feels more relevant than ever, and, with the latest film taking us back to the 50th Hunger Games, there's plenty for fans to scrutinize beyond the action itself. Personally, though, I can't stop looking at the plants.

If you've followed the franchise, you'll know that nature has never been merely decorative in Panem. From sinister plants and poisonous berries to the natural world providing food, healing plants, and shelter, knowing your botany in the arena can quite literally mean the difference between life and death.

There's also a long literary tradition of using plants as an act of resistance. After all, flowers have carried hidden messages for centuries, from the symbolism of roses in mythology to the elaborate Victorian language of flowers, when a carefully chosen bouquet could communicate everything from secret affection to heartbreak.

Watch The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Trailer:

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Even the names of some of the franchise's most memorable characters have botanical connections. Katniss is named after Sagittaria latifolia, a real North American aquatic plant also known as a swamp potato thanks to its edible tubers – making it a rather fitting namesake for a character whose survival instincts are so closely connected to the natural world.

Rue, meanwhile, shares her name with an aromatic herb traditionally associated with regret and sorrow (which is heartbreaking when you consider her story). And it seems the trailers and posters for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping suggest that the franchise's botanical language is far from finished.

From wildflowers carpeting the arena to carefully arranged floral displays around some of Panem's most recognisable characters, there are plenty of plants worth looking twice at in the posters and trailers alike.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some have fascinating historical meanings, others have surprisingly sinister botanical properties, and more than a few might offer clues about the story's characters and themes.

With that in mind, then, here are 12 botanical details I've spotted – and what they could mean.

The striking urn plant, Aechmea fasciata, is a popular bromeliad that's hard to miss in the above Sunrise On The Reaping poster thanks to its architectural rosette of silvery-green leaves and bright pink flower spike.

Its name comes from the distinctive cup formed by its overlapping leaves, which collects water in its natural habitat. This adaptation helps the plant make the most of the resources around it, even when growing conditions are challenging.

It's easy to see why it makes an interesting symbol in the Hunger Games universe. Urn plants are associated with resilience, adaptation and protection – qualities that are essential when survival is the ultimate prize. There's something particularly fitting about a plant that creates its own little reservoir of resources in a world where nothing comes easily, right?

Foxgloves (Digitalis purpurea) are among Britain's most recognisable wildflowers. Their tall flower spikes and bell-shaped blooms make them a favourite with pollinators and cottage garden enthusiasts... but there's a darker side to these pretty flowers. Every part of the foxglove plant is poisonous, containing compounds called cardiac glycosides that affect the heart.

Interestingly, those same compounds have played an important role in medicine. Digitalis-derived drugs have been used to treat certain heart conditions, making foxgloves a fascinating example of how the line between medicine and poison can depend on the dose.

In the Hunger Games, then, foxgloves could represent the duality of healing and danger – something that feels particularly at home in an arena where even the most beautiful things can be deadly.

White roses have long been associated with innocence, purity and remembrance. In Victorian flower dictionaries, their meanings included innocence, silence and even a holy death. Their appearance around President Snow is therefore particularly interesting, especially considering he's one of Panem's most ruthless figures.

Could they be a visual reminder of the innocence destroyed by the Capitol? Or perhaps a suggestion that even the most pristine-looking things can conceal something rotten underneath?

If white roses suggest purity, red roses are traditionally associated with passionate love and desire. They have been used for centuries as declarations of affection, but their symbolism isn't always straightforward. In the Victorian language of flowers, different shades and arrangements could carry different messages, from deep devotion to longing.

When red roses appear around President Snow, it's difficult not to consider the contrast between romantic passion and the bloodshed associated with his regime. After all, their vivid color also makes them an interesting counterpart to the white roses. Together, then, the two colors create a visual language of innocence, passion, power and mortality... which is very Hunger Games-coded.

The California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is instantly recognisable by its bright orange flowers. Native to western North America, it's also the official state flower of California. It's a hardy plant that thrives in sunny conditions and can tolerate relatively poor soils, making it a lovely symbol of resilience.

Poppies have different meanings across cultures, but they're frequently associated with remembrance, sleep and renewal. The California poppy's connection to the American landscape, though, makes it particularly interesting in the world of the Hunger Games, especially as it reimagines a future North America as Panem... especially as its bright and cheerful appearance feels so ironic against the darker world in which the Games take place.

Try the Burpee Sunset Mixed California Poppy Flower Seed from Walmart if you're in the mood for shades of orange, yellow, and cream in your own garden. You can even sow the seeds directly into gravel or cracks, too!

If you've spotted the sunflowers in the character poster for Percy Daggs IV as Ampert, you're not alone in wondering what they mean for the new Hunger Games film. After all, it's difficult to look at a sunflower (Helianthus annuus) without thinking of sunshine, happiness and optimism.

These towering annuals are often associated with hope, loyalty and resilience. Their ability to grow quickly and produce impressive flower heads makes them a familiar symbol of strength and positivity, and there's also a lovely modern interpretation of sunflower symbolism that centers on community and supporting one another through difficult times.

In a story where alliances can mean survival? Well, that sense of solidarity feels particularly poignant.

Canterbury bells (Campanula medium) are charming cottage garden flowers with tall stems covered in nodding bell-shaped blooms. And, fun fact, they're also the birth month biennial for May babies, too!

Their traditional Victorian flower meaning was 'acknowledgement', while other historical dictionaries associated them more generally with constancy. And, in a story about loyalty, friendship and the people we stand alongside when times get difficult, both interpretations feel rather fitting.

Celebrate the Tributes' attempt to break the machine, then, with a packet of Canterbury Bells Double Mix from Amazon.

The unusual pincushion protea, from the genus Leucospermum, has an unmistakable appearance. Its spiky flower heads look almost like elaborate fireworks or, as the name suggests, a pincushion.

Native to southern Africa, these evergreen shrubs are adapted to challenging growing conditions and are known for their striking flowers. Proteas more broadly, though, have become associated with transformation, strength, courage and diversity. As such, their unusual appearance also makes them a natural symbol of individuality.

Their presence around Effie Trinket is a possible nod to her flamboyant personality, as Effie has always been someone who embraces color, extravagance and standing out from the crowd, even when the world around her is anything but cheerful. Peersonally, though, this writer thinks it might be a nod to her eventual character arc...

Toadstools might not technically be plants – they're fungi, as we made very clear in our recent piece on birth month mushrooms – but they deserve a place in this botanical spotter's guide.

Fungi are essential to healthy ecosystems, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil. Some species, however, are highly poisonous, while others have medicinal or mind-altering properties, and that contrast gives mushrooms a fascinating symbolic role. They can represent decay and death, but also renewal, transformation and altered states of consciousness.

In the world of the Hunger Games, where the natural environment is often manipulated to confuse, frighten or kill its inhabitants? I suspect toadstools are a fitting reminder that not everything growing in the wild should be trusted.

Bee balm (Monarda) is a North American perennial loved by bees, butterflies and hummingbirds. Its colorful and nectar-rich flowers (particularly this stunning Pocahontas Purple Rose Bee Balm from Nature Hills) make it a wonderful addition to pollinator-friendly gardens, while the plant also has a history of traditional herbal use.

Today, bee balm is sometimes associated with compassion, empathy and comfort during difficult times. An RHS study of historical flower dictionaries, however, reveals that one nineteenth-century interpretation of this super-spreader was rather less affectionate: "Your whims are quite unbearable".

That's quite a contrast to the modern associations of care and kindness – and makes its appearance in the sinister world of the Hunger Games all the more intriguing... especially for those who remember the role they played in the Sunrise On The Reaping book.

Now here's a botanical detail I particularly love, as Nepenthes is a genus of tropical carnivorous plants, commonly known as tropical pitcher plants. Their distinctive modified leaves form hanging pitchers filled with digestive fluid, which trap and break down insects and other small prey.

The genus name has a fascinating origin. It comes from the Greek word nepenthes, associated with a mythical substance that banished sorrow or grief, which is an extraordinary name for a plant that catches and digests its victims.

In the context of the Hunger Games, the contrast is almost too good to ignore. A plant whose name evokes freedom from grief, but whose survival strategy involves trapping and consuming other creatures? Surely that's a dark metaphor for Panem itself (and almost worth buying a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Storein the run-up to the film, too).

A post shared by The Hunger Games (@thehungergames)

Spanish bluebells (Hyacinthoides hispanica) are popular spring-flowering bulbs, producing upright stems covered in clusters of blue, pink or white bell-shaped flowers. Unlike native blooms, though, these can spread vigorously in gardens and hybridize with native bluebells – something which hhis has raised concerns about the genetic integrity of native woodland populations.

The resulting hybrids can be difficult to identify, and experts advise gardeners living close to native bluebell populations to avoid planting Spanish bluebells. In terms of the Hunger Games, then, it's an interesting possible metaphor for displacement, hybridization and the arrival of an outsider that changes an established ecosystem.

In a story so concerned with power, territory and the destruction of existing communities, it feels like an idea well worth considering.

Beyond the individual plants seen across the posters and trailers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, it's the wider meadow-like landscape of the arena that deserves attention.

Wildflowers are usually associated with freedom, biodiversity and the natural world growing without human interference, and tend to evoke a sense of peace and escape from the pressures of modern life. This arena, though, turns that idea on its head, forcing nature to become a part of the spectacle. Its beauty is carefully presented, but the environment is ultimately controlled by the Gamemakers. A field of flowers might look like an idyllic meadow, yet it exists within a space designed to test, manipulate and endanger the tributes.

It's a clever contrast between the natural world as something beautiful and life-giving, and nature as something that can be manipulated into a weapon. And perhaps that's the biggest botanical message of all: in Panem, you should never assume that anything is harmless. Even something as simple and innocuous as, say, a flower.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7952. How to Wrap a Tree to Protect it From Winter Damage

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

It may sound like an odd practice, but wrapping a tree can be worthwhile. Once trees drop their leaves, they no longer benefit from their protective canopy, and hazards can damage young and thin-barked trees, along with some evergreen trees and shrubs. “Cold temperatures, drying winds, ice, and hungry wildlife can injure trees during winter,” says Fred Breglia, ISA, a certified arborist and author of the upcoming book titled Big Trees: A Tour of the World’s Biggest Trees.

And it’s not just the cold that makes trees susceptible to damage. Adding a tree wrap around the trunk can protect the bark from harsh winter sun when leaves no longer shade it. Ahead, learn why tree wrapping helps some trees flourish and survive colds—and how you can wrap trees for winter safely and effectively.

Young trees, like those that have been growing for up to two seasons, are especially susceptible to winter damage. Wrapping immature and thin-barked trees helps prevent trunk damage from sun and freeze-thaw cycles. Some evergreens also benefit from a full-tree wrap for winter or a screen to prevent browning foliage, and other young trees can be saved from animal munching or rubbing damage with a fence wrap.

Rapid temperature changes in winter combine with an empty canopy to expose trees to frost cracks or sunscald. Vertical frost cracks can make a tree more vulnerable to pests or diseases.  Sunscald is even more serious. “Sunlight warms frozen bark, then shade or nightfall causes it to refreeze and die,” says Breglia. Sunscald usually occurs on a trunk’s southwest side, where winter sun is most intense and the bark warms up the most. It can cause a jagged vertical wound along the tree trunk and dry, cracked, sunken, or dead bark.

Trees are more susceptible to sunscald include those less than 2 years old and species with thin bark, such as:

Another type of cold damage is winter browning, or desiccation injury, which “occurs when evergreen needles and rhododendron leaves lose moisture faster than frozen soil can replace it,” says Breglia. He adds that low temperatures, freeze-thaw cycles, sun, and wind can worsen winter damage on evergreens or semi-evergreens. “Browning often occurs on the south or southwest side of conifers, though wind exposure may also damage the north side,” Breglia says.

Trees and shrubs most susceptible to winter browning include broadleaf evergreens, needled evergreens, or those with scale-like leaves, such as:

Deer and other browsers can munch on buds of trees in winter when food is scarce, but they also can bite into tender bark. Even in early fall, bucks look for small tree trunks to rub against as new antlers form and cause itching. “Voles, mice, and rabbits can severely damage young trees and shrubs by eating their bark in winter,” adds Breglia.

As always, young trees are most vulnerable to severe damage, along with some trees that wildlife prefer.

If you have a young tree or a tree or shrub species vulnerable to winter damage, you generally need to learn how to use tree wrap so you can prepare it in fall before the first winter frost. The precise timing varies by region and the type of damage that can occur. For example, if deer visit your landscape, you might need to wrap young trunks by late summer or as soon as you see bucks growing antlers.

For potential vole and mice damage, wrap trunks before the first snowfall. Most young trees will benefit from wrap protection for at least two winter seasons. In all cases, be sure to remove tree wraps by spring and never leave them on all year.

The most common way to wrap a tree trunk for winter tree protection is with a poly or fabric tree wrap or plastic guard. A tree wrap should be breathable and a light color. Breglia says the material should “conform to the trunk but also allow airflow without trapping moisture.”

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Using a small trowel or shovel, gently scrape away any debris or leaves against the trunk and dig about 1 inch below the soil surface all around the trunk. This helps to set your tree wrap taut against the trunk and just below ground level.

Start at the lowest point of trunk exposure and begin to wrap around the trunk, ensuring each pass overlaps by at least ⅓ of the wrap’s width so there is no exposed bark.

If you’re using a plastic guard, widen the opening and place it around the tree, ensuring it sits just below ground level.

Continue to wrap the trunk until you reach the area just below the tree’s lowest branch. When you’re finished wrapping, secure the wrap with heavy-duty tape or twine. Do not staple or puncture the tree.

If using a plastic guard, add another guard above the lower one, cutting it if necessary to end just below the branches. Secure it to the bottom guard per manufacturer directions or with heavy-duty tape.

Check the wrap from time to time to make sure it remains secure at the top and has not loosened or been damaged below.

When the cold weather is over, carefully remove the wrap from the tree.

Although you can loosely wrap an entire shrub or tree in burlap to prevent winter browning, it is best to build a barrier around the plant, typically with stakes. “Use a burlap windbreak placed a few inches from the foliage, or loosely wrap multistemmed evergreens to block drying winter winds without trapping moisture,” says Breglia. If you wrap a tree or shrub in the fabric to protect it from wind or moisture loss, leave a hole at the top to allow sun and air to get in.

If you want to prevent winter wind damage like browning, install a burlap or shade fabric screen around the tree. Here’s how:

As long as your tree wrap is secure and at least 1 inch below ground, it can protect the trunk from most small animal damage. If you only need to protect against animals and not sunscald or browning, consider this method suggested by Breglia:

When wrapping trees for winter, always remember to remove the tree wrap in spring. Each spring, check trees and shrubs for any damage as growth resumes, like discolored needles, split bark, or areas that appear to have been nibbled on or stripped by animals. Breglia also advises watering trees well in spring and summer (and after planting a tree) so they are healthy when entering the winter season.

When properly placed, tree wrap can protect many trees and shrubs from winter damage. The trunks of young and thin-barked trees are particularly vulnerable to frost cracks, sunscald, and animal damage, so covering the trunk can keep a tree from the type of damage that could eventually result in taking the tree down and replanting.

Tree trunks are best wrapped in light-colored breathable fabrics especially designed for tree wrapping or plastic tree guards that surround a trunk. Some gardeners use burlap, but it can result in damage and is best used as a light wrap or screen to protect trees from winter browning or animal damage. Breglia recommends against the use of wound paint or dressing for young trees; paint will not protect trees from animal damage.

Always wait to wrap a tree in fall as it goes dormant and before the first hard frost. If you miss the first frost, wrap the tree as soon as the trunk has dried out to prevent repeated injury. Never wrap or leave wrap on a tree in spring or summer growth phases. And the best time to wrap a tree is when it is young (first 1 to 3 years of growth).

Some trees or shrubs need only temporary winter protection from unusual frosts or storms. A burlap screen or windbreak also can protect trees in winter. Spreading a 2- to 3-inch layer of mulch around the tree, at least the width of its root ball or canopy, can protect tender roots from repeated winter freezing and thawing. Breglia says that anti-dessicant sprays can help prevent drying out of trees and shrubs. Fencing can keep browsing animals away from evergreens.  “Proper placement of winter injury-sensitive plants, such as rhododendrons, boxwood, yew, or arborvitae can reduce the chance of winter damage,” adds Breglia. Finally, healthy trees can best survive winter, so watering and other care steps in spring and summer help protect tender trees in winter.

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7951. The Best Bathroom Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Published Oct 29, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Stepping into a chilly bathroom isn’t the most pleasant experience, but fortunately, there is a wide range of bathroom heaters that can quickly warm any bathroom. We researched nearly 50 different models and tested four in our own homes, and we found a favorite. Dreo’s wall-mount space heater took top honors for its quick heating, safety features, and its ability to be controlled remotely.

In addition to the units we tested, several others met our high standards for quality, safety, and innovation, and we’ve included them here as well. Keep reading to learn more about how the following models earned their spots on our lineup of the best bathroom heaters.

Bottom line: Discover the best bathroom heaters of 2026, from top-performing wall-mounts to budget-friendly options, ensuring a warm and comfortable space.

We tested the first four bathroom heaters on this list, and you’ll find a variety of options suited for various types of bathroom layouts and budgets. From wall-mount models that don’t take up floor space to small personal options for dressing nooks, these are some of the best bathroom heaters for keeping your space comfy.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Functionality 4.8/5; Noise 4.8/5; Value 4.8/5

Dreo has a winner with the Dreo WH517S smart space heater. We liked being able to hang this space heater on the wall, where it was up and out of the way, rather than sitting on a wet bathroom floor. Installation was simple: Dreo included a mounting template that indicated the location for the screws, and best of all, the template came with a bubble level so that we could ensure the heater would be perfectly straight.

Setting up the app was a snap. All we had to do was plug the Dreo WH517S into the wall socket and turn it on. We already had the Dreo app on our smartphone, which immediately recognized the heater. If you don’t have the app, a QR code walks you through the steps.

We tested the space heater in a small, 65-square-foot bathroom located at the end of an HVAC duct run, so it always felt cold during the winter—until now. On a day when the outdoor temperatures were in the single digits, the WH517S raised the bathroom’s temperature from a chilly 58 degrees to 70 degrees in about 20 minutes.

This heater also comes with an ALCI plug option capable of shutting the heater off when it senses abnormal electric flow. It also has an IP24 rating, so it can take an occasional splash of water. In homes with small children, this heater can be mounted high on the wall for added safety.

What our tester says: “On winter mornings, I love being able to turn on the heater in the bathroom from my smartphone without having to get out of bed. Just 15 minutes and the bathroom is warm and comfortable for my shower.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Dreo Wall-Mount bathroom heater at Amazon or Dreo.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4.5/5; Functionality 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Value 4.3/5

You don’t have to spend a lot to warm up a chilly bathroom. The Lasko 1500W bathroom space heater is compact, comes with an ALCI safety plug, and best of all, is affordable.

This Lasko heater doesn’t have many bells and whistles, but it’s a solid pick to heat a small- to medium-size bathroom. It measures just 8 inches tall by 6.25 inches wide and weighs just 3.35 pounds, making it small enough to sit on a bathroom shelf or countertop.

In our tests, this budget-friendly heater raised the temperature of our bathroom by 10 degrees in under 30 minutes when we ran it on high. We liked the option of choosing high or low power, and the heater’s 1-hour setting ensures it won’t continue to produce heat after an hour if someone leaves it running.

It comes with a cool-touch case that didn’t get hot after an hour of running the heater on high, but the grille on the front of the heater did get hot, so we’d suggest locating this bathroom heater out of the reach of pets and little hands.

Get the Lasko 1500W bathroom heater at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Performance 5/5; Functionality 5/5; Noise 5/5; Value 4.5/5

Thanks to its quiet operation, effective heating, and feature-rich design, this slim and stylish Dreo heater earned nearly perfect marks in all our tests. Though it weighs under 5 pounds and isn’t even 6 inches in diameter, it had no difficulty warming spaces significantly larger than its 200-square-foot recommended area. For that reason, we especially appreciate that it comes with a remote with an impressive 26-foot range, as we regularly have to turn it off during our baths in order to keep ourselves from getting too warm.

Still, remotes are fairly commonplace for these types of appliances, so Dreo upped the ante by adding 70-degree oscillation, a 12-hour timer, a programmable thermostat, three heat settings, and fan-only operation. The heater also features an ALCI plug, V-0 flame-retardant construction, overheating and tip-over protection, and an inline carry handle. While it did take us a bit of fumbling to figure out this unit’s touch-control buttons at first, it wasn’t so complicated that we needed to consult the manual, and we’ve now used it without issue almost every day for nearly 2 months.

Get the Dreo Solaris bathroom heater at Amazon or Dreo.

The following bathroom heaters were not personally tested, but we chose them for our lineup based on their quality, features, and consumer ratings. If you’re still looking for the right model, you’ll likely find it here.

A ceiling-mounted bathroom heater doesn’t use up valuable floor or wall space, and when properly installed, there should be no safety issues. The Panasonic WhisperWarm goes one better by integrating a bathroom vent with a heater in a single low-profile unit.

We like the exhaust fan, which can be set to run at 50, 80, or 110 cubic feet per minute (CFM) to suit a variety of room sizes. The heater has a fixed output of 1600W but can be connected to a thermostat, allowing full control over room warmth. The Panasonic WhisperWarm uses the brand’s own intelligent DC motor, making it an energy-efficient space heater. The grille can be adjusted to direct warm air.

A Flex-Z fast bracket is designed to simplify installation, and the Panasonic can be fitted to either 4-inch or 6-inch ducting. A dimmable LED is also an option (though at extra cost). If a ceiling-mount heater isn’t already installed, we suggest hiring an electrician, because this unit requires a dedicated electric circuit.

Get the Panasonic bathroom heater at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

The main draw of a bathroom heater with a fan is to spread the heat as rapidly as possible around the room, but a downside can be extra noise. The Stiebel Eltron wall heater is different in that it delivers warmth quickly while running at just 49 decibels, which is about the level of a modern refrigerator.

Its maximum output is 1500W, which Stiebel Eltron rates as sufficient for rooms up to 150 square feet. A built-in thermostat regulates performance, and we like its 60-minute boost timer, with the unit automatically reverting to its previous setting at the end of the period. There is also a frost protection setting and an on/off switch that shuts down the whole unit to prevent accidental use.

Keep in mind that this is a hardwired unit, so it can’t simply plug into an outlet. If there’s no existing hardwired heater, professional installation is a good idea.

Get the Stiebel Eltron bathroom heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Wall heaters for bathrooms can save valuable floor space, but they can also butt into the room, providing a frustrating obstacle. The Broan-NuTone Comfort-Flo is a recessed or in-wall bathroom heater that provides a low-profile solution that we love for small bathrooms where space is at a premium. The louvers direct the heat flow downwards, helping to spread warmth evenly, and a front-mounted knob controls the built-in thermostat.

The Broan-NuTone Comfort-Flo is factory-wired at 1500W and 120 volts. It can be converted to 750W at 120 volts or 1500W at 240 volts, which may suit some installations. Note that the choice of watts is final; it does not offer two output levels. Installation is fairly straightforward, but we suggest hiring an electrician if this heater isn’t replacing an existing bathroom with a dedicated circuit.

Get the Broan-NuTone bathroom heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

When we started researching modern bathroom heating options, we quickly discovered that there were hundreds of different models available. After carefully considering nearly 50 choices, we settled on eight top models, and then we chose four of those to test in our own bathrooms.

We also looked at how safe the various models were for use in standard bathrooms. Remodeling expert Benjamin Stenson, director of operations of Norsemen, a home remodeling contractor in Louisville, Kentucky, told us, “Safety features are paramount, so users must opt for heaters designed to withstand bathroom conditions.”

Hands-on testing consisted of assessing the quality of each heater’s build, trying out each of its features, and keeping records of how quickly each one heated a small bathroom during cold weather. We noted how hot the exterior of the heaters became after an hour of continuous use, and we awarded points based on a rubric—the better a bathroom heater performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we summed the points and used them to determine our best overall pick and assign relevant categories for the others.

While the appearance of a bathroom heater will always impact choice, there are a number of technical aspects to consider. The information below will help shoppers choose the most appropriate types of electric bathroom heaters for their needs.

The three general types of heaters for bathrooms include portable bathroom heaters, wall-mounted heaters, and ceiling-mounted heaters. Most (but not all) space heaters for bathroom use are electric. It’s harder to find non-electric heaters than electric heaters for bathroom use.

The term “portable” can refer to various bathroom heaters, including plug-ins, space heaters, and oil-filled radiators. These are usually among the most affordable bathroom heaters. Their distinguishing design feature is that they are not permanently fitted to the bathroom wall or ceiling, so they can be used in other rooms. Some are very light and easy to move. Space heaters often have carry handles. Although oil-filled radiators are heavier, they can still be moved if necessary. All of these might be good options for bathrooms not in regular use, such as in a guest accommodation.

The main advantage of wall-mounted bathroom heaters is that they don’t take up valuable floor space. They can also be very discreet. Wall-mounted exhaust fans are sometimes combined with heater elements, though these generally have more modest output.

Much like wall-mounted models, a ceiling-mounted bathroom heater can be both powerful and discreet. Its position also keeps it well away from small children and pets. Many are combined with an exhaust fan, which is a benefit but can complicate installation. Some ceiling models are infrared space heaters that use a large red bulb to radiate heat downward.

Physical size will have an impact on choice, especially in smaller bathrooms. Plug-ins and small bathroom heaters can be an effective option, though recessed wall units and ceiling models have no space penalty at all once installed.

Actual heat output can be difficult to assess on an electric heater. Most indoor room heaters are rated in watts. Opinions vary, but many experts quote 5 to 10 watts per square foot as optimal for comfortable warmth. However, manufacturer figures may contradict this rule of thumb and are perhaps a better guide. Models described as providing “supplemental” heat might also fall below this standard, but it does depend on bathroom size. Bathroom heaters that provide thermostats or two output settings offer greater control over personal comfort.

Water and electricity are a dangerous mix, with a risk of serious electrical shock. The descriptive materials for any heater intended for use in the bathroom should clearly state that it is for bathroom use, but we could not find any official guidelines. Ceiling heaters for bathrooms present little risk when installed correctly because there are no exposed heater elements or plugs.

Other units may be at risk of water splashes, so thought should be given to positioning. In addition, there is some risk at wall outlets. The usual solution is to fit either an ALCI or GFCI safety plug. Both will cut power in a fraction of a second and prevent harm. Many manufacturers provide these, but they can also be retrofitted.

Some use portable propane heaters in bathrooms and other interior rooms, but if you choose that option, make sure the heater is designed for inside use. Some will give off dangerous fumes.

There’s a lot of detailed information in the article above, and we hope it answers most questions that often crop up regarding choosing the best bathroom heater. While doing our research, we came across some queries of a more general nature, and we have addressed those here.

The best way to heat a small bathroom is often with either a portable heater, a fan-less wall panel, or a heated towel rack for the bathroom. These provide sufficient heat but are either very quiet or completely silent.

Bathroom heaters are absolutely worth it, as anyone who has had to bathe in a cold bathroom will attest. What’s more, many are very affordable as well as economical to run, so users can have a little luxury without a big bill.

Many different types of heaters are allowed in bathrooms, ranging from low-cost portable models to a variety of wall- and ceiling-mounted options. Our collection of top bathroom heaters listed above underlines the wide choice available.

Bathroom heaters are perfectly safe to use when installed and operated following the manufacturer’s recommendations. Sometimes it’s as simple as having an ALCI safety plug fitted. With others, the wiring is hidden and out of harm’s way.

It’s not a good idea if it’s a continuously running heater. However, if you have a permanently installed heater that runs on a thermostat, it’s probably okay. For trips to the restroom at night, consider a heated toilet seat and leave the space heater off.

Use 10 watts per square foot of floor space as a guide when sizing any kind of heater. For example, a 1500W bathroom heater will warm a 150-square-foot bathroom efficiently.

If it’s hardwired, probably. If it’s a high-capacity heater (1500W or up) that plugs into an outlet, it could overload the circuit if several other appliances are plugged in at the same time.

#7950. Supreme Court to Consider Successive Habeas Claim in Capital Case, Twenty Years After the Murder

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

This week, the Court will consider when a death-row inmate may file a second habeas application based on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.”

On Wednesday this week, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in Guerrero, Director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice v. Dexter Johnson. It is a capital case involving the kidnapping, rape, and murder of Maria Aparece that Johnson committed in 2006. The case does not involve any claim Johnson is innocent of these heinous crimes, but rather how to interpret provisions in the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA).

AEDPA prohibits successive habeas applications by state prisoners with only two narrow exceptions, including for claims that "rel[y] on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A). The question presented seems to answer itself. The Supreme Court has granted cert to decide whether a claim relies on a "new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable" when the Court announced the rule before the filing of the prisoner's prior federal habeas petition. As Texas persuasively argues in its merits brief, Johnson's Atkins claim (that he should not be executed because, he claims, he is borderline intellectually disabled) does not rely on any new rule of constitutional law. The Court decided Atkins v. Virginia in 2002—long before Johnson filed his initial federal habeas application, before his conviction became final on direct review—and even before he committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.

Instead of a change in law, Johnson's claim relies on a new factual predicate: the publication of a new diagnostic manual by the American Psychiatric Association (the DSM-5), under which he was diagnosed with an intellectual disability. But a claim in a successive application based on a new factual predicate must satisfy § 2244(b)(2)(B), which Johnson's Atkins claim does not, because his new evidence has no bearing on whether the jury would have found him "guilty of the underlying offense." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii).

Surprisingly, a Fifth Circuit panel accepted Johnson's argument that he could pursue relief on this "new" claim. And the Fifth Circuit en banc denied further review by a vote of 9-7. Judge Ho (joined by Judges Jones, Smith, and Engelhardt) wrote a dissent from this denial, pointing out that "[e]xtraordinary delays like this are, alas, extraordinarily commonplace in our criminal justice system. And they are far from costless. Never mind the expense to the taxpayer. Such delays also force the family and friends of victims like Maria Aparece to wait for justice—for over two decades, in this case."

I have filed an amicus brief in the case, along with counsel of record Allyson Ho and her colleagues at Gibson Dunn, Brad Hubbard, Matt Scorcio, Brandon Wolf, and Marquan Robertson. Our brief provides a fuller account of the cost to victims' families—such as the Aparece family—who must wait for justice in capital cases like this one. Here's the introduction to our brief:

Twenty years ago, in the early-morning hours of Father's Day 2006, Dexter Johnson abducted 23-year-old Maria Chrisalee Lopez Aparece—"Sally" to her family and friends—and her boyfriend, Huy Ngo, at gunpoint. After terrorizing them, Johnson raped Sally in the back seat of her car while his accomplice taunted Ngo. Johnson then marched Sally and Ngo into the woods, shot each of them in the head, and left them for dead. Johnson and his accomplices then took Sally's car joyriding and used her credit cards to fund a shopping spree. Earlier that evening, Sally had been at home making a card for her father, Protasio Aparece, while he worked a sixteen-hour shift as a registered nurse. After her murder, Sally's family found the unfinished card. They placed it in their living room, in front of the fireplace, alongside Sally's ashes—where it remains today. Johnson's vicious crimes inflicted unbearable pain on his victims and their families.

But that was just the beginning of their suffering. Johnson's serial litigation has robbed the families of even a modicum of peace or closure. It has been two decades since Johnson brutally murdered Sally, and nineteen years since a Harris County jury sentenced him to death—but justice still has not been served. This Court should vindicate crime victims' "important interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence," Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149 (2019), and "powerful and legitimate interest" in "real finality," Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998), by reversing the judgment below and ending an ordeal that has compounded the suffering of Sally's family for over two decades.

You can read the full brief for the Aparece family here, which discusses how excessive delays (like the one in this case) break AEDPA's promise of finality in capital cases and how research confirms that excessive delays in criminal cases harm victims' families.

I hope the Court reverses the Fifth Circuit's decision and brings the Aparece family one step closer to justice.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 2, 2010

Paul Cassell is the Ronald N. Boyce Presidential Professor of Criminal Law and University Distinguished Professor of Law at S.J. Quinney College of Law at the University of Utah.

Those tiny black flies are only part of the story. A raw potato slice on the soil can reveal what's underneath for next to nothing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You water your houseplant, and a little cloud of tiny black flies lifts off the soil. A minute later, they're on the window. Fungus gnats turn up in many homes once fall arrives, and they can hang around all winter. The next batch is already growing in the pot, and a fungus gnat potato trap is an easy way to find them.

Before you read up on how to get rid of fungus gnats, take a look at what's going on in the pot. The adult flies you keep swatting don't feed on your plants, but their larvae are a different story. Those live in the damp potting mix just under the surface, out of sight unless you go digging.

One raw potato saves you the digging. Lay a slice on the soil, and the larvae come up to feed on it. Lift it a couple of days later, and whatever is in the pot is often feeding on the underside. Odds are there's a potato in the pantry already, so finding out costs you pretty much nothing, really.

A fungus gnat's whole life happens in or around the pot. They're small flies, often in the genus Bradysia, and a female can lay up to 200 eggs in damp potting mix. Once they hatch, the larvae eat for a couple of weeks and pupate near the surface, and new adults show up a week or so later. At room temperature, that's roughly three to four weeks per generation – so a few flies in October can be a lot more by the holidays.

It's the larvae doing the eating. Their usual food is fungi and rotting organic matter, but they'll go after fine root hairs too. While a minor infestation won't usually do any harm, enough of them can damage roots and stunt growth, especially in seedlings and young plants. Watch for something like a tiny worm: clear or whitish, no legs, a shiny black head, ¼ inch (6 mm) long at most.

Cut a raw potato into slices about ¼ inch (6.4 mm) thick. Set one cut side down on the potting mix, and press it lightly so it sits flat. That contact is the whole trick. Larvae move up to the potato as a food source and gather on the moist underside where it touches the soil.

Give it a day or two before the first look. Flip the slice and check its underside, then the soil where it sat, for tiny clear larvae. Against dark, wet potting mix, they're hard to pick out, though, so a magnifying glass, like this Rongon 10X folding pocket magnifier from Amazon, helps a lot. Nothing there yet? Set it back down for another day or two. Sometimes larvae can take a few days to find the potato.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Don't leave it there for good, though. Raw potato breaks down in damp soil, and a rotting slice is just more of the decaying material larvae feed on. Toss the old one in the trash, larvae and all, and put down a fresh slice. Used like this, potato slices for fungus gnats let you track whether the numbers are dropping. Eggs won't show up on it. They don't feed, so they stay put in the mix.

So, do potatoes kill fungus gnats? Not really. The potato doesn't poison anything – it just draws feeding larvae up from the roots, and tossing a slice with larvae on it removes those ones. Eggs, pupae, and the adults flying around the room aren't affected.

Use the potato to check on things, then reach for something else to fix it. Say the slice comes up clean. That's nice, but it doesn't mean the pot's clear. Maybe there are only a few larvae, or they weren't feeding much. If flies keep hanging around, put down another slice.

Too much water keeps a lot of fungus gnat problems going. Short days and cool rooms slow houseplants down in fall and winter, so they use less water. Water like it's still July, and the mix stays wet, which eggs and larvae love. Let the top inch (2.5cm) dry before watering again. Empty the saucer, and make sure the pot drains. Old mix holds extra water as it breaks down. If a plant's due for repotting, look for a fresh mix with perlite for drainage, like the Back to the Roots Indoor Potting Mix, available from Walmart.

Yellow sticky traps are for the adults. Push a few into the pot – you can buy sticky traps cheaply from Amazon. Each female stuck to one won't lay any more eggs, and the count tells you if things are improving. Down in the soil, the larvae aren't touched. If the gnats won't let up, try Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis), a naturally occurring soil bacterium. Despite the name, it isn't the Bt sprayed on caterpillars. This strain targets only fly larvae.

Summit Mosquito Bits use Bti to control both mosquito and fungus gnat larvae. Rather than scattering the granules on the soil, it's best to soak them in water for about 30 minutes, then apply that water to your houseplant soil. Repeat application about every five days, since Bti doesn't last long indoors.

Beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae), such as BioLogic's Scanmask nematodes, are another organic option. These microscopic roundworms seek out fungus gnat larvae in potting soil. They enter the larvae and release bacteria that kill them, then feed and reproduce inside their bodies. It's pretty gruesome, but effective. They arrive alive in the mail, so use them right away. Keep the soil moist and the temperature between 60 and 90°Fahrenheit (16–32°C), or they won't work. Whichever you buy, check that the label allows indoor potted plants, then follow it.

Catching larvae early makes a fungus gnat problem much easier to control. A few larvae in one pot make for a far smaller job than a houseful of flies a month from now – and a potato slice is a cheap way to see whether your houseplant soil is hiding them.

So keep a potato around this winter. Set a fresh slice down whenever the flies show up again, and go easier on the watering while days are short. Fungus gnats have a much harder time of it once the top of the soil dries out between drinks!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7948. The Best Fireplace Tools of 2026, Picks from Our Editors

Published Oct 29, 2026 9:30 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Whether you have a traditional open fire, a wood-burning fireplace insert, or a wood stove, a set of fireplace tools is something of a necessity. Moreover, the right companion set can make an attractive addition to your room.

But with so many fireplace tools on the market—ranging from compact models for small, cozy fires to heavy-duty sets for outdoor fire pits—finding the right set isn’t easy. That’s why we researched a range of popular products across several categories to help you decide on the best fireplace tools for your home or yard before choosing the Enclume 3-Piece Steel Fireplace Tool Set as our top pick for its durable steel construction, attractive hammered finish, and ability to contain all the pieces you need.

Bottom line: Discover the best fireplace tools of 2026, blending function and style to suit any home or outdoor setting.

The following top picks feature both premium brands and budget alternatives as well as tool sets suited to indoor, outdoor, or interchangeable use. Read on to learn more about some of the best fireplace tools for any purpose.

In many homes, a log rack is an essential wood-burning fireplace accessory, so combining the rack and fireplace set is an obvious solution. This Enclume model offers good capacity with a separate kindling rack at the top, yet it requires only a little over 1 square foot of floor space.

The tough hammered steel is reminiscent of wrought iron, though it’s not as resilient; as a result, this set is not recommended for outdoor use. Four screws must be affixed for the feet, so the package includes an Allen wrench. Plastic foot sliders help prevent scratches on hard surface floors. This set doesn’t include tongs.

Get the Enclume fireplace tools at Wayfair.

When many options are available to suit individual preferences, this five-piece set from Amagabeli is appealing for its combination of desirable features and value for money. The tools are made from wrought iron, so they should last for many years. Featuring a classic style that’s smart, but not overly ornate, these fireplace tools can fit with a variety of decors.

The handles are comfortable and available in a black, brass, or gold-plated finish to match the other fireplace accessories. Tool reach is sufficient for large indoor fireplaces and outdoor pits. The support must be assembled, but that involves only tightening two nuts. Once together, the “gravity” base provides a sturdy platform.

Get the Amagabeli fireplace tools at Amazon.

Williams Sonoma is known for providing quality furniture and accessories, and this midcentury fireplace set is a fine example. Each piece looks finely crafted, and the corn stalk fiber broom shows particular attention to detail. The set is compact, but the curved support provides for easy access to each tool when needed.

These are fireplace tools that would look equally at home in front of a classic open fireplace grate, insert, or stove. Construction is steel throughout, finished in either matte black or burnished brass. The stand incorporates a tray so any ash that falls from the tools is contained. There are also rubber feet so it doesn’t slide around or mark flooring.

Get the Williams Sonoma fireplace tools at Williams Sonoma.

At the low end of the price scale, this log rack and tool set from Best Choice Products has a full set of tools, including tongs, yet it costs far less. While it looks less robust than some options, it’s reasonably well made. The rack requires a little more assembly than some, but it’s not difficult. If care is taken when putting it together, it will be sturdy enough for a weight rating of 150 pounds.

Both rack and the fireplace tools are described as wrought iron; however, many independent reviewers believe they are powder-coated steel. It’s still a durable material but not recommended for outdoor use.

Get the Best Choice Products fireplace tools at Amazon.

A good ash bucket is an indispensable fireplace tool for cleaning the fireplace or removing excess ash for better burning. While any steel bucket could do the job, the high-capacity F2C ash bucket is custom designed for the job and offers several advantages.

Construction is from galvanized iron, a material that has good resistance to corrosion. Durability is further enhanced with a powder coating, making the F2C ash bucket equally suitable for outdoor use. There’s a lid that keeps the contents secure, and it greatly reduces the chances of accidentally dropping hot ashes on the floor or hearth rugs. There’s also a wooden handle that makes it more comfortable to carry.

The long reach of some fireplace tools means gloves aren’t always necessary, but it’s a good idea to have some handy for when it’s necessary to get close or while opening a hot fireplace insert or stove door. These gloves from Rapicca have been designed for welders, so they need to be tough, and few materials are stronger than natural cowhide. For comfort, they have been lined with cotton.

Rapicca heat-resistant gloves are rated for up to 662 degrees Fahrenheit. Sleeves extend for 5.5 inches, providing protection up past the wrists in case of stray sparks. These multipurpose gloves can also be used for fire pits, barbecues, and outdoor grills. They have good bite and claw resistance for dealing with troublesome pets.

Get the Rapicca fireplace gloves at Amazon.

Those splitting their own logs into more manageable sizes or kindling want a good axe, and few can match the quality or performance of the Estwing Fireside Friend. This U.S.-made tool is forged from a single piece of steel, so it’s practically indestructible. It is also superbly balanced, making the 4-pound head easy to handle.

A 2⅜-inch hand-sharpened tempered-steel cutting edge ensures it slices through tough logs with minimal effort. A ballistic nylon sheath protects the edge when not in use. The handle is wrapped in a patented shock-reduction grip that absorbs up to 70 percent of the impact energy, dramatically reducing the chances of stress-related injuries.

Get the Estwing fireplace tool at Amazon.

When selecting the best fireplace tools, the challenge is finding the right blend of strength, durability, and style. What suits one person could be entirely inappropriate for another. In every case, manufacturing quality is the prime consideration, but caveats exist. Sometimes, high-value fireplace tools, while functional, may not have the strength of those manufactured by premium brands.

Nicole Cullum, interior designer and founder of the wallpaper and textile company Color Caravan based out of Taos, New Mexico, has helpful design advice when it comes to choosing fireplace tools: “Fireplace tools are most certainly an opportunity to blend function and design.” While they need to be long lasting, there is also the opportunity for “turning a basic tool into an artistic sculptural moment.”

Safety is also important. Fire Program Specialist Bruce D. Bouch, MPIO, of the U.S. Fire Administration says: “It is important to purchase quality tools that will not readily fail during use. Check the connections on the tools for stability and the quality of the stand if provided.” He also cautions that “ash collection should only be completed with a metal can with a tight-fitting lid designed for that purpose. Embers from a fire become insulated within the remaining ashes and can readily ignite combustible items.”

While every fireside tools set is designed to perform the same basic functions, a number of factors affect their suitability for a particular location, including decor style, size, material, number of tools included, and more. Below are details about key considerations shoppers often keep in mind while choosing the best fireplace tools.

While product photography can provide a detailed impression of the style of a particular fireplace tool set, it can be misleading in terms of size. For example, a set that looks heavy duty might actually be much shorter than depicted.

Always check the set’s physical dimensions. Tool length is not always provided, but knowing the overall height of the stand allows a reasonably accurate estimate. Width and depth of the set also can have an impact, depending on its intended location.

Fireplace tool sets usually include four pieces: a poker (or stoker), tongs, broom (or brush), and shovel (or pan), and the stand to complete what is typically called a five-piece set. Some sets omit the tongs.

Fireplace tools are usually made of brass, steel, stainless steel, or wrought iron.

Brass is decorative, but it has limited strength because brass sets were originally intended for coal fireplaces, not logs. Anyone installing a faux fireplace or gas fireplace might buy a brass set as decoration, but it’s not recommended for day-to-day use.

Wrought iron is more resistant to corrosion than brass and likely to be more durable, so it’s usually recommended for outdoor use. Wrought iron will rust eventually, and both plain steel and wrought-iron fireplace tools often have an additional coating for increased protection.

Stainless steel is highly resistant to rust but almost always more expensive. Considerable debate exists as to whether steel or wrought-iron tools are stronger. It depends on the steel composition and, with fireplace tools, that information usually isn’t available.

Consider how the shovel and broom are attached to their shafts as this also can impact durability. Shovels may be welded or riveted; the former is usually stronger. Brooms may have a replaceable head, but not always.

Traditional wrought-iron fireplace tools were naturally blackened or grayed during the forging process. Today, unless they’re handmade, the wrought-iron tools either will be painted or, more likely, have a tough powder-coated finish. The handles might be chromed or brass plated. While brass lacks strength on its own, as a coating, it is acceptable.

Style is very personal, and there are many designs to consider. Rope work is common, as are twists and scrolls. Other tools can be quite plain and minimalist. While decorative elements are always a key consideration, the functionality shouldn’t be overlooked. It’s particularly important that fireplace tools are easy to grip. If there’s an existing fireplace screen, consider tools that match that item.

Stability is also key. It’s almost inevitable that the fireplace tool stand will get bumped at some point. A flat base plate works well on a perfectly even floor but also check the material thickness. If it’s thin and lightweight, it might get knocked over easily. Those stands with four or five feet will probably balance better on surfaces that aren’t perfectly level.

When fireplace tools are purchased online, a modest amount of assembly may be required. The tool support stem may need to be attached to the base of the stand, for example. If a log basket is part of the set, it may need to be bolted together. Generally, a screwdriver and/or wrench is all that’s required.

If fireplace tools are left in the fire, it’s possible that they may get hot. However, generally, they are used briefly and then returned to the rack.

It can be. If you have a large open fire or an outdoor fire pit, short tools can bring your hands uncomfortably close to the flame. On the other hand, long heavy-duty tools can look out of place with a smaller fireplace.

A few are available, but the range is limited, and they frequently come close to the price of a whole new broom.

Many fireplace tools are designed to be used outdoors. A finish—like a powder coating—that protects them from corrosion or rust is a key feature. However, some are recommended for indoor use only, so always check the manufacturer’s recommendations.

Yellowing leaves this month are usually caused by the #1 seasonal mistake houseplant parents make. Here’s how to save your plant's life before it’s too late.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your houseplant leaves are turning yellow this November, your plant is sending urgent distress signals that you really need to heed. As days shorten and sunlight becomes less intense in fall, most houseplants use far less moisture as their growth dramatically slows. Continuing your summer watering routine during this shift creates waterlogged soil, quickly leading to root rot – and an avoidable trip to the compost bin. Catch that first yellow leaf early, however, and you can quickly reverse the damage to keep your houseplant happy and healthy.

Failing to adjust a watering routine in line with houseplants’ seasonal needs is the most common mistake we plant parents make, and unfortunately the root rot that results can be fatal. It takes a few weeks of waterlogged soil and rotting roots before the damage manifests with yellowing leaves, which is why this symptom usually shows up in November – and why once you spot a yellowing leaf you need to take swift action.

So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a yellowing leaf, and save it from an untimely death with a simple fix.

Take a closer look at the yellow houseplant leaf to see what tone, shape, position and extent of the discoloration is. Different plants show this early symptom of root rot in various ways: a Monstera will likely get a yellow halo on one of its monster-sized leaves while a ZZ plant leaf will turn bright yellow from top to bottom overnight. Peperomia foliage typically fades to a pale yellow while a snake plant leaf takes on a translucent yellow tone at the base. Matching up the symptoms to the plant species is a surefire way to tell if overwatering is the cause.

Match your houseplant to the symptoms and you have your diagnosis.

Large, thin-leafed tropical plants like monstera, calathea, anthurium and clumping philodendron typically show a bright yellow halo around a dark spot from overwatering. This happens because as roots begin to rot in soggy soil, fungal or bacterial pathogens in the potting mix travel up the plant and into the leaf tissue. Dead leaf cells show up as a black or brown area, and the bright ring of yellow around it is where the plant is attempting to stop the infection spreading.

ZZ plants (Zamioculcas zamiifolia), caladiums, and elephant ears (Alocasia and Colocasia) grow from potato-like rhizomes or tubers that store lots of water, so it can take these plants a little longer to show signs of overwatering. When they do, it's dramatic though! If these houseplants receive more water than they can process and rot sets in, nutrients are suddenly cut to a whole stem. The entire stalk and its foliage will quickly drain of color to turn a solid strong yellow, top to bottom.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Prayer plants (Maranta), peperomia, Chinese money plants (Pilea peperomioides), African violets (Saintpaulia), nerve plants (Fittonia) and Boston and maidenhair ferns all have a shallow network of very fine, fragile roots. Suffocating in overwatered soil, these thin roots quickly disintegrate and the leaves lose their lustre then become limp and fade through pale green to a matte yellow. Don’t expect these leaves to be mushy from all that water: because the root damage cuts the water supply off, leaves will become dry and brittle, snapping off immediately when touched or simply dropping from the plant.

Jade plants (Crassula ovata), snake plants, Christmas or Thanksgiving cacti (Schlumbergera), echeverias and aloe vera all store water in their stems or leaves, and excess moisture causes them to turn a translucent, sickly yellow at the base. The area will also feel mushy and this may happen where stems or leaves meet the soil, in which case stems may topple over, but also where leaves attach to stems or leaf segments join together.

Vining plants like pothos (Epipremnum aureum), English ivy (Hedera helix), wax plants (Hoya) and heartleaf philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) typically show overwatering symptoms on their oldest leaves near the base first. Unable to draw as many nutrients through suffocating roots, the plant strips nutrients from its older, less productive leaves to feed the fresh growth at its tips in the hope of finding a more suitable environment. Stripped of chlorophyll, the base foliage turns an even, uniform yellow while the newer growth at the stem tip remains green.

Overwatered houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants (Chlorophytum comosum) and ponytail palms (Beaucarnea recurvata) typically develop brown foliage tips with a yellow area separating them from the healthy green tissue. This happens because the leaf tips are at the very end of the plant's plumbing system so, when roots are damaged and can't take up water effectively, are the first to run out of moisture. The yellow color below the dead brown leaf tissue is the plant trying to salvage what nutrients it can. The leaves may lose their upright arch and start to droop, too.

If you spot yellowing houseplant leaves, immediately stop watering and let the soil dry out. Slide the pot off and if you see white roots, you’ve caught the problem in time. Pop the plant back into its pot and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry. A moisture meter like this from Amazon takes out the guesswork and helps you adjust your routine to the plant's fluctuating needs going forwards, and water houseplants properly.

If there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, and roots look dark, root rot has set in and you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp scissors or pruners or to snip off all roots that look dark or feel mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your houseplant.

It's vital the pot has a drainage hole so excess moisture can escape (and a saucer to save your surfaces). If you adore a decorative hole-less pot, use it as a cachepot with a holed plastic pot inside. For succulent plants that store water in their leaves or stems, fill your pot with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot. For everything else, use an indoor potting mix with coconut coir and perlite that evens out moisture levels while allowing good drainage like Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix For All Plants, available from Walmart.
