#7946. Promise to Apologize Might Be Enforceable—but Court Can't Order Apology if None Was Finally Agreed to

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Mia Roberts Perez (E.D. Pa.) in Souderton Area for All v. Souderton Area School Dist., decided Sept. 28:

This case began as a case about Plaintiffs' exercise of their First Amendment rights by protesting at a Souderton Area School District ("District") school board meeting. It then became a case about keeping promises. Now, it is a case about which promises this Court can enforce.

When Plaintiffs protested the Souderton Area School Board outside a September 2024 meeting, the government officials for whom their message was intended were not the only ones affected. One school board member was accompanied by her teenage daughter as they exited the meeting. In the parking lot, Plaintiffs Christopher Spigel, Helen Spigel, and Patrick Kitt confronted them. Rather than constraining their critical expression to the adult members of the school board, the protesters directed their ire toward the child, who the District has consistently maintained was frightened by the adult Plaintiffs' conduct.

Here are plaintiffs' allegations as quoted in an earlier decision:

According to the Complaint, in August 2024, Plaintiffs and other District community members learned that then-member of the Board of School Directors of Souderton Area School District (the "Board") William Formica posted lewd comments on social media about Vice President Kamala Harris, disparaging teachers and non-English speakers, and deriding diversity programs. In response, Plaintiff Souderton Area For All ("SAFA") encouraged its members to attend District Board meetings to protest and demand Mr. Formica's resignation.

The August 29, 2024 Board meeting saw high attendance of community members opposed to Mr. Formica's remarks, as well as a rally organized by SAFA to protest. But the Board did not allow SAFA or its members to demonstrate on District property, requiring them to gather on a public sidewalk 80 feet away from where the meeting was held.

At the same time, the Board permitted supporters of Mr. Formica to gather and counter-protest directly outside the meeting's entrance on District property. Due to increased attendance, the Board began requiring meeting attendees to provide photo-ID so that they could prioritize seating for District residents. Several individual Plaintiffs were excluded from meetings as a result of this new rule.

On September 26, 2024, as Board members exited a Board meeting, Plaintiffs Patrick Kitt, Christopher Spigel, and Helen Spigel protested by making cricket noises and accusing the Board of being complicit in Mr. Formica's misconduct through its silence. One Board member was accompanied by her teenage daughter, who was upset and intimidated by the protesters directing questions and accusations to her.

Two weeks later, the District issued cease and desist letters to Plaintiffs Kitt, Spigel, and Spigel, informing them they could not be on school property for the remainder of the school year, including for public meetings. On November 20, 2024, Plaintiffs filed this lawsuit, alleging the District's actions violated their rights to free speech and due process. In addition to the Complaint, on November 20, 2024, Plaintiffs filed a Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order ("TRO"), seeking to enjoin the District from enforcing its ban on Plaintiffs from entering school property for the remainder of the 2024–25 school year and allowing Plaintiffs to enter school property to attend school board meetings and other events on the same terms as other members of the public….

[T]he Court enforces the settlement promises …: continued livestreaming and archiving of Board meetings; rescission of the cease-and-desist letters; completion and maintenance of the designated protest/gathering area consistent with applicable law; and payment of the attorneys' fees already authorized.

What exactly was allegedly said to the daughter? According to a letter from the school district's lawyer attached to the Complaint,

It is my understanding that you … began screaming erroneously believing that [Board member Kim Wheeler's] daughter was Bill Formica's daughter. You screamed: "Tell your father he's an asshole" and "Tell her dad he's a fascist and needs to resign."

We are also advised that Jim Wheeler admonished you not to speak to her daughter because she is just a child and Bill Formica was not her father. You once again began yelling at Kim Wheeler's daughter to: "Then tell your mother to stop saying silent and she's just as bad as Bill."

On the other hand, the plaintiffs' counsel describes matters differently (in response to an e-mail from me):

As to the plaintiffs' position regarding what was said at the September 26, 2024, school board meeting, Chris Spigel recalled asking "does the child know her dad is a fascist?" and Patrick Kitt recalled that he called Board Member Formica a "coward" and a "beta male" but did not say anything to Board Member Wheeler's daughter, who was 15 at the time.

The e-mail also disputes other claims in the letter from the school district's lawyer, related to how close some of the plaintiffs were to Formica and her daughter; it cites surveillance video at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Th8y29iZjY0 (though noting that the video has no sound).

And now back to the Sept. 28 decision on the apology:

After the District retaliated against Plaintiffs and Plaintiffs brought this lawsuit, the parties engaged in lengthy settlement negotiations. At all times, the settlement terms included a promise by Plaintiffs to issue an apology to the child who was personally, adversely affected by their conduct.

The settlement negotiations ultimately broke down, and this Court granted the District's motion to enforce the settlement agreement on promissory estoppel grounds. The Court found that Plaintiffs promised to dismiss the lawsuit and apologize to the child, that the District relied on those promises when it took definite and substantial action to fulfill its own obligations under the settlement agreement, and that it would be unjust to allow Plaintiffs to walk away after the District's actions in reliance.

Plaintiffs move for reconsideration of one part of the Court's order, which was sealed due to the confidential nature of the parties' agreement. The Sealed Supplemental Order required Plaintiffs to keep their promise to apologize to the board member's teenage daughter, an innocent bystander who no one disputed was caught in the crossfire of the protest and experienced emotional distress as a result.

As adults, as community members, and as parents, people recognize the importance of teaching children by example: showing them kindness and respect, and taking accountability for their choices so that their children may follow those examples in their treatment of others. It is not controversial to acknowledge that the ethical thing to do when an adult harms a child is to apologize to that child, even if the harm was inadvertent.

The First Amendment, however, limits the Court's ability to compel an apology. A party may waive First Amendment rights through an agreement, but courts presume against waiver of fundamental rights. Any waiver must be voluntary, knowing, and intelligent, and supported by clear and compelling evidence.

Here, the record does not establish such a waiver. The proposed apology changed throughout the negotiations—including who would issue it, what it would say, and how it would be delivered—and Kitt's willingness to apologize was conditioned on resolution of all other settlement issues, a condition that was not met. For these reasons, and those discussed more fully below, Plaintiffs' Motion for Reconsideration is granted….

Plaintiffs argue the Sealed Supplemental Order violates their First Amendment right against compelled speech. Defendants oppose, asserting that the Order at issue here merely enforces a promise Plaintiff Kitt made, through which he waived his First Amendment right….

[G]enerally applicable laws do not offend the First Amendment simply because they have incidental effects on speech. See Cohen v. Cowles Media (1992) (finding that allowing promissory estoppel action based on promise not to disclose confidential source's identity did not violate First Amendment despite incidental consequence of inhibiting truthful reporting because "the First Amendment does not confer on the press a constitutional right to disregard promises that would otherwise be enforced under state law"). "First Amendment rights can be limited via contract."

However, there must be "'clear' and 'compelling' evidence of waiver and that waiver is voluntary, knowing, and intelligent." "[C]ourts must indulge every reasonable presumption against waiver of fundamental constitutional rights." In the context of the First Amendment, a waiver must also be "freely given."

Typically, courts lack the power to order litigants to apologize. See Devonish v. Atl. Cnty. Justice Facility (D.N.J. 2010) (collecting cases and dismissing claim for injunctive relief directing an apology because "the remedy of 'apology' is not cognizable, either within the meaning of a Section 1983 action or as a general legal remedy that a court has the power to order, under any provision"); see also Woodruff v. Ohman (6th Cir. 2002) (finding district court exceeded its equitable power when ordering defendant to apologize for gender discrimination because "[t]he apology will not provide any remedy … for which the damages imposed have not already accounted," and there was no authority "that would permit a court to order a defendant to speak in a manner that may well contravene the beliefs the defendant holds"); Ali v. Barton (N.D. Fla. 2020) (noting that the Court lacks the power to order defendants to issue "an unconditional apology")….

Throughout the settlement negotiations, the parties themselves disagreed about the nature of the apology. The apology was first raised as a term of the settlement at the settlement conference on January 16, 2025. The parties initially agreed that Plaintiff Stephanie Barnett Jamison would deliver the apology to the minor. The minor thereafter expressed that she would not accept an apology from Jamison because Jamison was not directly involved in the actions that frightened her. As of February 5, 2025, the parties were still negotiating the specifics of the apology.

Plaintiffs eventually agreed that Kitt was willing to provide the apology "so long as all other issues in the case are resolved." The issues were not fully resolved. Between February and May 2025, the parties continued exchanging drafts of the settlement agreement and making changes to certain provisions, including whether the parties would issue a joint press release, individual press releases, or no press release at all. That term was never resolved because the District did not accept Plaintiff's final proposal that the agreement be silent as to a press release until the offer was terminated. The Court already found that term material to the agreement.

As this Court previously explained, each of the drafts the parties exchanged contained materially different terms. Each constituted an offer or counteroffer, such that there was no settlement agreement that the Court could enforce under traditional contract principles. The Court agrees with Plaintiffs that Kitt could not knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waive his First Amendment right to be free from government compelled speech when his promise was conditioned on the parties' resolution of all other issues—a condition that was not met….

I am looking into getting unsealed the sealed supplemental order and the briefing related to objections to that order.

Emily Morgan and Joy Ramsingh (Ramsingh Legal, PLLC), and Solomon Furious Worlds and Sara J. Rose (ACLU of Pennsylvania) represent plaintiffs.

NEXT: Supreme Court to Consider Successive Habeas Claim in Capital Case, Twenty Years After the Murder

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7943. Some Surprisingly Tolerant Judges out There in Pennsylvania

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Commonwealth v. Outlaw, decided Thursday by Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice David Wecht, writing for a unanimous court:

In June 2022, Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington was holding a hearing on a motion to suppress evidence in Marquis McClain's criminal case. Seated in the gallery of the courtroom was McClain's acquaintance, Basile Outlaw. After Judge Covington announced that she would be denying McClain's suppression motion, Outlaw stood up and said "the judge is a cocksucker" loud enough for Judge Covington to hear. Judge Covington responded, "What did you say?" Outlaw replied: "Never mind. I'm leaving." Outlaw then exited the courtroom.

A deputy sheriff and a court employee began searching the building for Outlaw. The trial court recessed the suppression matter to allow McClain's defense attorney to confer with his client in the wake of the court's suppression ruling. The court subsequently adjourned, but Judge Covington asked McClain's attorney to "stick around for another moment … just in case." Around this time, Outlaw came back to the courtroom on his own, at which time he was taken into custody for direct criminal contempt.

Outlaw was tried and sentenced "to fifteen to thirty days' incarceration"; he served thirty days. But the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the conviction:

Specifically at issue here is Subsection 4132(3) [of the Pennsylvania Crimes Code]. A conviction under that Subsection "requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt: (1) of misconduct, (2) in the presence of the court, (3) committed with the intent to obstruct the proceedings, (4) which obstructs the administration of justice." This Court has held that, "[f]or conduct to constitute an obstruction of the administration of justice, it must significantly disrupt judicial proceedings." This means that "[r]emarks that are injudicious, or even disrespectful, will not, without more, justify a summary conviction for contempt of court." To illustrate these principles, consider Williams v. Williams, where a pro se attorney in a custody dispute reacted injudiciously to a trial judge's evidentiary ruling:

Opposing Counsel: I heard him say that you are such a fucking asshole. I heard it as an officer of the court. And the stenographer is nodding her head. That's exactly what he said, "He is such a fucking asshole." And he said it under his breath. And as an officer of the court, I am standing here, and I am testifying that that's exactly what he said.

The trial court held Williams in contempt. On appeal, however, this Court held that Williams' remark did not obstruct the administration of justice because, although "there was a momentary break in the proceedings" due to Williams' comment, "the hearing resumed quickly," "[t]he entire incident encompassed just three and a half pages of hearing transcript," and "[s]uch a transient delay is not an obstruction of justice." Expounding upon the statutory requirement that the contemnor must "obstruct[t] the administration of justice," we explicitly stated that "[i]nappropriate and even ill-mannered conduct which does not obstruct or delay the trial falls short of the misbehavior punishable under 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132(3)."

Consistent with Williams is Behr v. Behr, where a pro se litigant brought to family court a box of documents that had the word "DEATH" scrawled on it in faint orange highlighter. The box remained under the litigant's table for the entire hearing, and only after the proceeding concluded did anyone notice it. The trial court held the litigant in contempt, but this Court reversed, concluding that the litigant's conduct did not significantly disrupt the judicial proceeding. We also rejected the trial court's suggestion that a significant disruption occurred when the presence of the box triggered an investigation and subsequent contempt hearing. We called this "circular reasoning" because, if we accepted the argument, it would mean that "any time a court reconvenes a hearing to investigate alleged misconduct, the alleged contemnor has automatically obstructed the administration of justice." …

The circumstances of this appeal are analogous to those in Williams. The insult that Outlaw directed at the court here ("the judge is a cocksucker") is offensive in a manner similar to the remark made in Williams ("He's such a fucking asshole."). Both comments fall well below the expected standard of courtroom decorum, and both contemnors made their comments in response to judicial rulings with which they disagreed. Furthermore, the delay to the proceedings in this case was limited to the judge asking Outlaw "What did you say?", followed by Outlaw responding "Never mind. I'm leaving." This is the exact sort of "transient delay" or "momentary break in the proceedings" that we held in Williams cannot serve as the basis for a conviction under Subsection 4132(3). …

[A]t common law, judges had broad authority to impose contempt for insulting remarks that undermine the court's authority with the public. This sweeping authority continued to be enforced well into the twentieth century. In Appeal of Levine (Pa. 1953), for example, we affirmed the contempt conviction of a District Attorney who responded to a scheduling misunderstanding by saying to a trial judge: "that's the way with this court, always mixing things up; everything is set on one day." Upholding the contempt conviction, this Court described the inherent contempt powers possessed by trial courts in extremely broad terms, saying that: "[g]enerally speaking, one is guilty of contempt when his conduct tends to bring the authority and administration of the law into disrespect."

Appeal of Levine represents perhaps the zenith of judicial contempt authority in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. The Appeal of Levine Court itself admitted that the judicial power to punish all disrespectful conduct committed in the court's presence is "arbitrary in [ ] nature and liable to abuse." Following Appeal of Levine, the judicial contempt powers were codified and limited by the General Assembly's enactment of 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132. Our decisions interpreting that statutory codification, including Williams, Behr, and Campolongo, retreated from Appeal of Levine's maximalist approach and stressed that "[i]nappropriate and even ill-mannered conduct which does not obstruct or delay the trial falls short of the misbehavior punishable under 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132(3)." These decisions also emphasized that "trial judges are supposed to be persons of fortitude who are able to thrive in a hardy environment, and they must be on guard against confusing offenses to their sensibilities with obstruction of the administration of justice."

The OAG's [Office of the Attorney General's] argument cannot be squared with these contemporary precedents. Under the OAG's proposed approach, virtually all disrespectful remarks or profane language would be contemptuous, so long as the comment can be said to risk undermining the court's authority in the minds of the public. Indeed, the OAG maintains that "spewing" vulgar language of any kind while court is in session constitutes an obstruction to the administration of justice (even if it does not delay the proceedings) because such language "weakens the public's faithful adherence to a court's judgments and rules of decorum." The OAG's view of the law is not compatible with this Court's precedent, which holds that there can be no obstruction of the administration of justice within the meaning of the Judicial Code absent a significant disruption to the judicial proceeding. …

Justice Sallie Updike Mundy concurred, joined by Justices Kevin Dougherty and Kevin Brobson:

[W]e have not been asked to reconsider our holdings in [cases such as Williams], and absent such a request, this Court must adhere to these decisions…. I write separately to emphasize my agreement with Chief Justice Emeritus Saylor's dissent in Williams:

While not every intemperate remark will cross the line which separates zealous advocacy from contemptuous conduct, in my view the vulgar and insulting language at issue was appropriately punishable summarily as direct contempt. [Williams'] remarks were not only injudicious and disrespectful-the epithets directed at the Court were an affront to the authority and dignity of the tribunal and thus alone sufficient to constitute interference with the due and orderly administration of justice.

Like my esteemed former colleague, on a clean slate, I too would have found Williams' conduct punishable under Section 4132(3).

In fact, I find the use of the word "significant" throughout the majority in Williams, amongst other cases, when discussing disruptions that constitute "obstruction of the administration of justice" to be nebulous and subject to disparate interpretations. Merriam-Webster defines "significant" as, inter alia, "having meaning[,]" "large enough to be noticed or to have an effect[,]" and "having or likely to have influence or effect." Clearly, the trial court found the interruption caused by Outlaw's vulgar outburst to be "large enough to be noticed[.]"While I understand "that trial judges are supposed to be persons of fortitude who are able to thrive in a hardy environment," I find the act of calling a judge a "cocksucker" to be an "affront to the authority and dignity of the tribunal[,]"which was historically adequate to support a finding of contempt….

Keisha Nicole Hudson and Aaron Joshua Marcus (Defender Association of Philadelphia) represent Outlaw.

#7942. Firing for "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" Post Upheld

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

In Johnston v. County of Gila (D. Ariz.), Judge Dominic Lanza rejected, on procedural grounds, plaintiff's challenge to a Gila County Personnel Commission decision upholding his firing from his job as "a legal secretary with the Gila County Attorney's Office"; here's the factual and legal analysis from the Commission decision (see exhibit 10):

On September 10, 2025, at around 2:00 p.m. Arizona Time Appellant posted "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" on/via his Facebook account.

Multiple GCAO employees, including some who are not Appellant's Facebook friends and/or who do not personally use Facebook, saw and otherwise learned of Appellant's post on September 10 and in the days that followed. Multiple GCAO employees discussed the post with each other and complained about the post to GCAO's Chief Deputy Joseph Collins as well as to Gila County Attorney Bradley Beauchamp.

Beauchamp believed that the post appeared to condone murder based on the victim's political viewpoints and statements and became concerned that this post and perception would reflect on GCAO in the public's eyes and thereby undermine the public's trust in GCAO's official duty to prosecute homicides without bias and without regard to a victim's views, statements, or affiliations. Several other GCAO employees shared the perception that Appellant's post appeared to condone the murder of someone based on their statements and views and shared the concern that this would reflect poorly on GCAO and undermine public trust.

Multiple GCAO employees reported being offended or otherwise bothered by the post. Appellant's post resulted in immediate meetings and changes to office practices due to concerns of disharmony within the office and the effects it would have on GCAO operations.

Appellant's Facebook account was reportedly set to 'private' which Appellant believed would limit his post to only being seen by his existing Facebook friends and that all his friends had to do if they were upset by his post was 'unfollow' him. Notwithstanding Appellant's Facebook account setting and his belief as to the setting's effect on post-exposures, his post apparently reached multiple witnesses within a short timeframe, including some who either were no t his Facebook friends or did not use Facebook at all….

The evidence introduced in this matter demonstrated that Respondent's decision to dismiss Appellant for Appellant's social media post "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" was based on the following:

Accordingly, Respondent's reason for dismissing Appellant did not appear to have been decided at random or on a whim, to be founded in prejudice, or to lack a reasonable basis.

With regard to Appellant's assertions that his dismissal violated his rights under the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution, the evidence presented in this hearing did not support Appellant's claim, particularly in light of the close direct nexus between the central mission of Respondent's office—the fair and impartial prosecution of all criminal matters without regard to a crime victim's personal views, opinions, or affiliations and Appellant's post about a public homicide victim, Appellant's role in the office and exposure to members of the public, Respondent's concerns regarding inferences the public would make based on Appellant's post, the fact that almost immediately multiple parties complained regarding Appellant's post and their perception that it condoned murder and reflected poorly on the office, the immediate disruption it caused in Appellant's office, and the immediate and widespread knowledge of Appellant's post.

Here's a slightly adapted version of my analysis of the general First Amendment issue that I posted right after the Kirk shooting:

In such cases the government is acting as employer, and in that capacity it has more latitude to discipline and fire employees than it does to imprison or fine them. Generally speaking, the government may discipline an employee based on the employee's speech if

There is no categorical exception even as to government employment for speech that praises violence; indeed, Rankin v. McPherson (1987) (which Johnston cited in his arguments to the Commission) held that the First Amendment was violated by the firing of a law enforcement clerical employee for saying, after President Reagan was wounded, "if they go for him again, I hope they get him":

[The statement] plainly dealt with a matter of public concern. The statement was made in the course of a conversation addressing the policies of the President's administration. It came on the heels of a news bulletin regarding what is certainly a matter of heightened public attention: an attempt on the life of the President. While a statement that amounted to a threat to kill the President would not be protected by the First Amendment, the District Court concluded, and we agree, that McPherson's statement did not amount to a [punishable] threat … or, indeed, that could properly be criminalized at all.

The inappropriate or controversial character of a statement is irrelevant to the question whether it deals with a matter of public concern. "[D]ebate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and … may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials." "Just as erroneous statements must be protected to give freedom of expression the breathing space it needs to survive, so statements criticizing public policy and the implementation of it must be similarly protected."

But Rankin stressed that the speech actually didn't create much upset or disruption for the office, whether because of an internal reaction or an external one. To quote the concurrence by Justice Powell,

There is no dispute that McPherson's comment was made during a private conversation with a co-worker who happened also to be her boyfriend. She had no intention or expectation that it would be overheard or acted on by others…. The risk that a single, offhand comment directed to only one other worker will lower morale, disrupt the work force, or otherwise undermine the mission of the office borders on the fanciful.

Interference with work, personnel relationships, or the speaker's job performance can detract from the public employer's function; avoiding such interference can be a strong state interest…. [But w]hile McPherson's statement was made at the workplace, there is no evidence that it interfered with the efficient functioning of the office…. Constable Rankin testified that the possibility of interference with the functions of the Constable's office had not been a consideration in his discharge of respondent and that he did not even inquire whether the remark had disrupted the work of the office.

Nor was there any danger that McPherson had discredited the office by making her statement in public. McPherson's speech took place in an area to which there was ordinarily no public access; her remark was evidently made in a private conversation with another employee. There is no suggestion that any member of the general public was present or heard McPherson's statement.

Nor is there any evidence that employees other than [her boyfriend] who worked in the room even heard the remark. Not only was McPherson's discharge unrelated to the functioning of the office, it was not based on any assessment by the Constable that the remark demonstrated a character trait that made respondent unfit to perform her work.

Here, the Personnel Commission found that there had been disruption, based on "Testimony from multiple witnesses attesting to staff disharmony and disruptions occurring almost immediately after, and in the days following, Appellant's post—including staff complaints, colleagues being bothered and offended by Appellant's post, an office meeting, and an immediate change to office standards regarding political debate to avoid further disharmony and staff complaints." And the post, unlike McPherson's statement, was made to a considerable number of people; even if it was a Facebook page set to private, a lot more people were aware of it.

If one looks at later lower court cases, they have routinely turned on whether the speech created enough controversy, with the public or with coworkers. When the government is administering the criminal law or civil liability, such a "heckler's veto" is generally not allowed: The government generally can't shut down a speaker, for instance, because his listeners are getting offended or even threatening violence because they're offended. But in the employment context, the Pickering balance often allows government to fire employees because their speech sufficiently offends coworkers or members of the public. (The analysis may differ for public university professors, though it's not clear how much; see this post for more.)

This conclusion by lower courts applying Pickering might, I think, stem from the judgment that employees are hired to do a particular job cost-effectively for the government: If their speech so offends others (especially clients or coworkers) that keeping the employees on means more cost for the government than benefit, the government needn't continue to pay them for what has proved to be a bad bargain. Maybe that's mistaken. Maybe it's so important to protect public debate, including on highly controversial matters, that public employers should have to keep on even the most controversial employees (see this article by Prof. Randy Kozel, which so suggests in part). But that appears to be the rule.

We see this, for instance, with statements that are allegedly racist, sexist, antigay, antitrans, etc.: If they cause enough public hostility, or seem highly likely to do so, then courts will often allow employees to be fired based on them. But if they largely pass unnoticed except by management and perhaps just a few people who file complaints, then courts are much more likely to hold that the firings may violate the First Amendment (see, e.g., this post and this post, though there are many other such examples).

There are other factors that courts consider, to be sure: For instance, if the employer can show that a person's speech shows they are unsuited to the job, that makes it easier for the employer to prevail. (That seems to be part of the county attorney's justification here.) But even there the magnitude of public reaction is relevant, because one common argument is that one trait required for certain employees is the ability and willingness to instill confidence and respect in coworkers and clients, rather than to produce outrage and hostility.

And while some have tried to distinguish, say, racist speech from other speech on the grounds that it shows the speaker is likely to unfairly treat clients or coworkers who belong the groups he condemns, one can say that about many kinds of speech: Speech praising the killing of people who publicly advocate for certain views may be said to show the speaker is likely to unfairly treat members of the groups. (Such unfair treatment may often be illegal, especially by public employees, but in any event will often be unethical and contrary to the employer's mission.) As a result, the magnitude of the public reaction, which is often measurable rather than speculative, ends up playing a major role.

This creates an unfortunate incentive: Like any heckler's-veto-like rule, it rewards would-be cancellers, whether among the public or just among coworkers, if they only speak out often enough and with enough outrage. But rightly or wrongly, that is how these cases generally shape up.

Ashley E. Caballero-Daltrey, Derek Ryan Graffious, and Michele Molinario (Jones Skelton & Hochuli PLC) represent the County.

#7941. Firing of R.I. Governor's Staffer for Pro-Gaza-Ceasefire/"End to the Occupation" Post Violated First Amendment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Sanchez v. Almond, decided Wednesday by Judge John McConnell (D.R.I.):

Mr. Sanchez began working at the office of Rhode Island Governor Daniel J. McKee in May 2021 as a "constituent services" staffer. The office is "the first point of contact with the public for the Governor's office" where employees handled calls, emails, letters, walk-ins, constituent problems, requests, and questions about the Governor's positions.

Mr. Sanchez was not a member of senior staff, and did not formulate policy, or policy developments. While the scope of his employment is shaded differently by the parties, they all agree that his duties involved, among other things, helping Rhode Islanders access public benefits and triaging their concerns by referring them to the appropriate departments. The office received roughly 500 calls and 400 emails per month.

Mr. Sanchez's direct supervisor was David Barricelli, who reported to Joseph Almond, Senior Deputy Chief of Staff, who in turn reported to Antonio Afonso, the Chief of Staff in charge of hiring and firing in the Governor's office, including Mr. Sanchez. Mr. Sanchez's performance was never called into question, and he was never disciplined before his termination….

Sanchez was also a Providence City Council member (and his superiors had not objected to his running for local office).

On October 7, 2023, Hamas attacked Israel killing roughly 1,200 people and Israel responded with fierce military actions in Gaza, whose population is overwhelmingly Palestinian. That day, the Governor's office issued a statement condemning "the abhorrent acts of terrorism by Hamas against innocent civilians in Israel" and expressed solidarity with Israel.

The same day, Mr. Sanchez posted on his personal social media a call for "respect of all human rights, especially the Palestinian people who faced atrocities for decades[,] and at the same time condemn all attacks on civilians." Ten days later, Mr. Sanchez posted that the United States was "actively aiding in a genocide" and called for "immediate deescalation and cease-fire."

On October 22, 2023, while off duty, he posted on the platform "X" (formerly known as "Twitter"):

"prov did not disappoint … yesterday, I marched with thousands of people calling for an immediate ceasefire and a [sic] end to the occupation"

The video attached depicted scores of people marching in Providence, Rhode Island. Some members of the Governor's staff thought that rally participants had chanted "from the river to the sea." That said, nothing suggests that Mr. Sanchez adopted or repeated that phrase nor is there evidence to suggest he endorsed that chant, or is in favor of violence. {No one disputes Mr. Sanchez's account "@MSanchezPVD" represents his employment as a City Councilman not his employment at the Governor's office suggesting that he was acting outside his capacity in the Governor's office.}

The post led to concern at the Governor's office, and to media questions:

On October 23rd, the Governor's Director of Legislative and Intergovernmental Affairs, Rico Vota, counseled Mr. Sanchez not to make new posts reflecting his opinion, to keep a low profile, to speak to Mr. Afonso, and to tell the communications team about any media inquiries. He did not, however, ask him to remove the posts. Mr. Vota notified Matthew Sheaff, the Governor's Senior Advisor for Communication, who likewise recommended that Mr. Sanchez keep a low profile, which Mr. Sanchez did.

That same day, two media outlets, NBC 10 WJAR and The Providence Journal's Katherine Gregg, asked the Governor's office about the rally but did not mention Mr. Sanchez or his posts. In response, the Governor issued a statement that he "unequivocally condemn[ed] the despicable acts of war and terror perpetrated by Hamas against the people of Israel."

The next day Ms. Gregg asked the Governor's communications team to confirm that Mr. Sanchez worked for the Governor and Mr. Sheaff replied that "… [a] member of our senior staff has spoken with the individual, and the situation is under review." Ms. Gregg also contacted Mr. Sanchez, but he did not respond to her and instead told Mr. Sheaff about her inquiry, apologizing for "dragging you guys into this."

On October 25th, Ms. Gregg published an article identifying Mr. Sanchez as a Constituent Services associate; NBC 10 WJAR and a WPRO radio host then asked the office about him, and NBC 10 reported on the post. A state legislator asked Mr. Vota whether the employee in the article "worked downstairs."

On October 26th, Mr. Barricelli reported to Mr. Almond that Constituent Services had received three emails and two phone messages about Mr. Sanchez's post, all after Ms. Gregg's article. Mr. Almond did not consider these "to be a lot," and they did not interfere with the office's operations. Mr. Almond testified that addressing such matters was within his own regular duties, and Mr. Barricelli testified that fielding such comments is the associates' job.

Afonso and Almond demanded that Sanchez take the post down, but he refused; he was then fired. Sanchez sued, and the court held that Sanchez's First Amendments rights were violated (and so clearly that the defendants weren't entitled to qualified immunity):

The First Amendment protects the right of a public employee to speak on matters of public concern, and that right "is not lost when an individual chooses to work for the government." Public employees' speech on matters of public concern, on their own time, is speech long understood to "occup[y] the highest rung of the hierarchy of First Amendment values." Nonpolitical public employees do not "surrender" their First Amendment rights by accepting government employment. …

The Court "must balance the interests of the employee, as a citizen, in commenting upon matters of concern and the interest of the State, as an employer, in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees." "This balancing act is commonly referred to as the Pickering balancing" after the Supreme Court's decision in Pickering v. Board of Ed. (1968)….

On Mr. Sanchez's side, speech on public issues occupies the greatest of First Amendment protection, and the stronger the speech interest, the stronger the justification the employer must offer. {The interest by the employee and the public is heightened when the employee is also an elected official, as was Mr. Sanchez.} …

On Defendants' side, legitimate interests include avoiding unnecessary disruption and inefficiency, maintaining discipline and harmony in the workplace, and protecting close working relationships that depend on loyalty and confidence. A reasonable prediction of disruption receives significant weight, and an employer need not wait until disruption becomes manifest before acting. Courts are more willing to credit such a prediction where some disruption has occurred….

Defendants contend that the post sent "a mixed message on the Governor's public stance." Mr. Afonso testified that some constituents conflated Mr. Sanchez's view with the Governor's. Even so, there was little room for genuine confusion. Mr. Sanchez's account identified him as a city councilor and never mentioned the Governor. The press, not the post, connected him to the Governor's office.

Crediting Mr. Afonso's testimony, nothing in the record shows that constituents conflated Mr. Sanchez's position with the Governor's that was traceable to the post itself. Mr. Sanchez's account cannot be reasonably understood as speaking on behalf of the Governor such that it would cause confusion in either the Governor's office or the public's perception….

[As to actual disruption, c]rediting Defendants' version of the record, in the five days between the post and the termination, the Governor's office received: one Providence Journal inquiry following up on the social media posts; three emails and two telephone messages from the public; a question posed by a state legislator in the elevator to Mr. Vota; and a few other questions from NBC 10 and a WPRO radio host. The Court also credits Ms. Darocha's recollection that the Governor was asked about Mr. Sanchez at press gaggles that week; Mr. Sheaff's testimony that the matter "encompassed [his] day"; testimony that time spent on the matter was time not spent elsewhere; and the decision not to put an optional event on the Governor's calendar.

Mr. Almond testified the inquiries were not "a lot" and "did not interfere with the operation of the office" and Mr. Barricelli testified that handling such communications was essentially his associates' job. By its own account, that office spends roughly "85 percent" of its time responding to current events and media inquiries. Better said by Mr. Sheaff, "[i]t's very common that the Governor gives a statement or his thoughts on news of the day …[;] [i]t's just part of the job of being a governor." This is the ordinary business of a governor's office and nothing in the record suggests that the post affected the Governor's own work, his relationship with his staff, or the office's ability to serve constituents in an unusual way. Balancing these facts, and considering the Defendants' burden on this issue, the Court settles this score firmly against Defendants.

{Defendants also point to Mr. Sanchez's later acknowledgment that he had "put[ ] the [G]overnor in a tough situation" and that, "given my day job, these kinds of things can get messy quickly." Though affecting the Court's calculus, an employee's recognition that his speech is affecting his employer does not supply Defendants with the artillery they think it does.} …

Brian W. Haynes (Casner & Edwards, LLP) and Edward H. Trent, Gene C. Schaerr, and Miranda Cherkas Sherrill (Schaerr Jaffe LLP), and James A. Ruggieri (Higgins Cavanagh & Cooney, LLP) represent plaintiff. Note that I'm a part-part-part-time academic affiliated with Schaerr Jaffe LLP, but I didn't work on the case, and was indeed unaware of it until it came up in a Westlaw query of mine; no-one asked me to blog about it.

#7940. 5 Spots for a Water Leak You Might Totally Miss—But Can Cost You

Published Oct 29, 2026 4:05 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plumbing lines run throughout the home and the yard, bringing in fresh water for you to bathe, wash, water, and drink. However, when there is an issue with one of these plumbing lines or the attached appliances and fixtures, what seems like a small leak can quickly become a major problem as the growing accumulation of water causes water damage, encourages mold growth, and slowly ruins existing plumbing connections.

According to the EPA, the average household’s leaks can account for more than 9,300 gallons of wasted water per year, while some homes have leaks that waste 50 gallons or more per day. As a plumber and restoration expert, I have seen many issues that were easy enough to fix turn into major restoration projects simply because they were unseen or neglected for so long.

Even a single leak can destroy insulation, ruin drywall, and cause mold to spread behind your walls. Before your plumbing becomes a problem, use this guide to discover five water leak sources you might miss so that they don’t cost you in the long run.

Since this is a battery-powered unit, you don’t have to worry about missing a leak just because the power is out. Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Water-carrying appliance hoses, like those on refrigerators, dishwashers, and washing machines, are notorious for causing catastrophic, hidden water damage. Since these appliances are often pushed tight against walls or tucked inside cabinetry, a slow leak can be difficult to find as it quietly rots the subfloor for months before a puddle ever creeps out into the open room.

The wax ring or plastic flange connecting the toilet base to the waste pipe can degrade over years. Instead of leaking onto the bathroom floor, the water can seep straight down through the subfloor, rotting the ceiling framing of the room directly underneath, which is why you need to be aware of any potential signs of a water leak, especially in the bathroom.

Water leaks caused by frozen pipes hidden behind walls or under concrete slabs can go unnoticed for a long time, causing extensive water damage in the walls if you aren’t careful. Water lines running beneath a concrete slab foundation can corrode or shift, causing a slow leak. These are highly hidden and usually only identified by a warm spot on the floor, a spike in the water bill, or eventual foundation cracking.

Underground irrigation lines are one of the most common culprits behind massive, hidden water loss. Because irrigation systems are buried across a wide outdoor area, an underground leak can dump thousands of gallons directly into the soil without ever creating a surface puddle.

Like roof leaks, outdoor spigots can lead to unexpected damage over a long period of time. These spigots should be turned off during the winter to prevent them from bursting internally during winter freezes. However, they may also develop leaks during the warmer months of the year, and the leak can remain completely hidden inside the wall cavity or crawlspace, only letting water escape whenever the valve is opened.

#7939. A Stylish Indoor Herb Garden With Nearly Zero Effort: An Auk Mini 2 Review

Published Oct 30, 2026 8:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I was already a fan of the original Auk Mini after testing it for our guide to the best grow lights, so I was curious whether the new Auk Mini 2 actually improved on it or simply gave it a facelift. I tested the Espresso/Walnut model on the same kitchen counter where I used the original: an area that receives virtually no natural light. That meant the plants were entirely dependent on the Mini 2’s built-in grow light. I planted all four included pots with the supplied seeds, two basil and two parsley, and grew them for about a month.

The biggest change I noticed right away was the design. The original Auk Mini was already one of the best-looking growing systems I’d tested, but the Mini 2 feels more finished. Its corners are rounder, the transitions between components are smoother, and the whole thing has a more organic shape. I tested the Espresso/Walnut finish again, and it’s still my favorite. The pots have changed, too. Their bottoms are more rounded and extend farther into the reservoir, which appears to give the growing medium better access to water.

Setup is still wonderfully simple. Auk gives you exactly enough prehydrated coco coir for the four pots, and I’ve yet to use another coco coir product that’s as pleasant to work with straight out of the bag. I filled the pots, planted the supplied basil and parsley seeds, scattered the included (and new) small stones over the growing medium, added water and nutrients, and installed the light. That was basically it. The new top layer might seem like a minor addition, but germination and early growth seemed noticeably quicker than with my original Mini. Auk claims the Mini 2 produces 20 percent more growth, and while I didn’t conduct a controlled comparison, my experience certainly supports the idea that plants establish faster in this version.

After roughly a month, all four plants had grown into full, healthy herbs that I was able to harvest for cooking. That’s particularly impressive considering they received no sunlight whatsoever. I didn’t encounter algae, mold, or other growing problems during testing. Maintenance was minimal, too. During the first month as the plants were establishing, I didn’t need to refill the water reservoir.

Once the herbs became established and started drinking more, I simply topped off the reservoir as necessary. At that point, trimming the herbs to keep their growth under control actually became more work than maintaining the garden itself, and that’s hardly a complaint when the payoff is fresh basil and parsley whenever I want them.

There are other upgrades, including an optional app, a new Slow Mode, a larger reservoir, and optional pots designed for larger plants. Those additions make the Mini 2 more versatile, but I don’t think existing Auk Mini owners need to rush out and replace their current unit. The original is still really well made. My biggest complaint is that at $249, I wish Auk included the two larger pots and longer dowels rather than charging another $79 for them. Still, for someone buying their first Auk, I’d absolutely choose the Auk Mini 2. It’s super easy to use, grows plants effectively with minimal effort, and actually looks good while doing it.

#7938. My New Dispatch Article on the Legal Case Against Trump's Section 338 Tariffs Targeting Canadian Imports

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

It explains why the Section 338 tariffs are illegal, and part of a broader pattern of tariff power grabs.

Today, The Dispatch published my new article on the case challenging Trump's Section 338 tariffs against Canada. Here is an excerpt:

Courts have already ruled against two avenues President Donald Trump used to impose his tariff regime. That hasn't stopped his efforts to attempt to deploy obscure or outdated trade law provisions to justify new import levies.

His latest tool is the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, the notorious legislation that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression.

Section 338 of that law is the basis of Trump's massive 50 percent tariffs on a variety of Canadian imports, including motor vehicles, furniture, dairy products, and more. On October 20, Gellert Global Group Corp., a major food importer and producer based in New Jersey, filed the first lawsuit challenging those tariffs before the U.S. Court of International Trade, the federal court with jurisdiction over tariff cases.

Gellert, which imports Canadian cheese subject to the tariffs, is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, a public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). It resulted in the tariffs' invalidation in February by the Supreme Court, which not only ruled that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs but also emphasized that tariffs are a congressional power, and that the president does not have the power to "impose tariffs on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time." The Section 338 tariffs are a similar power grab.

They are illegal for multiple reasons, part of an ongoing effort by this administration to usurp Congress' constitutional authority over tariffs. In addition, they harm the U.S. economy and poison relations with a key ally. Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act has never been used by a president to enact tariffs before; Philip Zelikow, a conservative trade policy expert and former Bush administration official, has shown that Section 338 was superseded by legislation enacted in 1962 and 1974.

Even if Section 338 is still operative, Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods violate its requirements. As the complaint explains, the Canadian trade measures cited by Trump as justification for the new tariffs do not discriminate against U.S. goods; Section 338 can only be used against discriminatory policies. Some of the Canadian measures retaliate against previous tariffs imposed by Trump. Most do not actually treat U.S. goods less favorably than imports from many other countries. In addition, the Section 338 tariffs go well beyond "offsetting" Canadian measures, violating another requirement of the law….

The administration's interpretation of Section 338 also runs afoul of the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to "speak clearly" when authorizing the executive to make decisions of "vast economic and political significance." Under Trump's approach, Section 338 can be used to impose 50 percent tariffs whenever a trading partner imposes any restrictions on U.S. goods, or simply chooses not to buy them. And the resulting tariffs need not be calibrated to those they are supposed to "offset." This is a blank check to impose massive tariffs against almost any imports at any time—exactly the kind of power the Supreme Court, in its ruling on the IEEPA case, determined the executive cannot have…

If Section 338 is still valid and does grant the kind of nearly unlimited authority Trump claims, that would violate the constitutional "nondelegation" doctrine, which restricts delegation of legislative power to the executive…

The Section 338 tariffs are part of an ongoing series of import taxes Trump has instituted in the wake of the IEEPA decision, seeking to again usurp the unlimited tariff authority the Supreme Court denied him. He previously tried to use Section 122 and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to essentially replicate the IEEPA tariffs. In both cases, he sought to transform a narrowly limited tariff authority into a blank check to impose massive tariffs at will…

In addition to illegally usurping Congress' authority under the Constitution, these tariff actions raise prices for consumers, greatly reduce economic growth, would impose some $700 billion in new taxes on Americans over a 10-year period, and have failed to increase manufacturing employment, despite Trump's claims that they would achieve that goal.

The tariffs against Canada—combined with Trump's repeated threats to make Canada the "51st state"—have also poisoned U.S. relations with a key ally. The percentage of Canadians with a favorable view of the U.S. has fallen from 54 percent in 2024 to only 33 percent this year—a worse rating than even China's authoritarian regime…. Alienating a key ally and trading partner doesn't make America "great again." It makes us weaker, poorer, and more isolated.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.
