#7929. The Best Garage Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

By Tom Scalisi, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor, Timothy Dale

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:30 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

For DIYers and hobbyists, the garage is often a great place to store tools and work on a variety of projects—but without a garage heater, that can become a lot less comfortable as temperatures start to fall. But selecting the right model for your space depends on several factors, including the size of the garage, the preferred type of fuel, the importance of portability, and essential safety features.

After testing several popular options in our own garages, we chose the Comfort Zone Ceiling-Mounted Industrial Heater as our favorite for its flexible installation options, powerful heat, and easy maintenance. Read on to learn more about it and the rest of the models that made our list of the best garage heaters available today.

Bottom line: Choosing the right garage heater depends on your space, budget, and heating needs, with top picks offering a range of features and safety options.

The lineup below includes some excellent heaters that we hand tested in real-life situations. They proved to be top-notch in their heating method for heat output, safety, and overall quality. Organized by category, this list can help folks find the best garage heater to stay warm while working.

The Comfort Zone electric garage heater is a semipermanent option that mounts on a ceiling or a wall. It can be hardwired into the home electrical system, or fit it with a plug-in cord for a 30-amp outlet. The heater’s durable steel body is resistant to impact damage, and a dual-knob thermostat at the base makes it easy to control the temperature in the garage.

This 7,500-watt forced-air electric heater has adjustable louvers and a variable-angle mounting bracket to direct airflow wherever necessary. A built-in sensor in this garage heater ensures that the unit won’t overheat. If the temperature gets too high, the device switches off immediately to prevent internal or external damage. It proved to put out plenty of heat.

While the Comfort Zone is a quality garage heater, setting it up was a bit of a mixed bag. It didn’t come with the 240-volt pigtail or box entry (the cable clamp that secures the wire to the box), so these must be separate purchases. Otherwise, it was very easy to set up. Another plus: Removing the grill is simple, making future cleanings a breeze.

While the Comfort Zone is a quality garage heater, setting it up was a bit of a mixed bag. It didn’t come with the 240-volt pigtail or box entry (the cable clamp that secures the wire to the box), so these must be separate purchases. Otherwise, it was very easy to set up. Another plus: Removing the grill is simple, making future cleanings a breeze.What our tester says: “The Comfort Zoneput out plenty of heat, and the adjustable louvers make it easy to direct warm air right where you need it.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Comfort Zone garage heater at Amazon.

The Lasko ceramic space heater is well suited for the garage—or any indoor location where a bit of extra warmth would be welcome. Just pick it up by the built-in handle and find a suitable location with an accessible power outlet. The heater can be adjusted via the control panel on the top of the unit or with the included remote.

Once the heater is turned on, users can opt to set an automatic timer that will turn it off when it reaches the scheduled time, or let it run nonstop until it is switched off manually. The 1,500-watt heater boasts several additional features, including oscillation, overheating protection, and a cool-touch exterior so that users can maneuver the unit while it is in use without getting burned.

During testing, the Lasko proved to be a surprisingly powerful (and very quiet) heater. While it wasn’t able to heat the whole garage, it did make a significant difference in the immediate area. We also liked that it has a remote control for adjusting the temperature and swapping through modes. The oscillation mode is particularly nice for spreading a bit of heat over a larger area, like a workbench or a shop floor. The only complaint is that this fairly tall heater doesn’t have any tip-over protection. We left it face down on the garage floor for over a minute, and it just continued to heat.

Midrange electric garage heaters like this are a good choice for those who prefer a ceiling-mounted heater. This powerhouse has a built-in overheating detection system that will shut down if the temperature gets dangerously high.

Control the heat output with the simple analog dial at the base of the unit and redirect the flow of warmth with the adjustable mounting bracket and louvers. This 5,000-watt heater comes with a built-in thermostat and a thermal safety shutoff. However, the unit does not include a power cord, so it must be direct wired to a dedicated 240-volt outlet with a 30-amp breaker.

During testing, the Fahrenheat FUH electric heater proved to be a solid choice in a compact design. The hanging bracket was easy to install, and adjusting the angle of the heater was as simple as loosening the two mounting nuts and positioning the unit. Also, this model’s shroud aims the heat downward, warming the space below it. But its lack of a 240-volt wire or cable clamp means shoppers will have to make separate purchases

Get the Fahrenheat garage heater at Northern Tool + Equipment.

If infrared or fan-forced heating is more appealing than convection heat, then this Dr. Infrared garage heater is a great choice. It has a dual heating system that incorporates a radiant infrared heating element, which can quickly warm up physical objects, like people and tools, and it has a fan-forced heating system to warm up the air in the garage.

The heater needs a 208-volt or 240-volt connection to function properly, allowing it to run at up to 5,600 watts. Once the garage heater is set up in a safe location away from flammable material, the temperature dial can be set between 37 and 113 degrees Fahrenheit, and it will automatically maintain this temperature as long as the heater switch is on “auto.” The heater will run continuously with the switch set to “on.”

If ample heat is the primary goal from a compact heater, the Dr. Infrared Heater can deliver. Although this is an industrial-grade heater, there isn’t much setup or installation to do: Just remove it from the box. However, this unit does run on 240-volt electricity and uses a NEMA #6-30P plug, which many users may not have on hand (we didn’t); budget some extra cash for the outlet and an electrician, if needed.

Get the Dr. Infrared Heater DR-988 garage heater at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

When it comes to heating large barns and garages, Mr. Heater’s propane convection heater might be the top choice. This large, barrel-style heater produces between 75,000 and 200,000 BTUs, meaning it can heat up to 5,000 square feet of garage space. And since the heater works on convection, it will start a cycle that helps warm the space evenly.

This Mr. Heater model features a collapsible upper section that slides down over the lower section when not in use. This makes it easy to store. It also has a thermoelectric safety valve to shut the unit off if the flame goes out.

If there’s one thing our test revealed, it’s that this heater is built for wide open spaces (within a barn or garage, of course). Even at its lowest setting, it produces 75,000 BTUs, filling the space quickly with heat. We felt our small test garage heat up within a few minutes, and it raised the temperature 15 degrees Fahrenheit in 20 minutes. However, it’s likely too much heater for a small garage, but the fact that it doesn’t require electricity means it can be used to keep horse barns, construction sites, and other similar off-grid buildings warm.

Get the Mr. Heater garage heater at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Acme Tools.

The Dr. Infrared 240-volt commercial heater might be a great option for those in the market for a high-quality heater with ample output. This model features two modes: 3,000 watts and 6,000 watts. It has an adjustable thermostat built into the heater, but it also comes with an additional thermostat to install on the wall for better control of the temperature. It is a direct-wire application, meaning that instead of a cord to plug in, the installer hardwires it into a 240-volt circuit.

We’ve tested a few of these wall- and ceiling-mount heaters, and this Dr. Infrared hardwired shop heater is one of the nicest. The design is smooth and appealing, rather than overly boxy like most other models. The oversize plastic knobs make it easy to lock the heater in place once users find the ideal angle. This makes a big difference, as these knobs were easier to use than smaller hardware typically found on other similar heaters. If the unit is to be ceiling mounted, its louvers are adjustable to direct airflow down or away from the work area.

Although the built-in thermostat doesn’t indicate temperature values that users can set precisely, once they get an idea of how much warmth they need in their garage, they’ll know where to set it. The biggest concern with this model is that most folks will have to hire an electrician to run 240-volt service to the heater so it can function in the majority of garages. Also, the product description makes it sound like it comes with a separate wall thermostat, but our test model did not.

Get the Dr. Infrared Heater DR-966 garage heater at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Dr. Heater.

Anyone looking for a flexible garage heater that they can also use outside to keep the chill at bay will want to consider the Briza infrared electric indoor/outdoor heater. This infrared heater is weatherproof, allowing it to withstand rain, snow, sand, and dust. It also has three output settings.

The Briza boasts flexible mounting options. It comes with hardware to attach it to a wall or ceiling and also includes a portable telescoping tripod so that it can stand alone and be adjusted for height wherever it is placed. It has a remote control so users can adjust the temperature or set a timer without having to reach up to the unit (the timer is only available through the remote, in fact).

In testing, we were impressed by the amount of heat the Briza produced while also being incredibly quiet. It got so warm on the highest setting that we could barely stand in front of it, yet it emitted a barely audible hum. We also found infrared heat more comfortable than having a fan blowing hot air at us. Though at first we were a little skeptical of the tripod, it proved to be very sturdy and telescoped to the perfect height. Our only complaint is that while there are three settings, this heater doesn’t have a thermostat to turn it on and off when the room meets the desired temperature.

Cold snaps can spell disaster for garages with water or sewer lines, but the Bio Green Palma fan heater lets folks avoid this problem. This heater can maintain temperatures around 48 degrees Fahrenheit—considerably lower than most space heaters. This allows the forced-air unit to run less often while still preventing frozen pipes. It features a 5,118 BTU 1,500-watt output and a digital thermostat for easy temperature setting.

During our test, we realized that the Palma heater’s value lies in its ability to maintain very low temperatures without allowing freezing—it’s not intended to give a garage Florida Keys-level warmth. And we found that it does this job quietly and very well. It’s well built, with a tough stainless housing, and it’s splash-proof to prevent damage from a bit of water. It doesn’t have a tip-over safety switch, but given its compact, stout size, it would be tough to knock it over by accident. Our only complaint about the Bio Green was the off-gassing smell it produced when it was first turned on.

Get the Bio Green garage heater at Amazon.

Flame King’s portable propane forced-air heater is another small garage heater that’s worth considering. This smaller model features an output range between 30,000 and 60,000 BTUs, allowing it to heat medium-size garages. It features a plug-in electronic ignition and an adjustable output dial to help users achieve the perfect temperature in their garages.

This model from Flame King has tons of safety features. It has a low-oxygen fuel shutoff that activates when there isn’t any flame as well as a fire detections system and a tip-over switch.

The Flame King portable propane forced-air heater did quite well during our tests. It was easy to set up and use and produced plenty of heat for our small test garage. Temperatures started to feel comfortable after around 25 minutes of runtime. We also liked that this model is lightweight and extremely portable, though it is loud just like the other forced-air propane heaters in the test. Another point to consider is that the Flame King is relatively good on fuel, stretching a 20-pound tank to 8 hours while most heaters in the range take just 7 hours to empty a bottle.

Get the Flame King garage heater at Amazon.

We put these garage heaters through their paces, considering installation, output, and (to a degree) safety features. First, we removed each unit from the box and set it up according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Many didn’t need any setup, while others required attaching legs, hanging brackets, and installing wiring. We took note of each, relative to the type of heater, as we expected gas and 220-volt heaters to be a little more involved.

Then, the heaters were tested for output. We turned each heater on inside the garage, taking note of how long it took to reach the desired temperature. At this point, we evaluated the additional features, such as humidifiers, thermostats, and timers.

Finally, we checked each heater’s safety features, such as cool-touch surfaces and tip-over shutoffs. Replicating the low-oxygen cutoff would’ve been dangerous, so we took the manufacturer’s word for it.

Before choosing the best heater for the garage, take a few minutes to learn about some of the most important shopping considerations, including heating method, fuel source, and heat output. There are also critical safety features that can help keep users safe while enjoying a garage heater.

DIYers will want to determine what’s most valuable in their garage: freed-up space on the counter or the floor, or the ability to work at a few different workstations. Knowing this should help when deciding whether to purchase a stationary or a portable garage heater.

Busy DIYers may appreciate being free of the trip hazard that electric cords on the floor can create. Stationary garage heaters most often attach to the ceiling, but there also are options that mount to a wall.

There are a wide variety of energy options, sizes, and prices that range from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. The downside to mounted heaters is that they typically cost more than their portable counterparts because they’re closer to commercial quality.

No matter the type of heating or fuel used, portable heaters focus warmth where it’s needed the most. Like space heaters on steroids, forced-air options feature large horizontal tubes that house the heating element and a powerful fan that delivers blasts of hot air.

While portable electric units often cost less, they can be less powerful than their multifuel counterparts. Alternatively, portable units can distribute warmth through radiant heat and convection.

Not all garage heaters control the temperature in the same way. There are three primary heating options: forced air, convection, and radiant.

Consumers have a wide range of energy options from which to choose when shopping for a garage heater. While heaters are most commonly fueled by electricity, propane, or natural gas, there are also those that run on diesel and kerosene.

Since electric garage heaters pull a lot of power, these usually require a designated electrical circuit on its own breaker. An electrician can tell if existing garage wiring is adequate to run an electric heater or if a new circuit should be installed.

If there is already natural gas service to a home, there is an option to install a natural gas heater. Propane-powered heaters can be installed on a home’s propane line, or individual tanks of propane to fuel smaller heaters can be purchased.

The best garage heater for a space can produce enough heat to be comfortable, without breaking the budget. Heat output for gas-powered heaters is measured in BTUs. Gas garage heaters typically range from 12,000 to 30,000 BTUs or more.

When trying to determine the heat output of an electric heater, a general guideline is to provide 10 watts of output for approximately every square foot of space. For example, a 100-square-foot room will require a heater with 1,000-watt output for adequate comfortable warmth.

Most heaters advertise the maximum square footage the unit can adequately heat with a standard 8-foot ceiling. If a garage has a higher ceiling, take that into consideration and pick a size up. Insulation will also affect the warmth factor in a garage. Even a high-capacity heater cannot prevent icy drafts from entering through poorly insulated doors and windows.

Safety must be a primary consideration when deciding on the best garage heater. To help keep the space safe and comfortable, manufacturers have added several features, including cool-touch exteriors, overheating protection, and automatic shut-off systems.

Various different features may add to the convenience and efficiency of a garage heater. These include programmable thermostats, oscillation, and remote controls.

Portable garage heaters only need to be positioned and provided with fuel or electricity to function. Wall- and ceiling-mounted garage heaters typically come with the hardware required to install the heater, but some products don’t have mounting brackets. Also, for hard-wired installations (these heaters don’t have plugs), it may be necessary to hire an electrician.

Mount a heater in the coldest corner of the garage, ensuring that ceiling-mounted models are at least 24 inches from the walls to reduce fire risk. Direct the heater toward the center of the garage and follow the manufacturer’s steps to make sure that the heater is installed according to its specifications.

Even after becoming familiar with the best garage heaters, there may still be some lingering questions about the type, efficiency, and appropriate size. Below are answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about garage heaters to provide additional info.

The best type of heater for the garage depends on your needs. Large garages benefit from a natural gas or propane heater because of the high heating capacity, allowing the heater to adequately warm the space. However, an electric garage heater is a safer alternative and the heating capacity is suitable for smaller garages.

Depending on where you live, the answer to this question can vary. Areas with mild winters will naturally require less heat production to warm a space than locations with harsh, freezing winters.However, an electric garage heater with 3,000 watts is usually needed to heat a 2-car garage. The best gas garage heater for a 2-car garage typically has a rating of about 18,000 BTUs to adequately heat the space.

Efficiency can be difficult to determine because an electric infrared heater technically has 100 percent efficiency, but it may actually cost more to operate than the best natural gas garage heater. This is due to the cost of electricity over natural gas or even propane. If you are looking for a heater that uses almost every watt of energy for heating, then an infrared heater can be the best option.

Yes, a garage heater can be too big. If it is too big, the excess heat produced quickly makes the garage feel uncomfortable, forcing you to open the door to release some heat. If you have a smaller garage, consider using a portable heater to keep the space warm.

It depends on the size of the garage. Typically, a good general guideline for electric heaters is that they provide 10 watts of output for every square foot of space. This means that as long as the garage is 150 square feet or smaller, a 1,500-watt heater is more than adequate.

Portable garage heaters can be placed anywhere. Fixed or mounted garage heaters should be installed in the coldest corner of the garage, directing the heat and airflow toward the center of the space. Make sure that heaters are installed at least 24 inches away from the walls, and always check the manufacturer’s directions so you install and use the unit properly.

Tom Scalisi is a full-time DIY and construction writer for many of the largest websites in the industry, including Bob Vila, This Old House, Family Handyman, and Forbes as well as his own pest control blog. His uninsulated garage makes winter projects tough in the Northeast, so he knows a thing or two about keeping warm out in the shop.

#7928. Journal of Free Speech Law: "Protecting the Thinking Process in Human-AI Interaction: The Forum Interstitiale Between Thought and Expression," by Caroline De Cock

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

International human rights law protects freedom of thought absolutely and freedom of expression subject to limitations. The relevant established doctrine calls the two sides of that line the forum internum and the forum externum. However, the line was drawn when thinking left no trace, and with current technological developments, it no longer holds.

Within the span of six months in 2026, a United States court ordered that 20 million ChatGPT conversations be provided as evidence under ordinary discovery rules, two federal courts reached opposite conclusions on whether a litigant's exchanges with a chatbot were protected at all, and the Supreme Court held that location records kept by a third party remain constitutionally protected. Records of where a person's body had been were protected, while records of how their mind worked were not.

The law currently has no category for the search query, the exploratory prompt, the unfinished draft, or the confession made to a machine. The U.S. answer has been a quarrel about privilege: Courts refuse to grant AI exchanges between users and chatbots protection because the machine is not a professional, like a doctor or a lawyer, and the industry asks for a new privilege because it claims the model behaves like one. Both the courts and the industry assume that protection depends on what the person is using, i.e., what the machine is. This Article argues that it depends on what the person who uses the machine is doing.

It proposes the forum interstitiale, a third zone between the two classical fora, which can protect the thinking process under a standard stronger than ordinary expression law but short of absolute. Every candidate analogy to interactions with AI chatbots in existing law is tested herein, from search queries and confidential dialogue to protected reading, aggregated records, the European law on correspondence and data protection, private diaries and drafts, and neural data. Each fails for the same reason, namely that the protection it offers relates to a relationship, a disclosure, a recording, an addressee, or a data type, and never to the function of the act as thinking.

The interstitial zone this Article proposes only flows upwards. It lifts acts abandoned by the current binary approach into protection and displaces nothing from the absolute core of protected thought. The Article also sets out what acts belong in the liminal zone, five elements of the protection standard, the duties those elements impose on AI providers, and a map of individual AI interactions across the three fora. This classification determines what records of thought can be demanded, kept, filtered, and used against the person who was engaged in the process of thinking.

NEXT: Prof. Francesca Gino's Contract and Discrimination Claims Against Harvard Business School Dismissed

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7926. 40 Home Tasks to Tackle Before the First Frost

By Caitlin Castelaz, Michelle Ullman, Theresa Clement

Published Oct 30, 2026 10:16 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When the dog days of summer give way to autumn’s cooler temperatures, it’s time to get your house in shape for the change of seasons. Fall is the ideal time of year to work outside because there’s just enough of a nip in the air to make being outdoors pleasant, but not so much that you need a heavy coat. Before Old Man Winter comes calling, take advantage of these temperate days to tackle this seasonal to-do list.

As the weather gets cooler, it’s time to put your garden to bed under a blanket of mulch. Protect annuals and perennials from the cold by covering them with a 2- to- 4-inch layer of organic material, such as shredded wood or wood chips, shredded leaves, or straw. For shrubs, trees, and rosebushes, wait to spread mulch until later in the season, when the soil is cool but not yet frozen.

Insects love nothing better than overwintering beneath dead flowers, leaves, and other plant material. Roll up the welcome mat by raking away fallen leaves, deadheading annuals, pruning perennials and roses, and clearing out your summer vegetables before the first frost.

Once nighttime temperatures sink below 50 degrees Fahrenheit, it’s time for your tender container plants to move indoors for the season. Before carrying them into your house or to a protected spot in the garage, first clip away any dead or damaged leaves and branches, and then check carefully for insects.

Nothing says spring is coming like colorful tulips, daffodils, crocuses, irises, and hyacinths, but if you want to enjoy these beauties in your spring garden, you need to plant bulbs in the fall. As a general rule, northern gardeners plant spring-blooming bulbs in late September through mid-October, while southern gardeners can wait until mid-October or early November.

Keep warm air in and cold air out, and reduce your heating bills at the same time, by sealing up leaky doors or windows now. Check for drafts by turning off fans or air conditioners, then holding a lit stick of incense near doors and windows. If the smoke wavers or is sucked outside, you know you have a problem. The solution is simple: Caulk any cracks or chips around windows, and install weatherstripping to ward off drafts around doors.

According to the National Fire Protection Association, three out of every five residential fire deaths occur in a home that either has no smoke detector at all, or a smoke detector with nonfunctioning batteries. Don’t let your family become a statistic. Check your smoke and carbon monoxide detectors at the very least twice a year, once in the fall and again in the spring.

The X-Sense detector has a photoelectric sensor to detect smoke particles and a display that indicates when CO is higher than 30ppm. Read the review.

It’s a good idea to have your home’s chimney inspected and swept before fireplace season gets underway. This job is best done by a pro—expect to pay around $150 to $200 for a professional chimney inspection—but if you’re comfortable on the roof, you can do some preliminary work yourself. First, clear out any fallen leaves, birds’ nests, or other debris from the chimney, and repair any small cracks in the masonry with refractory cement, which is formulated to withstand high heat. Ensure that the damper moves smoothly and isn’t cracked, rusted, or warped, and then clean away soot, creosote, and ash.

If you’ve been thinking that your entry door could use a refresh, a new coat of paint on the surrounding door trim can help. Entry doors and trim are hard workers in most homes, and they have the scuffs and smudges to show it. Just painting the trim and cleaning the door will give the entry a more polished look. Clean the trim, let it dry, and then apply exterior paint. Most homeowners choose gloss or semi-gloss when painting trim. Two coats should be enough to protect the trim and keep it looking fresh for a year or more, depending on the weather and how busy your household is.

Want your lawn to look its best come springtime? Then sow grass seed in early through mid-fall. Reseeding the lawn gives gardeners in cold-winter areas a head start on spring. As the weather warms up, the grass will germinate, crowd out weeds, and develop a strong root system before the high heat of summer. If you live in a warm-winter region and want to keep your grass green all season long, sow annual ryegrass in the early fall. This quick-sprouting grass will look great through the chilly months and then die down once higher temperatures return in the summer.

If you have an asphalt driveway, reseal it in the fall when temperatures are between 50 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit and no rain is in the forecast. For most areas, that means late September to early October. To start, sweep away dirt, leaves, and other debris from the asphalt, and then pour asphalt sealant over the driveway. Using an asphalt squeegee, evenly spread the sealant across the driveway’s entire surface. Let the sealant cure for at least 24 hours before parking on the driveway.

Winter can be hard on your roof, when rain, snow, freezing temperatures, and high winds all take their toll. That’s why fall is the best time to make sure to inspect your roof and complete any necessary roof repairs before cold weather sets in. You can hire a professional for this service or, if you’re up to the task, do it yourself.

Autumn means raking leaves, and raking leaves can mean back pain. Make the job easier on yourself by buying a good rake. The right one is long enough so you don’t need to bend over, has flexible yet durable tines to easily scoop up debris, and has a comfortable, ergonomically designed grip so your hands don’t feel the strain. Our researched guide to the best leaf rakes contains some terrific options, whatever your needs and budget.

In most regions, fall brings rain—and a parade of muddy shoes. Get your mudroom ready for the season by setting out a large mat to absorb water and a tray to hold wet, muddy boots and shoes. If you don’t already have one, add a bench where you can sit and pull on your boots, and consider including a coat rack or wall hooks to hold jackets, umbrellas, and scarves.

As they say, the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, and the second best time is now. If “now” happens to be autumn, you’re in luck: The cooler temperatures and moisture help the tree establish roots before the hot and stressful summer weather.

To ensure success, mulch your newly planted tree to keep the roots insulated. Water regularly if there’s not enough rain, but don’t fertilize until spring. Avoid heavy pruning, other than trimming away any broken branches. And if a severe cold snap is in the forecast, wrap a blanket or piece of burlap over the tree for a little extra protection while it gets established.

With summer fun in the rearview mirror, fall is the time for getting back to business. Creating an organization HQ for the whole family is a great way to help you stay on task. Put it in a central location like the kitchen, mudroom, or back entryway, where the whole family can see it.

Include a large wall calendar or weekly schedule, a dry erase board for appointment reminders or shopping lists, and a bulletin board for important announcements or incoming and outgoing school forms. If your family uses a chore chart or meal planning chart, this would be the place to put it. Set up caddies to collect keys and other daily necessities so they’ll be easy to find and won’t clutter up the rest of the house.

Drain your hot water heater to remove accumulations of lime and other minerals that naturally occur in your tap water. When left untreated, this buildup can keep your appliance from functioning its best and put your system at risk for leaks and other problems. It’s an easy enough job to do yourself, but if you’re not confident in your DIY abilities, call a pro to do it for you. Simple though it may seem, this one task can lengthen the life of your water heater and prevent the system from malfunctioning down the line.

As temperatures drop, mice and other pests will be looking for a warm place to bunk, which is all well and good unless they choose your home as their winter retreat. Stay pest-free by doing a walkabout around the exterior and through the interior of your house, plugging any potential points of entry with caulk or steel wool. Keep in mind that mice can enter your home through a dime-size hole, so pay attention to even the smallest cracks.

Fall leaves and winter snow can cause your patio furniture to fade, stain, and rust. Protect it with a tarp or patio furniture covers, or place it inside your shed, garage, or screened porch. Before you stow it for the season, give patio furniture a proper cleaning with mild soap and water to remove dust, pollen, and mold. Treat wicker with lemon oil to keep it moisturized over the dry winter months and protect it from mildew.

Core’s heavy-duty tarps have a smooth undercoating a good pick for outdoor furniture covers that won’t leave behind scuff marks. Read the review.

Soak and scour the grates, clean under the hood, remove any foil or food particles from the interior, and wipe down the exterior. When foul weather moves in for good, you can quickly cover the grill and store it for the season.

Keep mowing your lawn in the fall until the grass stops growing. Then, when it’s time to put it away for the season, make any necessary repairs the lawn mower to ensure that it will be in good working condition when you pull it out again in spring. Wipe away any grass or other debris that clings to the machine, and consider having the blades sharpened by a professional. If you have a gas lawn mower, use up the last of the gasoline in the tank or add fuel stabilizer to prevent damage (check the manufacturer’s instructions).

If your lawn receives a lot of foot traffic, it could be at risk for soil compaction, a condition that prevents the proper circulation of air and nutrients. To keep your turfgrass nourished, aerate cool-season grasses in fall by using a manual aerator, or a spike or plug aerator (available for purchase or rental at many home centers). Before you aerate the lawn, make sure the soil is moist but not soaking wet, because it can be difficult to aerate dry soil.

Cool-season grasses, like bluegrass and tall fescue, benefit from a fall application of fertilizer. Fertilize your lawn with a slow-release formula about 1 week before you mow for the last time in the season. High-nitrogen formulas that offer winter weather protection are helpful in colder climates.

That stunning fall foliage may look good on the trees in your front yard, but when those leaves drop they can make a mess of your gutters. More than unsightly, leaves and other debris can clog the gutters, posing a real hazard in winter when rain and snow thaw and freeze inside gutters and form dangerous ice dams.

Protect your home from damage by removing leaves, sticks, and other debris from gutters now, and consider installing a leaf guard to keep your rain gutters clean with very little effort on your part.

Button up the house and get ready for windy winter by swapping out your window screens for storm windows (if you have them). If you don’t have storm windows, particularly if you have vintage single-pane windows that you’re trying to save, consider installing them.

Storm windows offer an additional layer of insulation against cold weather and drafts, help keep your home more comfortable, and can help lower energy bills.

You don’t want to wait until snow is falling and frigid winds are howling to discover that your home’s heating system is on the fritz. Call a pro to come out and evaluate your heating system now. If the HVAC specialist detects any issues, have them fixed promptly to save yourself from a potentially chilly disaster later in the season.

It may seem counterproductive to turn on a ceiling fan during the coldest months of the year, but a ceiling fan helps maintain comfortable temperatures even in the winter. Starting in the fall, set your ceiling fan to rotate in a clockwise direction (opposite the operating ceiling fan direction in summer), and run it on low speed to create an updraft. This tactic draws the room air up and forces the warm air near the ceiling down and through the room.

Because water expands as it freezes, it’s important to disconnect and drain garden hoses before temperatures drop to prevent them from bursting or leaking. Be sure to disconnect hoses from the outdoor spigots to which they’re attached; store hoses in a covered area like the garage or a tool shed to protect them from harsh weather. Turn off and drain your sprinkler system and shut off your outdoor faucets before nighttime temperatures dip below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

It’s easier to identify dead limbs before your trees drop their leaves, so early fall is a good time to trim back dead branches. Trimming your trees now is more than an aesthetic choice, and doing so can protect your home from damage. In freezing conditions, dead limbs can become heavy with ice and break off, ending up on your roof or lawn, or posing a safety issue for family and passersby alike.

For as long as there have been air conditioning covers, people have debated whether they’re a good idea. Advocates love covers for the way they keep ice and debris out of the machinery, while detractors fear that covers can create ideal habitats for rodents and other pests that can nest within the wiring. Homeowners who live in colder regions may want to consider at least covering the top of their outside AC condenser unit with a tarp or sheet of plywood, even if they leave the rest of the unit exposed. Window air conditioning units, on the other hand, should be removed, cleaned, and stored in a safe place until they’re needed again in the summer.

Give your HVAC system a fresh start with a new furnace filter. Furnace filters help maintain cleaner indoor air and keep a home heating system in good working order. Continue to change the filter every few months until you turn off your heat for the season.

A clogged dryer vent can cause a perfectly good appliance to operate more slowly and less efficiently, but more importantly it poses a serious fire hazard. Clean out your dryer vent at least once a year to speed up laundry day, keep energy bills low, and protect your home from fires. You can do the job yourself with a vacuum cleaner and a long dowel or wire hanger (if you’re careful not to damage the vent), or hire a pro to do the job for you.

Mold counts are on the rise at this time of year, exacerbating indoor allergies. Mount an effective defense by giving your carpets a thorough cleaning. Rent a carpet cleaner or hire a professional service to deep clean your carpeting, paying special attention to the bedrooms and high-traffic areas. If you’ve been thinking about removing your carpeting in order to breathe more easily, now might be the time to do it. Who knows—you may even have pristine hardwood floors hiding under those old carpets!

Don’t wait until the first snowstorm of the season to stock up on snow removal supplies. Buy an emergency stash of ice melt, salt, and sand (or kitty litter, in a pinch) to give you traction in slippery situations. Some home centers start selling these supplies as early as September and October, but if your local shop doesn’t carry them, you can certainly buy them from online retailers.

Have you ever cranked up the heat in late fall and waited for your radiators to circulate warm air through your home, only to discover that one or more of your radiators remains cold to the touch? If one radiator isn’t working when the rest of your system is operating normally, it’s usually a sign that air is trapped inside. This problem can be avoided by bleeding the radiators at the beginning of the season. To do this, first turn off the heat, then engage the bleed valve with a radiator key. Wait for the hissing sound to stop and a stream of water to pour from the radiator before closing up the bleed valve.

Cracks happen, and it’s important to take care of them before winter freezes make them worse. To repair cracks in concrete walkways, patios, or driveways, first clear away any dirt or debris from the damaged area, and then fill in the crack with masonry crack filler or concrete patch. Once you’ve filled the crack, smooth the edges of the new material with a trowel, and let the repair cure overnight.

Be ready for the next big storm before it strikes with a “go bag” of emergency essentials, and give serious thought to buying a generator for the house if you don’t already have one. Generators are available in a variety of sizes and types, including portable generators and models that can be wired into a home’s electrical system. The larger the generator, the more power it provides. Before you make a purchase, be sure to determine which features and which fuel type best suit your household’s needs.

If you live in an area that sees a lot of snow and where a snow thrower or snow blower is a must-have, fall is the ideal time to make sure your equipment works. Have clean, stable gas at the ready, and then take the snow blower out for a quick test run. Fill the tank, start it up, and make sure all of the features work. Always be certain to have a spare spark plug on hand so you won’t be caught by surprise during a winter storm.

An easy way to get ready for cold, wet fall weather—and spruce up your entry while you’re at it—is to invest in a new doormat. With the return to school and a faster pace of life, fall is a time of year when many homes experience an uptick in foot traffic. A ragged, worn doormat may no longer do the trick, and it might not exude the welcoming vibe you desire. Because there are so many options in materials, sizes, designs, and styles, consider switching your doormats out seasonally so they won’t wear out as quickly.

In the colder months, as darkness begins to fall earlier in the day, having adequate light on a front porch or entryway becomes even more important. If you’ve had the same porch light bulbs for a long time and they aren’t LEDs, think about swapping them out for new ones. After all, an entry light fixture isn’t much help when it doesn’t turn on.

Landscape lighting elevates the look of a home’s facade and helps set a welcoming tone. With a range of available colors and options that include solar-powered landscape lighting, it’s easier than ever to line a walkway or driveway, or to spotlight trees and other landscaping or architectural features, creating a custom look for the exterior of your house.

Caitlin Castelaz worked at BobVila.com for several years, writing, editing, or researching about nearly every aspect of home improvement and maintenance.

Michelle Ullman has been writing about just about everything related to home, garden, and lifestyle since 2011.

Theresa Coleman Clement is a freelance editor, writer, and home designer who specializes in home improvement, aging in place, sustainability, lifestyle, and home design. She has been writing and editing for BobVila.com since 2021. Her work has also appeared in Remodeling Magazine, Architect Magazine, Builder Magazine, Professional Deck Builder Magazine, DIYNetwork.com, and Habitat.org.

#7925. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us, but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s Zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I really like the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. And I’m with you on already thinking about spring—I’d love to see what you decide to grow over that new arch!

#7924. Declutter Your Garage Space With These Smarter Solutions

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:12 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Upgrade your garage from a cluttered mess to a highly organized space you can use with the help of ATLAS Shelving’s next-generation heavy-duty industrial storage unit that features a clean, open, and adaptable design capable of holding up to 2,500 pounds per shelf and 10,000 pounds total, evenly distributed.

Decluttering the garage is a crucial step toward creating a safe, accessible, and high-functioning extension of your home. Because a garage serves as the main entryway for many households—as well as the storage hub for heavy tools, seasonal gear, sports equipment, lawn and garden supplies, and more—an unorganized space can quickly become an eyesore and safety hazard that makes daily routines frustrating and hard to maintain.

As professional organizer Abriana Sanford, founder of Sorted and Styled in Atlanta, Georgia, notes, “Garages tend to become the catch-all space for anything that doesn’t have a designated home. Over time, this can make it difficult to find what you need, but decluttering allows you to reassess what you’re storing, eliminate unnecessary items, and reclaim valuable square footage.” By turning a disorderly pile into a streamlined, easy-to-maintain setup using strategic organization solutions, you can eliminate everyday hassle, restore peace of mind, and ensure that every tool and bin serves a clear, functional purpose. Sanford shares her garage organization tips below so you can get the most out of your garage storage space.

The first step in any garage organization project is to assess what you have and to get rid of what you no longer need. “One of the most common mistakes homeowners make is purchasing storage products before evaluating what they actually need to store,” says Sanford. She recommends first sorting belongings into categories. Then eliminate duplicates and materials that you no longer need. Finally, take inventory of what’s remaining. “This allows you to create a system that works for your belongings, rather than trying to make your belongings fit a particular system.”

Once you narrow down what you have, spend some time grouping belongings by how they’re used, such as lawn care, sports equipment, tools, automotive supplies, beach and pool gear, and seasonal decorations. “Creating designated zones makes it easier to locate items and return them to their proper places,” says Sanford. She also recommends considering the frequency of use when determining placement. “Everyday essentials should be easily accessible, while seasonal belongings can occupy higher or less convenient storage areas.”

Garage floor space is valuable, especially when you park your vehicles inside, so choose a variety of storage solutions that use open areas on the walls and ceiling. “Wall-mounted shelving, pegboards, overhead racks, and vertical tool organizers allow homeowners to maximize storage without sacrificing usable floor space,” Sanford explains.

When choosing the right organizational tool, be sure to consider the weight capacity of shelving, wall-mounted systems, and overhead racks. “Heavier belongings are generally best stored on lower shelves, while lighter, less frequently used items can occupy higher storage areas,” notes Sanford. Always follow the manufacturer’s installation and load requirements.

It’s also important to consider how flexible and adaptable storage products are. “I encourage homeowners to think beyond their immediate storage needs. Adjustable shelving, movable racks, and modular systems provide flexibility as hobbies, equipment, and family needs change,” notes Sanford. As household needs evolve, the garage should be able to evolve with them. “For example, a family storing strollers and toddler toys today may need additional space for bicycles, sports equipment, or recreational gear in a few years.”

One of Sanford’s favorite approaches to garage organization is incorporating adjustable shelving and modular storage systems. The ATLAS 7304K builds on this idea with an open-frame design that allows convenient side access, including in tighter garage spaces. Its clean, streamlined structure also provides a modern appearance. Another idea is to make the most efficient use of drawer space by either buying or making dividers. You can also add labeled stackable bins to open shelves or closed cabinetry to maximize storage.

Convenience is a core component of organizing a garage. Storage placement should reflect how frequently an item is used, says Sanford. “Homeowners shouldn’t have to move multiple bins or climb a ladder every time they need something,” she explains. “The more convenient a system is, the more likely everyone in the household will maintain it.”

Here are some tips for organizing in a way that takes accessibility into account:

Plastic storage bins with tight-sealing lids are the best choice to protect items. “In humid climates, moisture can be particularly problematic,” notes Sanford. She recommends using appropriate moisture-resistant storage containers and keeping belongings elevated off the floor when possible. “Clear, durable bins with secure-fitting lids also help protect belongings from dust and debris, while allowing homeowners to identify contents quickly.”

Sanford suggests avoiding cardboard boxes for long-term garage storage, especially if pests are a concern. “Cardboard can absorb moisture and provide hiding places for pests, so durable plastic containers with secure lids are often a better alternative.”

Storage needs have changed, and storage products should evolve with them. By combining heavy-duty industrial strength with a clean, open, and adaptable design, the ATLAS 7304K is built not only for what homeowners need today, but for how those needs may change over time. Its next-generation design makes better use of the existing space while offering flexibility for the future. It’s built for heavy loads. Designed for changing needs.

#7923. Will Alito or Thomas Retire if Democrats Win the Senate?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

While the Ginsburg example looms in the background, the answer depends on what values the justices are trying to maximize

Will Justice Thomas and/or Alito retire if Democrats take the Senate in tomorrow's election, hoping that the lame-duck Senate will confirm a nominee chosen by President Trump? In recent conversations, I've heard increasing speculation and support for this possibility among some judicial conservatives. And I hear corresponding worry among progressives.

Both sides think the election may create a brief, very consequential window for a Republican Senate to replace two aging justices. The GOP Senate would have to confirm their replacements before January 3, 2027. There would be political costs and procedural obstacles, but it could be done. Justice Barrett was confirmed by a Republican Senate within a month of her nomination on the eve of the 2020 election.

The rationale for retirement is straightforward: Don't get trapped in the actuarial straitjacket Justice Ginsburg found herself in when she failed to retire in 2014 (when she was 81). That was her last clear chance of retiring with a Democratic president and Senate.

Thomas is 78. Alito is 76. Neither has disclosed a serious health risk, and both have indicated they have no plans to retire this year.

But if Democrats take the Senate (prediction markets currently give them a 75% chance to do so) and if they play the sort of constitutional hardball over Supreme Court confirmations that Republicans have played in the past ten years, there's very little chance the new Senate would confirm any likely Trump nominee. Democrats needn't reject every possible Trump nominee--just those who would be likely to satisfy the conservative legal movement. So the president might not get another Supreme Court appointment before he leaves in January 2029. Calls for the eldest conservative justices to retire would surely intensify.

It's worse than that for judicial conservatives. If a Democrat wins the White House in 2028, the next opportunity for a Republican president to make an appointment might not come until January 2033. There are some important "ifs" packed in there, but they are well within the range of reasonable possibilities.

In January 2033, Thomas would be 84, Alito 82. Even assuming both remain healthy and active, that's a substantial amount of succession risk for conservatives to accept when they could potentially lock in their seats for another generation this winter.

A rational justice who prioritizes preserving his seat for something close to his judicial philosophy might well retire. But a rational justice might prioritize (or at least see himself as prioritizing) other things: continued service, jurisprudential influence, institutional reputation, and personal legacy. Justices do not see themselves simply as strategic agents of the political coalitions that produced their appointments.

For purposes of predicting what Alito and Thomas might do, the Ginsburg example cuts both ways. It illustrates the risks of refusing to retire when one's political allies control the presidency and Senate. At the same time, it illustrates the limits of assuming justices will subordinate their personal preferences regarding tenure, legacy, and judicial responsibility to the interests of that coalition.

Like Ginsburg, Thomas and Alito would probably resist renewed and intense calls for their immediate retirement. They might figure that:

(1) one of those additional "ifs" won't come to pass—that Republicans will retake the Senate in '28 or retain the White House;

(2) in any event, they'll outlast whatever period of Democratic control ensues (i.e., the mirror of the Ginsburg gamble);

(3) they've all but publicly committed themselves to staying on for now (Justice Alito says he will stay on through this term and Justice Thomas may want to pass Justice Douglas' record tenure, which would happen in May 2028); and/or

(4) a lame-duck retirement immediately after an electoral defeat would be seen as an unseemly concession to the sort of overtly political behavior by judges they've long publicly decried.

Progressives may dismiss this last consideration. Many critics see Thomas and Alito as essentially unscrupulous political actors who wouldn't hesitate to time their retirements in order to preserve another generation of conservative control. But that assumes they understand their own judicial behavior the way their harshest critics understand it. I doubt they do.

They may regard voting in accordance with their understanding of the Constitution—even when the results consistently advance conservative policy objectives—as fundamentally different from announcing their retirements right after voters have elected a Democratic Senate. On this view, they might think the former is acceptable judicial behavior while the latter is not.

On the other hand, they could see strategic retirements, which are hardly unprecedented among justices, as distinguishable from the politicized judging they've denounced. Choosing the circumstances and timing of retirement is compatible with their judicial philosophies. And many conservatives might well applaud their retirement decisions as responsible constitutional stewardship.

But a retirement announced immediately after the election to permit the outgoing Republican majority to confirm a successor, would be unusually conspicuous. Whatever their views about strategic retirement as a general matter, I'm guessing Thomas and Alito would regard the reputation cost to the Court—and to themselves—under these circumstances as too high.

The irony is that Ginsburg's cautionary example supplies the strongest argument for Thomas and Alito to retire, but also a good reason to doubt they actually will. Justices may be political actors in some respects, but they are not necessarily the political instruments their allies wish them to be.

#7922. How to Use a Shop Vac to Clean Up Wet Messes

By Tom Scalisi, Updated by Theresa Clement

Updated Oct 30, 2026 12:26 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

It’s not just dry messes that shop vacuums can handle. When unexpected wet messes happen, like a water main break, leak, or flood, a wet/dry shop vac is an indispensable tool that can quickly suck up the liquid into a canister for easy disposal. And, the variety of attachments that come with most shop vacs make them ready for flat surfaces, carpet, or even hard-to-reach crevices. The trick is knowing how to use a shop vac for water removal the right way. Here’s what you need to know.

Built for demanding cleanup jobs, DeWalt’s 9-gallon AC/DC et/dry vacuum combines heavy-duty suction power with the flexibility of corded or cordless operation. Whether you’re clearing water from a flooded basement or tackling a serious renovation mess, its large-capacity tank and dual-powered motor help reduce interruptions and keep projects moving.

Water and electricity don’t mix. Although modern shop vacs are typically double-insulated, it’s never a bad idea to plug yours into a GFCI outlet for extra assurance and if you use an extension cord, make sure it’s wet-rated.

Also, when using a shop vac for water, keep in mind that you will need to lift the shop vac’s canister to dump out the water when you are finished cleaning up a mess. It’s usually easier to dump out the water before it’s full.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

A shop vacuum can handle a ton of jobs like sawdust collection, carpet cleaning, and gutter cleaning. Here’s how to use a wet vac and how to suck up water with a shop vac.

If your model has a bag, remove it before using your shop vac for water. If you don’t, it will fill up with liquid and rip, making a nasty mess in the canister. These bags are typically very easy to remove and reinstall, so don’t throw yours out if it isn’t full.

Then remove the air filter. (If your shop vac has a wet filter, insert the model’s foam filter that’s designed for liquids.) If the air filter is installed when sucking up water, it will clog quickly and reduce airflow. The motor will then work harder than normally necessary, which could shorten the lifespan of your shop vac.

It’s easier to remove water from a surface if the end of the vacuum is compatible with the surface. For flat floors, look for the wide, T-shaped attachment. This attachment does the best job of removing water from hard floors of all types. Some of these floor attachments even have rubber squeegees that you can insert to increase their effectiveness.

Consider using the crevice tool for vehicle floors, tight spaces, depressions, or other spaces where the floor attachment won’t fit. You can also shop for a handheld wet vac meant specifically for small spaces.

Place the shop vac near the spill, and then run the cord to the closest GFCI outlet to extra protect yourself from any possible shock during use. If the cord doesn’t reach a GFCI outlet, then run an extension cord that’s wet-rated. You’ll see a W on the cord’s jacket if it’s wet-rated.

Pushing the vacuum attachment back and forth across the floor rapidly will spread puddles and make them harder to clean up. Here’s how to start vacuuming water.

For carpets and areas that require the crevice tool, adopt the same approach but on a smaller scale. Work in small areas, and give the vacuum a few seconds at each location before moving it to a new space.

Your shop vac has a built-in safety device that stops the vacuum when it’s full. There is a ball or puck in the filter attachment that floats, and when the water reaches an unsafe height, this device blocks the suction. To keep vacuuming, you’ll have to empty the canister.

After you finish cleaning up the water, you will still need to clean and dry the shop vac to prevent mold and mildew.

Using a shop vac for something wet usually means it’s a surprise and an urgent situation. From plumbing emergencies to severe storms and accidental spills, a wet-rated vacuum is a handy tool that can help contain wet messes and speed-up the return to normal. Here are some situations when a wet vac is a smart tool that can help.

There are a variety of shop vacs that are designed to handle different types of messes. Since everyone’s situation is different, consider your needs so you can choose the best shop vac for you. Here are some popular types of shop vacs.

Watch BobVila.com’s tool tester vacuum up water on a concrete floor using a wet/dry shop vac:

If you have a surprise basement cleanup to tackle, it may make sense to rent a shop vac, since big box stores also rent shop vacs by the hour or day for less than the cost of a new one. However, it might make sense to purchase one if you expect that you’ll use it at least several times a year.

Experts suggest running a shop vac for 2 hours or less before giving the motor a break to cool down, which can help extend the life of the tool. It’s also important to keep in mind that tools have an expected lifetime. For example, Ridgid says their vacuums expect a life of about 500 to 700 hours.

Yes, a wet vac can suck up liquids beyond just water as long as the liquid is not toxic or hazardous.

A shop vac is a great first response tool, and it’s useful for smaller messes. However, for substantial flooding or when water’s been present for long enough to cause structural damage or mold and mildew issues, you might need to call in the experts.

#7921. A November Garden Walk in Downtown Milwaukee

November is definitely settling in here in downtown Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Zone 6a). Most of the summer flowers are gone, leaves are piling up, and plenty of perennials are heading into dormancy. But there’s still so much to appreciate. Today we’re staying close to home for a walk around my neighborhood. I walk these streets with my dog all the time, and there are a handful of gardens I always slow down to admire.

Starting off strong with this one! This prairie-inspired garden is always buzzing with pollinators in summer, and it’s one of my favorites to walk by. In fall, the large sweeps of switchgrass (Panicum virgatum, Zones 4–9) and little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, Zones 3–9) really come forward. And wow, those fluffy switchgrass plumes make a statement when planted en masse.

From the other side, the pinkish-copper tones of little bluestem become much more prominent. The planting even carries across the sidewalk into the curb strip, making this small garden pretty hard to miss.

A few houses down is another garden that inspires me. The whole yard is planted so elegantly, with interest no matter the season. Bare spaces are usually filled with annuals. But even in November, we still get to see roses in bloom and hydrangeas giving it their all to remain relevant. The urn in the background with the pumpkin is a lovely seasonal touch.

This garden might look messy to some, but this is the kind of fall mess I truly enjoy. The hostas (Hosta cvs., Zones 3–9) spilling over the stairs, surrounded and covered by fallen red maple leaves… I love it!

This deep burgundy shrub covered in bright red berries certainly caught my eye. Unfortunately, it’s Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii, Zones 4–8), an invasive shrub here in Wisconsin. If you like the look, consider one of these native alternatives to Japanese barberry, including chokeberry, fothergilla, Virginia sweetspire, summersweet, and inkberry.

This Siberian crab apple (Malus baccata, Zones 2–7) is absolutely covered in clusters of warm orange fruit. Once so many summer flowers have disappeared, fruiting trees like this become some of the strongest color in the landscape.

It’s nice to see another garden extend beyond the front yard and into the curb strip. These often-overlooked spaces have so much potential. They can become a small garden, pollinator planting, or even a bee lawn.

And, of course, who can resist a strip of marigolds (Tagetes cvs., annual)? Especially when they’re still looking this good!

And one final reminder to leave the leaves this fall! Fallen leaves provide important overwintering habitat for pollinators and other beneficial insects, so leaving some in garden beds gives them a place to shelter until spring.

Thanks for coming along on my afternoon walk! While I wish this were a fall update from my little concrete jungle of a backyard, it’s all packed up now… because I’m moving to Georgia in just a few short weeks! I’ll definitely miss these neighborhood gardens, but I’m excited to see what new gardens and plants catch my eye down South.

#7919. Full Court Denies DOJ Petition In California Election Case In About 7 Hours, No Reply Needed

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Justice Kagan likely orchestrated the shadow execution before the petition was even filed.

I think we have seen a new record for speed on the emergency docket. Today, shortly before noon, the Solicitor General filed an emergency application in the California election law case. The brief was about 20 pages long. Circuit Justice never even bothered calling for a response. Shortly before 7:00, the petition was referred to the full Court, and was denied.

Rick Hasen calls it a mercy killing. I think shadow execution is more appropriate.

Indeed, this ruling was likely orchestrated by Circuit Justice Kagan before the petition was even filed. The government's case was dead on arrival. And Kagan spared California the fate that befell Missouri, which had to file a pointless brief that no one would read.

#7918. Winter Container Inspiration From New Jersey

Hi GPOD! Today we’re returning to New Jersey to see more from Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick. After sharing their beautiful fall containers with us, Ellen is back with some winter inspiration using colorful branches, evergreens, berries, pinecones, and more.

This beautiful antique lead planter in Ridgewood, New Jersey, always calls for a generous amount of greenery and nice height. We try to change what we do from year to year. This time we used curly willow, artificial white berry picks, magnolia leaves, red winterberry (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), and frosted pinecones. Silver bell eucalyptus, silver brunia stems, noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8) fill out the arrangement.

This is the same antique planter and house as in the previous photo, but from another winter. That year we used a combination of yellow twig dogwood (Cornus sericea ‘Flaviramea’, Zones 3–7) and red twig dogwood (Cornus sericea cvs., Zones 2–7) for lots of winter color. We also used artificial berry picks in pink and white and natural brown pine cones.

We like to use real berries, but sometimes the birds eat them before the season ends. Artificial berries give the client guaranteed color for longer. For greenery, we used desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), balsam fir (Abies balsamea, Zones 3–6), and incense cedar.

This slim planter sits on a small sliver of a step at an entry in Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey. It is simple but one of my favorites, with stunning red twig dogwood stems. We buy these from a farm that also grows and sells the more common darker-red stems.

Beneath the red is a froth of desert juniper. Dried lotus pods (Nelumbo cvs., Zones 4–10) and clusters of silver brunia punctuate the greenery. The finishing touch is a frilly skirt of bright chartreuse incense cedar.

This one sounds like an outfit, doesn’t it?

One of a pair of pots on the front porch of a Mission-style house in Teaneck, New Jersey, these had plenty of space for tall branches. We liked the combination of golden curly willow (Salix matsudana ‘Tortuosa’, Zones 4–8) and redtwig dogwood against the creamy tan stucco.

We tucked in shiny magnolia leaves with taller silver bell eucalyptus, then added natural brown pinecones and small clumps of silver brunia. A generous, draping swath of incense cedar finishes the bottom of the arrangement.

This is a window box in Englewood, New Jersey. A classic house calls for a classic planting. We used red winterberries, magnolia leaves, frosted pinecones, and silver brunia clusters. Some noble fir and our favorite evergreen, incense cedar, finish the arrangement.

This is a close-up detail of a planter in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey. Dark red twig dogwood stems are mixed with curly willow and branches of multiflora rose hips. We love using the rose hips, but they are sometimes hard to find.

This pot also had artificial white berry picks and Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus, Zones 3–8). Silver brunia on longer stems, noble fir, and incense cedar complete the arrangement.

Thank you for sharing more of your beautiful container designs with us, Ellen and Tracy! I love seeing how many different looks can come from a relatively small palette of winter materials. Changing the color and shape of the branches, berries, cones, and evergreens gives each container its own personality.

We have even more of Ellen and Tracy’s winter containers to share, so we’ll be back tomorrow with another round of inspiration!

#7917. Snow Thrower vs. Snow Blower: What’s the Difference?

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When a winter storm dumps a thick white blanket of the white stuff on your property, a snow blower or snow thrower can be your best friend. But which one do you need? Many often use the two terms interchangeably to describe snow removing power tools, but snow blowers and snow throwers are actually two distinct types of machines. While they serve the same purpose, they differ in size, power, snow removal ability, and price. Understanding the difference between the two is key to choosing a snow thrower vs snow blower to handle your winter snow clearing duties. Here’s what you need to know about.

Snow throwers and snow blowers clear snow in the same way: Both have a spinning auger that lifts the snow and launches it through a chute as you guide the tool along a driveway or walkway. But while snow throwers do this in a single step, or stage, a snow blower uses multiple stages to move the snow. There’s also a size difference: Snow throwers are smaller, more nimble machines that can handle moderate snowfall on smaller driveways, while snow blowers are larger and capable of clearing deeper snow from bigger driveways.

Snow throwers are ideal for removing small amounts of snow that are not extremely deep.They are single-stage machines that scoop up snow with an auger and launch snow out of a chute in a single action. Depending on the size of the snow thrower, they can clear a path that’s 18 to 24 inches wider and between 6 and 12 inches deep. Many can hurl it a distance of 15 to 20 feet, while some can send snow as far as 40 feet.

This Greenworks snow thrower weighs just 32 pounds and, in our tests, was powerful enough to clear snow up to 12 inches deep. Read the review.

Snow blowers are more powerful than snow throwers, making them a good choice for those who need to clear larger driveways or live in areas with harsher winters that receive higher snowfall totals. Like snow throwers, snow blowers have a rotating auger that scoops up snow, but they use two or three stages to clear snow. But instead of launching snow, it sends it to a separate impeller which blows the snow out through a chute and launches it 25 to 40 feet away. Some can even send snow as far as 50 feet away.

A three-stage model is even more powerful. This type of snow blower has an accelerator that breaks up the snow, allowing it to cut through compacted icy snow and large piles of snow more quickly than a two-stage model. Snow blowers can clear a path of snow ranging from 24 to 32 inches wide and 1 to 2 feet deep. With their two stage design in optimal conditions, some are capable of launching snow up to 60 feet.

Ryobi’s two-stage snow blower is easy to maneuver in tight spaces, has a powerful auger, and even works on gravel driveways. Read the review.

Choosing between a snow thrower and snow blower comes down to several factors, including snowfall totals, driveway type and size, ease of use, and price.

The average snowfall totals of the winter storms passing through your area are a big factor in determining whether to go with a snow thrower or snow blower. If snowstorms routinely drop snowfall of more than a foot of snow that’s wetter and more compacted, you’ll need a snow blower’s power and capacity to clear it. If your snowstorms are typically under a foot and consist of fluffy to moderately heavy snow, you can take on winter with a snow blower.

Keep in mind that the depth a snow blower or snow thrower can handle can vary from model to model, so make sure to check the manufacturer’s ratings. Some lighter-duty snow throwers max out at 6 inches, while there are compact snow blowers that might only be able to handle up to a foot of snow.

The type of driveway you’re clearing determines the type of snow removal machine you need. If you’re clearing a gravel driveway, don’t use a snow thrower. Since snow throwers have paddles that scrape across the ground, they can pick up and throw gravel, damage the auger, and send the gravel into your yard.

Snowblowers, in comparison, have skid shoes that prevent the auger housing from coming into contact with the ground, making them capable of clearing gravel driveways. But unlike snow throwers, which clear snow down to the pavement, snow blowers leave a thin layer of snow–about 1/8 of an inch–on smooth pavement.

The size of your driveway largely determines whether a single-stage snow thrower or multi-stage snow blower is the best choice. Snow throwers can cut a swath through snow that’s 18 to 24 inches wide, which makes them best suited for the typical two-car driveway.  Snow blowers have wider clearing widths of up to 32 inches, so they can cover significantly more ground than a snow thrower with each pass. They are a better choice for larger driveways.

Throwing distance is also an important factor when deciding between a snow blower and snow thrower. Most snow throwers can launch snow a distance of 15 to 25 feet away, though there are some single stage models that can throw snow up to 45 feet. A snow blower’s multi-stage design allows them to launch snow further, typically up to 50 feet, which is useful when clearing wider driveways or large patios.

With their ability to remove a wider swath of snow with each pass and launch it further, snow blowers are best suited for handling long winding driveways or larger driveways that hold three or more vehicles. While snow throwers have a narrower clearing width, their small size makes them easier to turn and maneuver, allowing you to clear 4 to 8 inches of snow over a smaller one- to two-car driveways.

However, these are recommendations. You can certainly use a snow thrower to tackle a larger driveway. Just plan on spending more time out in the cold to get the job done. Likewise, you can use a larger snow blower on a small driveway, but it may end up taking you longer. These larger machines require more room to turn and are more difficult to maneuver around smaller driveways.

Snow throwers are smaller and lighter, which generally makes them easier to maneuver, especially in tight areas. The controls on a snow thrower are also relatively simple, so there’s less of a learning curve when operating them.

Snow blowers are much heavier but are usually self-propelled and have power steering, so there’s less physical effort to operate them than a snow thrower. However, they are very difficult to move when the engine is off, which makes it more difficult to get in and out of storage.

A snow blower usually has more controls on the handlebars than a snow thrower, so expect a longer learning curve when learning how to use a snow blower.

Both snow throwers and snow blowers come in battery-powered and gas-powered versions. Cordless electric snow blowers are easier to maintain and start than gas models, operate with less vibration, and don’t produce exhaust. While gas-powered machines were once prevalent, today’s cordless electric models are comparable in clearing width, throwing distance, and snow capacity. That said, gas-powered machines still dominate when it comes to runtime. While it takes minutes to refill a gas tank, it can take hours to recharge a battery.

Snow throwers generally cost less than snow blowers. The transmission, large engines, and self-propelled system on these machines adds to their expense. Single-stage snow throwers are simpler machines, so they cost less. Snow throwers generally cost $500 to $1,000, while snow blowers can range between $800 and $2,000, with battery-powered snow blowers typically costing a couple hundred dollars more.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.
