#7843. 20 Ways to Keep Warm Without Turning on the Heat

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:38 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When winter winds blow, some homeowners dread the accompanying—and often outrageous— heating bills that Jack Frost brings with him. Heating oil prices for 2026, which are topping $6 a gallon, are particularly painful; overall, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), homeowners can expect to pay an average of 8.7 percent more to heat their homes than they did last winter.

While you probably won’t get away with not turning on the heat at all this winter, these smart solutions can help minimize winter’s impact on your budget.

Drafty windows are some of the biggest culprits when it comes to heat loss, which is why it’s important to insulate them properly. For an inexpensive fix, cut a piece of bubble wrap to fit perfectly inside the window frame, spray a thin film of water on the window, and press the bubble wrap into the glass. The layer of plastic will let the sunlight in while keeping the warmth where it belongs: inside.

The 3M window insulation kit is 0.75 mils thick and comes in one cut-to-fit sheet that measures 17.5 feet long by 5.16 feet wide.   Read the review.

Warm air rises, which isn’t great news for our heating bills. Although it might seem as though switching your ceiling fan on would make your room colder rather than warmer, turning on the fan can actually make a room toastier so long as you set the blades to spin in a clockwise manner.

To reverse the direction of your ceiling fan, check for a switch at the base of your fan. This change of direction creates a slight updraft that will push the warm air toward the walls and back down into the room.

Air leaks are a major source of heat loss. Check your home for possible gaps with this easy test: Hold a piece of toilet paper in front of your window and door frames. If the toilet paper moves, you’ve found a crack that needs to be sealed. Use weatherstripping to fill the gaps so that the heat stays tucked inside, and consider adding foam insulation to outlets to reduce heat loss even more. Caulk, too, is a useful weapon against leaks. “Use caulk for stationary cracks and gaps, especially around window frames or where siding meets the home’s foundation,” says HVAC technician Josh Mitchell, who works with AirConditionerLab in Nevada City, Calif.

RELATED: The 20 Best Products for Surviving Winter

If you have radiators in your home, try fashioning reflective plates out of aluminum foil and placing one behind each unit. Instead of just heating up your wall, the radiator will heat the foil, which will reflect warmth back into the room and allow you to maximize the unit’s output.

Exhaust fans are effective at ridding your bathroom of humid air during and after a hot shower. But leaving the fan off altogether when you shower is a good strategy for room heat generation, one that works particularly well if you leave the bathroom door open while you shower. The steam warms the air in the bathroom, and in adjacent halls and rooms.

If you have drafty doors, craft an inexpensive DIY fix from foam pipe insulation. Cut the foam to size, and wrap it around the bottom of your doors—yes, even the interior ones!—to prevent heat from escaping and utility costs from going up. If you’re not up for a project, there are plenty of affordable draft dodgers you can purchase. Draft dodgers are easy to slide off the door when the weather warms up, so you have no excuse not to try this budget-saving solution.

If you don’t have a jacket for your water heater, odds are you’re letting its warmth go to waste. Consider insulating your unit to reduce heat loss and save a little cash—about $20 a month, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. To see if your water heater needs additional insulation, just touch it. If it feels warm, it could probably use a water heater blanket, but check your owner’s manual first to make sure it’s safe to cover your model.

RELATED: Solved! When to Replace a Water Heater, Explained

This is by far the easiest thing you can do to lower home heating bills: Raise the blinds and open the curtains when the sun is out. It’s especially important to keep window coverings open on south-facing windows, because they bring in the warmest afternoon sun. Just remember to close your curtains again at night to keep all the toasty air inside until the sun returns.

Consider replacing your thermostat with a smart thermostat, which “allows you to set different temperature schedules throughout the day based on your occupancy patterns,” according to Justin Bohannon of Affordable Solutions HVAC & Electrical in Durham, North Carolina. “By utilizing setback temperatures during times of lower demand, such as when you’re at work or sleeping, you can save energy and reduce heating costs,” he adds.

Iced coffee or iced tea may be your go-to beverage to help you get through the day, but come winter it might be time to make the switch to a warmer beverage. Hot cocoa, tea, and coffee will warm you up on the inside and still give you that kick of caffeine you need.

A top sheet and comforter might be plenty comfortable from spring to fall, but in winter, it’s time to burrow under multiple layers. Try making your bed with flannel sheets and fleece or electric blankets, then drop your thermostat down a couple of degrees at nighttime to stay warm without burning through extra cash.

Cozying up next to a roaring fire is a way to warm up that comes with a caveat. In traditional fireplaces, about 80 percent of the heat generated escapes up the chimney. In fact, an open fireplace can even suck warm air out of the room. So while you do get some warmth from a fire in the fireplace, it may be less than you might think. To maximize your fireplace’s heat output, consider upgrading it with energy-efficient, wood-burning inserts.

If you do light a fire in the fireplace, remember to close the flue after you have put the fire out (keep the flue open, of course, while the fire is burning). Otherwise, all the warm air will go up and out of the house and let in the frigid air from outside.

RELATED: 11 Mistakes You Should Never Make With Your Fireplace

Layering clothing can goes a long way toward keeping you warm. While you’re at home, wear long sleeves, and wear socks (maybe even heated socks) and slippers around the house. Fashion retailer Uniqlo sells shirts, undershirts, long underwear, leggings, and socks with Heattech technology that traps heat to keep you warm. When you can’t shake a chill, throw your sweatshirt in the dryer for a quick spin to warm it up.

Check all your air vents to make sure they aren’t covered by window treatments or furniture. “Rearranging furniture is a surprisingly effective way to reduce home heating bills,” says Guy Sharp, a relocation manager at Andorra Guides who help residents settle into new homes, with a special focus on staying warm on a budget in the chilly temperatures that characterize the small European country nestled in the Pyrenees mountains.

“When you position your furniture away from radiators, baseboard heaters, and vents, you allow the heat to circulate freely throughout the room,” he adds. Blocked vents also makes your furnace work harder than it should and increases air pressure in the ductwork, which can lead to cracks. If it’s not possible to rearrange your furniture, you can use vent extenders to direct air around obstructions.

If you have an attic, it’s a good idea to confirm that there’s sufficient insulation up there and that the insulation is properly affixed. Look for gaps around pipes and ducts, and make sure that there aren’t any loose bits. Add more attic insulation if you find that what’s there could use some shoring up.

If your floors feel cold, throwing down some area rugs can will warm your feet up in a jif. Rugs offer a barrier against chilly air rising up from your concrete foundation, or from the crawl space under your home. For even more insulation (and to keep the rugs from slipping), use rug pads under your rugs.

If your home has seldom-used rooms, close them off. There’s no sense in heating the guest room, for example, if you’re not expecting visitors for a while. “Also make sure that you close any vents in little-used rooms,” says Leonard Ang, CEO of iPropertyManagement, an online company that offers advice for landlords, investors, and tenants throughout the United States.

For a thorough evaluation of how to best protect your home against winter’s chill, consider scheduling an energy assessment or energy audit. In such an audit, professionals use special equipment that draws in air through any gaps in your home’s exterior, allowing them to pinpoint areas that should be sealed or insulated.

When you do eventually turn on the heat, make sure your furnace is ready for a season of use. Having your furnace serviced in the fall is an often overlooked step that can help you save money on winter heating costs. “Regular maintenance of your heating system ensures it operates at peak efficiency,” says Brad Roberson, president of Aire Serv, an HVAC service company that has locations around the country.

#7842. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7841. Court Dismisses Claims Over Alleged "Doxing" and Criticism of Homelessness / Needle Exchange Activists

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Stabbin Wagon v. City of Medford, decided Sept. 30 by Judge Mustafa Kasubhai (D. Ore.):

The Court assumes the following alleged facts are true. Stabbin' Wagon is a Medford non-profit that provides clean needles, food and aid, and outreach services to unhoused people, particularly those suffering from drug addiction and mental illnesses. Plaintiff Jones was the founder and executive director of Stabbin' Wagon and Plaintiff Strong was an employee. Plaintiffs frequently criticized the City's arrests of unhoused individuals and its failure to provide outreach services to those individuals.

Defendants Brian Sjothun, Randy Sparacino, Justin Ivens, Darrel Graham, Geoff Kirkpatrick, Trevor Arnold, Arturo Vega, and John and Jane Does (collectively, "City Defendants") are current and former Medford city officials and police officers. City Defendants have criticized Plaintiffs and their needle exchange program. Starting around 2021, Defendants Graham, Kirkpatrick, and Sparacino monitored the Plaintiffs' social media activities, protest attendance, and interviews with newspapers. City Defendants removed Plaintiffs from police communications which alerted local outreach services when the police swept an encampment of unhoused individuals. Medford police have also stopped, arrested, and cited Stabbin' Wagon employees on several occasions from 2020 to 2023.

In 2023, Plaintiffs received a $1.5 million grant from the Oregon Health Authority ("OHA") to open a 'respite center' to provide more outreach services to unhoused people. Defendants Sjothun, Ivens, Arnold, and Kirkpatrick attempted to persuade OHA to rescind the grant. Plaintiffs allege that these Defendants "disseminated inflammatory, false, and disparaging information about Plaintiffs to other providers, state officials, and community leaders" in their attempt to reverse the grant.

Defendant Ryan Mallory is "a law-enforcement-adjacent figure in Southern Oregon" who operates social media platforms and companies that investigate, report, and consult on matters related to law enforcement, including the Medford Police Department. Defendant Mallory supported City Defendants' attempt to rescind the grant. He expressed his opposition to Plaintiffs' OHA grant on his Facebook group which has over 100,000 followers. His followers commented in support, and on September 13, 2023, one approached Plaintiffs while they were working and threatened to call the police. On August 4, 2023, Defendant Mallory posted Plaintiffs' personal information, including their home addresses and birthdays, in a graphic with Plaintiffs' likenesses resembling "law enforcement booking records." On September 7, 2023, Defendant Mallory posted a video and a comment that urged the public to oppose the OHA grant, stating in part:

Unqualified people that fill our Parks in greenways with needles, keep people addicted by promoting drug use, and misappropriate grant money by using it for public protest of the police rather than helping people are about to get a massive paycheck …. Ask for an audit of the stabbin wagon organization…. These folks are intending on renting a building to perpetuate drug use …. Melissa Jones and her marketing director [Sam Strong] have openly stated that they get grant money and use it to protest police and others.

Defendant Mallory and his followers continued making posts that "fomented animosity and disinformation regarding Plaintiffs and their services." On May 21, 2024, Defendant Mallory posted an article that discussed Plaintiff Jones's sentencing in municipal court and commented that she "[d]efinitely hasn't learned her lesson based on that. Guess we'll see how probation goes." In March 2025, Defendant Mallory posted a video that showed needles on the ground in downtown Medford and commented that Stabbin' Wagon "shouldn't be in business at all, it worsens the problem."

OHA delayed Plaintiffs' grant but ultimately awarded the funds. "[M]unicipal and zoning barriers and Defendants' subversion campaign" forced Plaintiffs to end their attempt to open the respite center. Plaintiffs Jones and Strong resigned from Stabbin' Wagon due to the Defendants' "harassment, surveillance, doxing, and retaliatory pressure." …

The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims (which related to doxing, criticism, surveillance, and retaliation) on various grounds, including that they were filed too late, but also added this:

Plaintiffs also allege that Defendants retaliated against Plaintiffs advocacy by opposing their grant from OHA and publicly and privately disparaging them. Plaintiffs allege that immediately after OHA awarded Stabbin' Wagon the grant, the City and Medford police, including Defendants Sjothun, Ivens, Arnold, and Kirkpatrick disseminated false and misleading information to state officials, community leaders, and other organizations. Plaintiffs allege the City sought to portray Stabbin' Wagon as extreme and unqualified, lobbied OHA, and coordinated with other nonprofits hostile to Stabbin' Wagon like OnTrack Rogue Valley and the Addictions Recovery Center.

Courts take a cautious approach with retaliation claims involving government speech like those here.

Restricting the ability of government decisionmakers to engage in speech risks interfering with their ability to effectively perform their duties. It also ignores the competing First Amendment rights of the officials themselves. The First Amendment is intended to "preserve an uninhibited marketplace of ideas in which truth will ultimately prevail." That marketplace of ideas is undermined if public officials are prevented from responding to speech of citizens with speech of their own.

The Ninth Circuit has accordingly set a high bar for when government speech gives rise to a First Amendment retaliation claim. For example, an act of defamation does not give rise to a retaliation claim if it does not affect the plaintiff's rights, benefits, or status with the state. Government speech that results in reputational harm and ultimately a loss in employment also does not meet the high bar for adverse action….

False accusations may give rise to a retaliation claim in certain contexts, however. In Mendocino Env't Ctr. v. Mendocino County (9th Cir. 1999), police officers falsely accused members of an environmental organization of criminal activity in connection with a criminal investigation. The officers made false accusations to secure arrest and search warrants. The Ninth Circuit held that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a First Amendment retaliation claim because the inclusion of the accusations in warrant affidavits permitted the inference that the acts would chill a person of ordinary firmness from future first amendment activities.

At the outset, some of Plaintiffs' allegations fail because they seek to hold Defendants accountable for protected speech. For example, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants Ivens and Arnold "expressed outrage over the award and attempted to mobilize public opposition and influence OHA to rescind the grant." They also allege that the City portrayed "Stabbin' Wagon as untrustworthy, unqualified, and politically extreme." These allegations are insufficient to give rise to Plaintiffs' retaliation claim because the government must be allowed to express its own views, even when it is critical of some of its citizens….

Plaintiffs [also] allege that OHA delayed Stabbin' Wagon's grant in response to Defendants' conduct but ultimately awarded it. Plaintiffs Jones and Strong resigned from Stabbin' Wagon and Plaintiffs had to close their peer respite program. Plaintiffs, however, do not allege that Defendants had any control over the grant process and conceded that point at oral argument. This is fatal to Plaintiffs' allegations that Defendants "disseminated inflammatory, false, and disparaging information about Plaintiffs." Cf. Gini v. Las Vegas Metro. Police Dep't (9th Cir. 1994) (holding defamatory statements did not give rise to a First Amendment violation where the officials "could not, and did not, make any decision or take any state action affecting [the plaintiff's] rights, benefits, relationship or status with the state")….

And the court had this to say about plaintiffs' civil rights conspiracy claim:

A plaintiff bringing a Section 1985 claim to vindicate rights secured by the First Amendment must "prove that the state was somehow involved in or affected by the conspiracy" because the First Amendment "restrains only official conduct." Plaintiffs remaining allegations are that unspecified Defendants coordinated "with anti-activist social media groups that published private information and incited public backlash" and disseminated "Plaintiffs' private identifying information, obtained through law enforcement channels, to more than 100,000 followers in order to incite harassment and vigilantism against Plaintiffs."

Plaintiffs make numerous allegations attributing this conduct to Defendant Mallory who is not a City official. Much of Plaintiffs' allegations center on Defendant Mallory's speech via social media and other outlets. Digital communications like these generally fall within the First Amendment's protections. Speech is generally protected unless it falls into a category of unprotected speech [such as the category of "true threats"]. Some of these allegations seek to impose liability for protected speech and therefore fail. E.g., SAC [Second Amended Comalaint] ¶ 121 (alleging Defendant Mallory criticized Plaintiffs' qualifications). Plaintiffs summarily allege categories of potentially unprotected speech by Defendant Mallory. E.g., SAC ¶¶ 129, 131 (alleging Plaintiffs experienced harassment); SAC (alleging defamatory statements); SAC ¶ 203.e (incitement). To the extent Plaintiffs seek to hold Defendant Mallory liable for these acts, Plaintiffs must identify the alleged unprotected speech with more specificity and without relying on broad legal conclusions.

Plaintiffs also allege Defendant Mallory published Plaintiffs' names and home addresses in a "[b]usted" graphic, mimicking booking log services. A party generally cannot maintain a claim for disclosure of publicly available information that is lawfully obtained. Florida Star v. B.J.F. (1989). Plaintiffs do not allege their names and home addresses were not publicly available or unlawfully obtained. Plaintiffs therefore have not alleged an overt act by Defendant Mallory.

With respect to the City Defendants, Plaintiffs allege that the "City Defendants, in particular the members of the Medford Police Department, were aware of Defendant Mallory's pro-law enforcement social media influence." Plaintiffs further allege that Defendants Kirkpatrick and Sparacino appeared on Defendant Mallory's podcast. Plaintiff makes the general allegation that "Defendants … reached a tacit understanding that Defendant Mallory would" amplify the City Defendants' retaliation against Plaintiffs.

Viewed in light of the Court's rulings above, these allegations are insufficient to allege the participation of the City Defendants in the alleged disclosure of Plaintiffs' personal information. A plaintiff must allege a conspiracy with facts that rise above allegations of parallel conduct and sympathetic viewpoints. Plaintiffs' general allegation of tacit agreement is insufficient. The Court has found that Plaintiffs have not adequately alleged the City Defendants retaliated against them, so Defendant Mallory cannot be said to have amplified it at this time. Plaintiffs' Section 1985(3) claim is dismissed because they must allege that "two or more persons conspire[d]" and that a state actor is "at least one of the wrongdoers." …

Stephanie C. Kucera and Zachariah H. Allen (Hart Wagner LLP) and Casey S. Murdock (Frohnmayer Deatherage Law Firm) represent defendants.

NEXT: Crime in Texas, Trial in Texas, Confession to Clergy in North Carolina: Which Law Applies?

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7839. How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a new car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

Use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin says. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

Vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”

Even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical issues with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

#7837. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, “Trump’s Transportation Department Makes Commonsense Updates to Vehicle Lighting Standards for AVs”

#7836. From a Life-Long Republican Contemplating the Election Results

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Yesterday's events put me in mind (as I have been on other occasions) of Kipling's The Lesson; it was discussing England's very poor performance in the Boer War (though after England ultimately won that nasty conflict), but it applies to many other contexts as well. Its opening and closing stanzas seem especially apt:

Let us admit it fairly, as a business people should, We have had no end of a lesson: it will do us no end of good.

Not on a single issue, or in one direction or twain, But conclusively, comprehensively, and several times and again ….

It was our fault, and our very great fault—and now we must turn it to use. We have forty million reasons for failure, but not a single excuse. So the more we work and the less we talk the better results we shall get— We have had an Imperial lesson; it may make us an Empire yet!

Change what needs to be changed (the lesson is political, not Imperial), and it's good advice for many situations. The question is whether enough of us will take the advice—and, of course, whether the lesson we learn is the correct one.

#7835. Justice Department and FBI Seize Vulnerability Scanning and Spear Phishing Tools Operated and Used by China-State Sponsored Hackers

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorized seizures to deny malicious cyber actors access to two hacking tools, “Microscan” and “FishHub,” used to scan and, in some cases, hack, U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure systems and other networks. As alleged in court documents unsealed in the Western District of Pennsylvania, malicious cyber actors working for Integrity Technology Group (Integrity Tech), a company based in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), operated and used the tools. Integrity Tech has contracts with the PRC government.

“The United States will not allow China or its proxies to operate against United States interests with impunity in cyberspace,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division will continue to respond decisively and use every tool at our disposal to disrupt the Flax Typhoon threats, dismantle the infrastructure sustaining them, and protect the critical networks that power our daily lives and on which our Nation’s security depends.”

“These state-sponsored hackers continue to aggressively target and access networks and systems throughout the world in an effort to identify and steal files and otherwise exploit victims’ vulnerabilities,” said U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti for the Western District of Pennsylvania. “These seizures, our second disruption of Integrity Tech’s massive operations in as many years, send another clear message to cybercriminals from the PRC and elsewhere of the Department’s dedication to defending and maintaining cybersecurity in the United States and abroad.”

“Integrity Technology Group provided China-linked threat actors with capabilities used to conduct widespread vulnerability scanning and, in some cases, intrusions targeting U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “The PRC relies on contractor and enabling companies to expand the reach and scale of its malicious cyber activity. By exposing and disrupting these enablers, we make it harder for the PRC to target American networks and infrastructure.”

“Today’s seizures underscore the FBI’s unwavering commitment in disrupting PRC state-sponsored cyber criminals who threaten our critical infrastructure and national security,” said Special Agent in Charge Mark Remily of the FBI San Diego Field Office. “FBI San Diego and our law enforcement partners around the world will continue to employ the full force of our investigative authority to protect the American people and safeguard our networks from malicious foreign cyber actors.”

According to court documents, Integrity Tech created and used a botnet of internet-of-things devices infected with a variant of Mirai malware. Among other things, this botnet facilitated Integrity Tech’s computer vulnerability scanning using Microscan. Integrity Tech developed Microscan to conduct reconnaissance, via the botnet and otherwise, of victim computer networks for vulnerabilities that its clients would later exploit. Targets of Microscan vulnerability scanning include a U.S. power company based in South Carolina, a multi-national Non-Governmental Organization, Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies in the natural gas and power sectors, and two Taiwanese universities. Integrity Tech accessed Microscan through one of the seized domains, c0cc[.]cc.

A second Integrity Tech tool, FishHub, is alleged to have facilitated the exploitation of computer networks through spear phishing. After an initial network compromise, FishHub downloaded additional malware to the victim network. This malware provided Integrity Tech’s clients with unauthorized remote access to the victim network or searched for specific files and sent them to servers controlled by Integrity Tech. Confirmed victims of FishHub activity included approximately 20 Taiwanese universities. Five of the seized domains helped deliver this malware: 98aicai[.]com, 98aicode[.]com, outlook3650[.]com, youtubecard[.]com, and linkedinns[.]net.

Today’s action marks the Department’s second public technical disruption of Integrity Tech’s hacking infrastructure. In September 2024, the Justice Department announced the court-authorized disruption of Integrity Tech’s Mirai malware botnet which consisted of more than 200,000 consumer devices in the United States and worldwide. In conjunction with the seizures announced today, the FBI, along with other U.S. and foreign-partner agencies, published a cyber security advisory. This advisory provides indicators-of-compromise associated with Integrity Tech intrusion activity and is designed to help network defenders identify and respond to Integrity Tech’s malicious activity.

The FBI San Diego and Baltimore Field Offices are investigating the case, in coordination with the FBI’s Cyber Division.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan McKenna for the Western District of Pennsylvania and Trial Attorney Jacques Singer-Emery of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case. Substantial assistance was provided by Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Sullivan for the District of Maryland and the National Police Agency of Japan.

#7834. Get a Head Start on Your Spring Garden by Planting These Perennials Now

By Nina Malkin, Gretchen Heber, Updated by Teresa Odle

Published Nov 4, 2026 4:04 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Perennials can live for years or even decades, beautifying your garden with very little care. Flowering perennials typically produce blooms by the second year, though some will burst with color the very first year. Spring-blooming perennials signal the coming of warmer weather and more colorful gardens.

However, fall, with its combination of still-warm soil and cooler, wetter weather, presents an ideal opportunity to encourage root growth in new spring perennials. So admire this list of perennials to plant in fall, pick your favorites, and take advantage of planting spring-blooming perennial flowers before winter strikes.

Planting perennials in the still-warm fall soil gives the plants a chance to get established underground, building a strong root system that will prepare them for vigorous aboveground growth—and flowering—come springtime. This helps lessen the risk of heat and water stress in spring. In addition, fall planting is beneficial in drought-prone areas. According to High Country Gardens, “as plants begin to go dormant in fall, and their energy shifts from top growth to root growth, they use much less water.”

With cooler fall soil and typically less windy conditions than spring, weather tends to stress young plants less in autumn. If you live where it’s still blisteringly hot, wait until temperatures cool down, but don’t wait so long that the plants have little to no chance to get somewhat established before a freeze hits.

Many perennial plants fare better with a fall planting and are better able to produce flowers in spring. Several of the plants on this list are herbaceous perennials, which typically die back to the ground in winter anyway, but remain alive underground and leaf out in spring, so they are well suited for fall planting. As with any new plant, don’t expect your fall-planted perennial to reach its mature size and full flowering in its first year, but give it some time to establish.

If you get impatient for posies as the winter drags on, put in hellebores now. Summer is too hot for them, so these are among the best perennials to plant in fall. Also known as Lenten rose, this is one of the first flowers to appear each year, often poking through the snow in late winter or early spring with big, bowl-shaped pink, yellow, or maroon blooms. Hardy hellebores do best in slightly shaded spots and neutral to alkaline soils with good drainage. Though deer and rabbits avoid munching on hellebores, the plants’ leaves, stems, and sap are poisonous if ingested.

Best For: Early blooming in a mass planting or ground cover.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 8Size: 12 to 15 inches tallLight: Dappled sunlight to partial shade

Certainly no shrinking violet, pasque flower is a showstopper with purple bell-shaped blossoms that is native to dry meadows in parts of Europe. Pasque is the Old French word for “Easter,” and this perennial is bound to bloom in time for the holiday (fortunately, it is also rabbit-resistant). The gorgeous garden star, which is also known as windflower and meadow anemone, flourishes in fertile soil with good drainage for easy purple spring flowers. Plant it in August if possible to give it time to produce blooms.

Best For: Winter to early spring color in cooler zones.USDA hardiness zones: 4 to 8Size: 4 to 10 inches tallLight: Partial shade to full sun

For colorful ground cover, consider creeping phlox. Phlox is the Greek word for “fire,” and this mat-forming plant will set your landscape ablaze with small, flat, fragrant blooms in purple, pink, red, or white beginning in March. It’s a favorite for filling in rock gardens and can be especially pretty draping over a wall. Choose a spot that receives dappled sun and has sandy soil that drains well. Though phlox might need dividing if it gets too crowded, it is a low-maintenance ground cover.

Best For: Colorful spring-blooming groundcover or to drape over walls or rocks.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 6 inches tallLight: Dappled shade to full sun

Gardeners who don’t like a lot of toil may love growing Virginia bluebells. Plant them in fall and In early spring, the perennial pops out flowers that start pale and turn a rich, true blue. They thrive in moist soil and mostly shady conditions, eventually establishing a colony of pollinator-friendly ground cover filled with foolproof flowers that require virtually zero care.

Best For: True blue color in moist woodland gardens. USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 1.5 to 2 feet tallLight: Partial to full shade

Prized for its graceful, nodding blooms, columbine is a woodland perennial, so it likes a partly shaded location and consistently moist soil. Its white, yellow, red, or blue flowers appear in early spring and bloom through midsummer. These native flowers also are deer- and rabbit-resistant, a plus in gardens visited by wildlife. The only caveat is that columbine is one of the shorter-lived perennials; if you love them, add a few plants every year or so to keep their color going and the butterflies and hummingbirds happy in mountain, forested, and cooler growing zones.

Best For: Spring color in natural and woodland gardens or meadows.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 1 to 3 feet tallLight: Partial shade to full sun

Tall, resilient false indigo (also known as blue wild indigo) flowers in late spring through fall with thick stalks and spires of small dark-blue blooms. If blue isn’t your bag, check out hybrids in other colors, including yellow and pink. False indigo likes full sun but can deal with some shade and is best planted in fall in hotter climates. The drought-tolerant native that’s a member of the pea family beckons bees and butterflies, and is unlikely to get nibbled by deer and rabbits.

Best For: Blue flowers above oval blue-green leaves in drought-tolerant gardens USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 3 to 4 feet high and wideLight: Partial shade to full sun

It must be those long, fuzzy, pale-colored flowers that give Astilbe its common nickname: false goat’s beard. This practically trouble-free plant that blooms from spring through summer is especially popular as a shady border plant and for its deer resistance. Its flowers contrast well against broad, leafy foliage. Astilbe thrives in loamy, slightly acidic soil and usually needs dividing every 3 to 4 years.

Best For: Border plant for part shade in gardens with acidic soil.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 1 to 4 feet tallLight: Shade to part shade

Attention gardeners in the Southwest who can’t get by on cactus alone: Hartweg’s or Texas sundrops are a perfect perennial pick, flowering in March through October. Also called evening primrose, this night-blooming perennial features flowers with bright yellow petals that open around sunset and remain through the next day. Once classified as Oenothera, the low-growing plant thrives in regions with hot prairies and plains. Sow seeds or plant in partly shaded areas for earlier opening times.

Best For: Large yellow flowers that bloom in the evening for rock gardens or moon gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 9Size: 1 to 1.5 feet high and 2 feet wideLight: Part afternoon shade to full sun

Shade happens—and that’s not a problem for lamium. This lovely yet tough ground cover can easily take on bare spots like those beneath trees. Lamium boasts variegated foliage in silver, gold, and green along with dainty pink and purple flowers that appear in late spring and summer. This rugged plant can thrive in clay and alkaline soils, and it actually prefers dry conditions. Deadhead the flowers once they fade to encourage a new crop of blooms.

Best For: Ground cover under trees or other areas where sun transitions to shade.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: Less than 12 inches high with 2- to 3-foot spreadLight: Partial to full shade

For a flowering perennial that smells as nice as it looks, let dianthus adorn your landscape. Some dianthus species are biennial (living about 2 years) and they require fall planting so they can gain energy over winter. All types offer clusters of spunky spring-through-summer blooms in a range of hues, including pink, white, yellow, and red against blue-green leaves. Dianthus loves sun and well-draining soil, and is ideal for rock gardens, containers, and borders. Its rich nectar will attract pollinators, yet deer and bunnies won’t bother with it.

Best For: Sun-loving flower for rock gardens, containers, and along rock walls. USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 6 to 12 inches high; 6 to 24 inches wideLight: Full sun

This cold-hardy daisy can add a touch of elegance to borders and garden beds. In late spring and early summer, the daisy comes alive with large white flowers with yellow centers, adding a contrast to other perennial garden flowers. The flowers fare best in rich soil with good drainage and are among perennial flowers to plant in fall (or sow from seeds). Shasta daisy is a flower that can handle heat. And while it does well with regular watering, it handles short periods of drought better than soggy soil. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the blooms coming, and even cut fresh ones for flower arrangements.

Best For: Sunny butterfly or cutting gardens or in containers. USDA hardiness zones: 4 to 9Size: 1 to 4 feet high; 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun

Add a pincushion plant to your garden and enjoy the springtime reward of delicate lavender, pink, or white flowers borne on gangly stalks that rise from a clump of gray-green leaves. Perennial in all but the coldest regions, pincushion flower is moderately drought-tolerant, attracts butterflies and hummingbirds, and thrives in sunny spots of the garden. The cut flowers of this plant make a wonderful, somewhat quirky, addition to a bouquet. Sow the seeds in fall.

Best For: Rock gardens or sunny fairy gardens and along walkways.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 9Size: About 1 foot high and wideLight: Full sun

A springtime profusion of plum-colored blooms greets those who plant purple coneflower or sow its seeds thickly in fall. The large, daisy-like flowers sit high above the medium-green foliage on this clumping plant. This hardy perennial can take a bit of shade but needs some sun to produce its stunning blooms. Purple coneflower is not terribly picky about soil, but will do best in soil that drains well. It’s also fairly drought-tolerant once established, and wilts a bit when it needs water. Harvest the blooms to add to indoor flower arrangements.

Best For: Native and butterfly gardens or meadows, or behind lower-growing flowers.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 3 to 4 feet high; 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun but can handle partial shade

Occasionally referred to as tickseed, and recently reclassified as Anacis, this pretty flowering plant is most commonly known as coreopsis. It comes in both annual and perennial varieties. If you’re planting in the fall, be sure to look for a perennial variety. The profuse bloomer produces scads of yellow flowers throughout spring and summer, and even into autumn. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage this long bloom time. Coreopsis is drought-tolerant and deer-resistant, but it will attract pollinators and songbirds.

Best For: Natural areas in rocky or sandy soil, rock gardens, and butterfly gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 3 to 4 feet tall; 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun or light shade

The delicate, intricate flowers of Oenothera lindheimeri (also known as gaura or whirling butterflies), are said to resemble supercharged butterflies. With white-tipped pink “wings” that surround long white stamens topped with yet more pink, gaura provides an elegant feature in the garden. This loose, shrubby plant is native to Texas, Louisiana, and Mexico, and it’s drought- and heat-resistant.

Best For: Native or prairie-style gardens or areas with sandy, well-draining soil.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 9Size: Flower stems to 4 or 5 feet; about 2 feet wideLight: Full sun

This member of the mint family offers both attractive purple flowers for bees in late spring and aromatic foliage is considered an herb that can go into teas or savory dishes. It’s a reliable plant that can stand alone in a rock garden or spread to form a border along a path. Catmint needs no fertilizer and will rebloom if you shear the plants to remove the first bloom of flowers. Plant it in fall in time to establish some roots before frost. It prefers good drainage and can thrive in rocky or sandy soil. It’s also drought-tolerant and deer-resistant.

Best For: Borders and walkways or in pollinator rock gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 1 to 3 feet high, 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun

Add bleeding heart to your garden in fall, and come springtime it will bring arching stems bearing delicate 1- to 2-inch-long heart-shaped pink flowers. An herbaceous, bushy plant formerly known as Dicentra, bleeding heart has clumps of foliage that can go dormant in heat while flower stalks rise above it. Plant this one in part shade, in moist, well-draining soil with plenty of organic material. As summer wears on, bleeding heart will likely retreat, but it will be back on display after winter subsides.

Best For: Woodland gardens, interplanted with foliage ground covers.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 2 to 3 feet high and about 2 feet wideLight: Partial to full shade

A sprawling, almost vine-like shrub, lantana decorates hot landscapes in late spring and summer with masses of delicate flower clusters in purple, orange, pink, yellow, red, or white. It is drought-tolerant once established and although it loves heat, it can feature in summer annual flower beds or containers in slightly cooler climates. Depending on where it grows, lantana can become shrub size. Butterflies flock to this hardy plant, which is deer-, pest-, and disease-resistant. Bear in mind that lantana is toxic to livestock, cats, and dogs.

Best For: Hot areas and drought-tolerant gardens to attract butterflies and hummingbirds.USDA hardiness zones: 7 to 11Size: 1 to 6 feet high; 3 to 5 feet wide where perennialLight: Full sun

Yarrow blooms from spring to fall with masses of umbrella-shaped flower heads gracing the tops of tall stems bearing fern-like foliage. Popular as a cut flower, yarrow is also beautiful in the landscape. You’ll find yarrow in a rainbow of colors, including yellow, pink, red, white, and gold. It’s drought- and heat-tolerant, but yarrow seeds need a cool period to germinate, so it’s best to sow seeds in the fall. Yarrow can spread aggressively, so plant it in a place where you’d like to see a sea of color.

Best For: Naturalized areas like meadows and drought-tolerant butterfly gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 1 to 3 feet high and wideLight: Full sun

Many spurge types offer early spring color, and cushion spurge is no exception. Its small yellow flowers are surrounded by yellow/pale green bracts, creating the impression of a larger flower. The mounded plant can grow in poor soil like sand or in loamy soil. Although the plant thrives in sun, it might need a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates. It’s drought-, deer-, and pest-resistant, and easy to grow and maintain. However, its milky sap is slightly toxic and can cause itching on contact.

Best For: Small spaces in rock or cottage gardens, containers.USDA hardiness zones: 4 to 8Size: 1½ feet high and wideLight: Full sun with some partial shade

Create the feeling of your own “poppy field” or Georgia O’Keefe painting with oriental poppies. Though the flower petals are paperlike, they are large and full of interest around the center. Look for varieties in classic deep red, orange, coral, or even white. Sow seeds or plant nursery transplants about a month before your first expected frost to aim for blooms in late spring to early summer. Note that these flowers do best in cooler and drier regions of the country and require soil that drains well.

Best For: Asian or cottage garden mixed in with late summer bloomersUSDA hardiness zones: 3 to 7Size: 3 feet high and nearly 2 feet wideLight: Dappled to full sunlight

Gardeners in warm regions might want to consider planting Mexican bush sage or other salvias in fall to establish good root systems before spring. In its northern ranges, this big beauty might go all the way to the ground in winter, but it will come roaring back in spring. Mexican bush sage forms an ever-expanding clump of stalks bearing long leaves and velvety purple flower spikes. It thrives in sunny, hot locations and is drought-tolerant once established.

Best For: Borders, mass plantings, or butterfly gardens, especially on slopes.USDA hardiness zones: 7 to 10Size: 3 feet high and 3 feet wideLight: Partial shade to full sun

Spring is typically the time that plants are plentiful from nurseries, and that’s usually when many gardeners are ready to improve their landscapes. But there are garden centers and online sellers that have stock through fall (and even end-of-season sales) or seeds for fall sowing. Keep these tips in mind for fall planting:

The earlier you can plant spring-blooming perennials in fall, the better. This typically is 6 weeks before the average first frost, so you can often plant perennials in September. This gives plants warm soil with cool nights and time to set roots, which can help prevent frost heave. This happens when thawing of frozen ground pushes plants up out of the soil. If some roots have taken hold and you have mulched the ground, the plant has a better shot. However, avoid planting on hot days or less than a month before frost is expected.

Although rule is a strong word for this principle and doesn’t apply to all flowering perennials, knowing about the “3 years” can help gardeners care for their new plants with realistic expectations about how they will look.  • The first year, most perennials need to grow roots, so they might not show much growth above the ground or flower as advertised; give them extra water to help the roots establish.  • In their second season, plants begin to grow a little more but modestly and might display more flowers.  • By the third year, perennials begin to shine and flower as expected; they also might need pruning.

Yes, fall is a good time to plant many, but not all, perennials. One reason is that you have lived with your landscape for a summer and might be ready to add some color for the next year. Most of all, the combination of still-warm soil but cooler nights helps transplants ease into their new home without the stress of heat or cooler spring soil so the roots have a chance to establish for better spring health. Just be aware of your average first frost date and be sure to count backward when adding spring-flowering plants in fall.

It’s best to wait and plant bare-root plants in late winter to early spring while they still are dormant, not in fall. This can include roses and other shrubs or fruiting trees. Perennial bulbs to plant in fall will bloom in spring, but wait until spring to plant summer-flowering bulbs. Some flowering plants are less hardy to cold and freeze than others. It is best to avoid planting those in fall, especially if you are on the low edge of their hardiness zone. If you live in a cold, damp area, you might want to wait until spring to transplant any flowering perennial subject to root rot, which can occur when roots sit in moist, cool soil.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

Nina Malkin is a published novelist and magazine veteran who has been contributing to BobVila.com since 2016.

Gretchen Heber is a writer, marketer, and entrepreneur based in Texas. A former garden editor and designer with the Austin American-Statesman and Lexington Herald, she is passionate about succulents, herbs, and fruit trees, as well as lighting, energy efficiency, and all things home.

Teresa Odle is a writer and editor who has lived and gardened throughout the mountains of arid New Mexico. She joined the BobVila.com team as a freelancer in March 2020, editing and writing helpful articles mostly on gardening and outdoor living.

#7833. The Best Holiday Decorations Across the U.S., and How to Steal the Look

These homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

Outdoor holiday decorating is an art. And while we love a tasteful string of white Christmas lights or a few pumpkins placed by the front door, why not really go for it when the holiday season rolls around? Over-the-top outdoor holiday decorations make the whole neighborhood get in the festive spirit! To help inspire you, we found some of the best maximalist holiday homes from coast to coast.

From extra spooky Halloween displays to dazzling Christmas spectacles, these homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

A post shared by jessica archibald (@jessicarchibald)

Halloween 2026 has come and gone, but it’s never too early to start thinking about next year! Known simply as The Pumpkin House, @jessicarchibald lines her roof, porch, and yard with hundreds of jack-o’-lanterns every Halloween season. The piles of pumpkins make a big impact both during the day and at night.

Steal This Idea: All you need is pumpkins! Attach faux pumpkins to long boards to make them easier to display on the roof.

The Kraken House (@krakenhousenola) captured here by @amournola, uses blow-up decor to explore the haunted seas. The blow-up tentacles hint at a sea monster hiding beyond the windows, but the dramatic lighting is what really makes this house shine.

Steal This Idea: Skip the kid-friendly Bluey holiday inflatable this year, and attach these terrifying tentacles instead. Then turn up the drama with solar up-lights in green and purple.

Can you believe this amazing black cat is a DIY project? To transform this front porch into a Halloween stage, @allset_bygabrielle hand-carved the cat figure out of wood and painted every detail.

Steal This Idea: In addition to the vintage-inspired cat, the spooky forest framing the door was made with a mix of dead branches and faux botanicals; providing texture and a subtle sparkle.

This front entry in New York City (photographed by @victoria.nycvisit) uses dark drapery, black roses, and a wide variety of unique pumpkins and squashes to create a gothic masterpiece. Trick-or-treaters beware!

Steal This Idea: It’s amazing what a few swathes of black and burgundy fabric can do. Drape the fabric around your front door to make an eerie entrance. Then use pumpkins and vases full of dark flowers to complete the look.

This viral townhouse @stoopandthecity, is dressed to the nines for every holiday. This autumn harvest display features patterned pumpkins and cascades of fall foliage. It’s perfect for Thanksgiving or for those that prefer to skip the ghosts and goblins.

Steal This Idea: Choose faux and glass pumpkins in a cohesive color scheme, and don’t hold back on the fall foliage. Use faux stems to make the display last all season long.

A post shared by Marissa Fiala | Houston, TX (@houstonhotspots)

When it comes to Christmas lights, you can’t find much better than the extravagant homes in the River Oaks neighborhood of Houston, Texas. Each home goes all out with sparkling lights on its exterior, wrapped around every tree.

Steal This Idea: The secret to this colorful tree, captured by @houstonhotspots, is wrapping the lights tightly around the trunk and every single branch. The technique takes time but makes a big impact. Use LED lights to cut back on electricity use.

This famous house on Castro Street in San Francisco does not hold back! (Photo by @415urbanadventures.) Every exterior surface is covered in decor. The symmetrical layout keeps it looking classy instead of gaudy. And of course, the star of the show is Santa hanging in the middle, ready to deliver gifts.

Steal This Idea: The key element of this display is the garland covered in shiny Christmas ornaments. When you think you’ve gathered enough baubles, you’ll probably need even more!

The historic mill in Clifton, Ohio, is known for its over-the-top Christmas light display, featuring over four million lights! While you might not have a historic mill to decorate, the lighting techniques can be used on your own home to dazzle the entire neighborhood.

Steal This Idea: The most memorable element of this display is the iconic red lights cascading down the hillside. Try laying strings lights in rows along your entire yard to get a similar look.

A post shared by Joe Yost | Yost Team -Compass Pittsburgh (@joeyostteam)

Make your house look like one giant Christmas present by adding a larger-than-life red bow. This Pittsburgh mansion is famous for its red Christmas bow that looks beautifully whimsical in the daytime and lights up at night.

Steal This Idea: You don’t need a mansion to recreate this look. Get your own giant red bow and hang it above your front door. Here’s one available on Etsy!

A post shared by Pink Dreams Collection (@pinkdreamscollection)

One way to set your house apart for Christmas is to use a non-traditional color scheme —like pink! This darling cottage from @pinkdreamcollection is a frosted pink confection complete with pink trees and pink nutcracker figurines.

Steal This Idea: Pink or pastel Christmas decor will make your home look playful and unique. Use different shades of pink to add dimension.

A post shared by The Hazard’s Gingerbread House (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse)

This spectacular residential light display by Walter Hazard (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse) makes his home look like a technicolor gingerbread house. The secret is the wire-fencing frames he uses to create methodical light patterns. Visitors come from all over the area to witness the gorgeous lights in action.

Steal This Idea: We might not all have the same light-manipulation talent as Walter, but you can get the same grid-like coverage with LED curtain lights like these.
