#7832. The Best Propane Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

By Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Timothy Dale, Bob Beacham

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Propane heaters are an incredibly effective way to quickly heat a medium to large living space using liquid propane (LP) as fuel, making them suitable for a range of heating needs.

We researched more than 30 propane heaters and then selected several top-rated models for hands-on testing by the Bob Vila test team. We also consulted Alex Rushwin, technical service manager for Enerco Group, manufacturer of the ever-popular Mr. Heater line of propane heaters.

Today’s propane heaters burn cleaner and are safer than early models. “Mr. Heater patented the first indoor propane heater back in 2000,” Rushwin says, “and that was a huge step forward for portable propane heat.” Since then, Mr. Heater has improved on the technology, and their indoor heaters are safer than ever.

Finding the best propane heater for your purposes depends on how you will use it, where it will be used, the heat output you need, and the important safety features included. Our favorite of the bunch was Mr. Heater’s MH9BX model for its portable design and quick heating capabilities. While intended use varies, each of the following models excelled in our hands-on tests and earned its spot in this lineup of the best propane heaters.

Bottom line: Propane heaters are versatile and efficient, with models suited for various spaces and needs. Safety and portability are essential considerations.

The following are some of the best propane heaters on the market in their respective categories. They were selected for quality and price, with a focus on the shopping considerations mentioned above.

Rushwin says that Mr. Heater’s Buddy series is one of its most popular sellers, and it’s been one of our favorites for years, as it was our standby heater for mountain camping adventures. The MH9BX was new to us though, and we were impressed right off the bat by the new swivel-connector feature that allowed us to twist the 1-pound propane bottle into position with ease. Some of the older models didn’t have the swivel connector, so good going, Mr. Heater! That’s a huge plus.

The Buddy MH9BX has an attractive design with a sturdy fold-down carrying handle that makes it easy to pick up and take wherever it’s needed. The heater has a choice of two heat outputs, either 4,000 or 9,000 BTUs, making it capable of heating up to 225 square feet of space. We tested the MH9BX in a 180-square foot room, and on high, it raised the temperature from 70 to 78 degrees Fahrenheit in just 30 minutes. It’s a radiant heater, so it warms objects, not the air, but the heated objects in turn warmed up the room.

This heater is able to burn propane at near-100 percent efficiency, which makes it an option for indoor applications. Its oxygen-depletion sensor (ODS) ensures that the oxygen level never drops to a dangerous point. Plus, its tip-over safety mechanism immediately shut the heater off when we tipped it over.

Read our full review: Mr. Heater MH9BX Portable Buddy Heater

Get the Mr. Heater MH9BX propane heater at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

Our second Mr. Heater pick is the Little Buddy MH4B, which provides instant warmth at an attractive price point. Not only is the Little Buddy easy on the wallet, but it’s also simple to carry along when tailgating or just spending a little time bird-watching on a chilly day. It’s an excellent pick for supplemental indoor emergency heat, too. It burns clean and comes with a low-oxygen sensor that shuts it off if the oxygen level in the space drops to an unhealthy level.

The Little Buddy is designed to heat spaces up to 95 square feet, so we tested it in a bathroom, where it raised the room’s temperature by 15 degrees Fahrenheit in 30 minutes. Keep in mind that temperature increases will vary depending on the type of space, starting temperature, and whether the space is insulated or if it is being used as a tent heater without any insulation.

Like its big brother, the Buddy heater, Little Buddy is a radiant propane heater, and it warms nearby objects—and people. We found it excellent for warming our gloved hands outdoors, but it doesn’t blow hot air. The tip-over shutoff turned the heater off immediately when we laid the Little Buddy on its side.

While this little propane heater isn’t powerful enough for warming up large rooms, it’s an excellent small heater that’s safe for indoor use.

Get the Mr. Heater Little Buddy propane heater at Walmart.

Tank tops aren’t just sleeveless attire for hot summer days. The Camplux Tank Top propane heater attaches to the top of a 20-pound or larger propane tank, and it quickly warms nearby objects or people—making it a handy heater for outdoor use or in ventilated shops and garages.

This is not an in-home model; the manufacturer suggests having a 0.5-square-foot opening for fresh air for every 15,000 BTUs being used. For example, if using both burners simultaneously on the highest setting (total of 30,000 BTUs), opening a 24-inch wide window just 1 inch would be sufficient. A door does not need to be wide open; just crack a window.

It comes with two radiant burners and attaches securely to the steel collar at the top of a standard propane tank. It was easy to connect to the tank and held firmly throughout our tests. We tested the Camplux dual-burner propane heater in a mobile workshop with an open-end wall.

It was simple to connect to the top of the propane tank and easy to light—but be aware this is a manual-light heater; we had to insert a lit match in a hole in the side of the reflective cover and then slowly turn on the propane. It fired right up. Each side lights and operates independently.

The Camplux Tank Top heater provided a lot of radiant heat—so much that we couldn’t stand any closer than about 4 feet without feeling uncomfortably hot when running it on the high setting. On the low setting, it was more tolerable, but it still puts out a lot of heat. It didn’t appreciably raise the temperature in the mobile shop, but that was due to one end of the shop trailer being completely open, which allowed cool breezes to blow through.

This is a powerful, no-frills propane heater for use in a ventilated workshop or on a jobsite.

Get the Camplux propane heater at Amazon.

The East Oak patio heater offers ambience and is a stunning focal point for a chilly outdoor winter gathering, but plan on spending at least an hour or more assembling all the parts. As we were setting it up, more than once we wondered whether the heater would be worth the hassle of trying to peel off the stubborn protective blue film—with some pieces coming off in tiny bits rather than sheets—and then putting together literally everything on the unit.

Once we got the East Oak pyramid heater together and fired up, we changed our minds—it was worth it. The glass cylinder in the pyramid’s center showcases beautiful dancing flames that rise to the upper vent, where the heat is reflected downward and outward toward anyone standing nearby. The outdoor temperature and breezes will affect its heating range, but we could feel warmth when standing about 10 feet away.

This is strictly an outdoor propane heater, so don’t take it in the house—it needs ample ventilation. It comes with tip-over shut-off protection and also shuts down propane flow if the flame goes out to keep propane gas from leaking into the air. We tested both, and they worked well. It connects to a 20-pound propane tank that fits right inside its base.

The East Oak pyramid heater also provides a good amount of light, so it can be used as supplemental lighting for outdoor entertaining. We really liked this tower heater, but we would have been happier with our experience if it had come at least partially assembled. It’s a lot to put together for even those familiar with assembling tools and appliances.

Get the East Oak propane heater at Walmart.

For many DIYers, the garage is the only covered space available for working on projects. Losing that space to cold weather is avoidable when using a propane heater like this one from Mr. Heater, which can heat a space of up to 450 square feet. The heater has three radiant-heat output settings, including a low setting of 6,000 BTUs; a medium setting of 12,000 BTUs; and a high setting that reaches 18,000 BTUs.

We put the MH18CH in a corner in a three-stall garage for testing. It was a chilly day, and also cold the day before testing, so the temperature in the garage was 53 degrees Fahrenheit. We turned the MH18CH on the high setting, and within 30 minutes, the temperature in the nearest stall rose to 61 degrees Fahrenheit, but the farthest stall registered just 54 degrees Fahrenheit. This was in an uninsulated garage, and results would vary in different-size garages or an insulated garage.

The propane heater has a space in the back designed to accommodate a 20-pound propane tank so that users can move the entire unit around easily on the four attached swivel wheels. This product also has a tip-over safety mechanism and an ODS sensor to automatically shut down the heater if the oxygen level gets too low.

This is a nice portable little propane heater that can be rolled around a garage or shop, which is a convenient way to heat the space where work is being done.

Get the Mr. Heater MH18CH propane heater at Lowe’s, Ace Hardware, or The Home Depot.

We examined several factors when choosing the propane heaters we wanted to test. Safety was essential, and beyond that, we looked at heat output (British thermal units, or BTUs), heater type (convection vs. radiant), ease of use, and cost. We considered the brand; after all, Mr. Heater and Dyna-Glo are well-respected names in the propane heater world. Still, we didn’t automatically dismiss smaller niche brands if the heaters were durable, safe, and highly rated.

The actual testing of the heaters was pretty simple; after all, they serve one primary purpose: to warm up a space or warm up nearby objects and people. We noted how easy (or challenging) the heaters were to assemble, and then we connected them to propane tanks or bottles, as called for by the manufacturer.

We tested the heaters’ ignition features and noted how much heat they produced and how quickly. Each propane heater was scored using a rubric. The better the heater performed on a test, the more points we awarded. After testing, we averaged the points to determine our top pick and to establish the best uses for each model.

Before choosing the best propane heater for a patio, garage, or home, take a look below to learn about some of the most important shopping considerations that can help you select a heater that suits your needs.

Propane heaters must have the pilot light ignited before the unit will produce any heat. Keep in mind that igniting the pilot light requires the gas to be turned on. These units typically have one of three different ignition methods: manual ignition, push-button ignition, and continuous ignition.

One of the main benefits of having a propane heater is that they are usually portable and can be connected to a small or large propane tank. It’s relatively easy to take a portable propane heater to another room, to the garage, or to the outdoors. However, if the heater will be used in one or two main locations, the product needs to be suited to those main areas.

In general, only heaters that accommodate 1-pound propane bottles are suitable for use indoors. Those that connect to 20-pound or larger propane tanks should be connected to a hose that’s long enough to locate the tank outdoors. The exception is models designed to hold 20-pound tanks that can be used in ventilated garages or workshops. Read the manufacturer’s safety precautions carefully.

The best outdoor propane heaters have enough heating power to deal with the rapid dissipation of heat that will naturally occur in a wide-open space. For those who want a great camping heater, a large outdoor option might be best. An alternative is a handheld propane heater that will keep people warm instead of heating the entire area. Some users may prefer to have a wall-mounted propane heater to save floor space and to keep the heater out of reach from kids and pets.

Portability is one of the features that sets propane heaters apart from electric or natural gas heaters, but not all propane heaters can really make the claim that they are portable. Some propane heaters that have built-in fans or other electronic components will typically need to be plugged into a power source, despite their main fuel being propane.

If portability is a key personal factor, then a propane heater that doesn’t need an electrical power source is often a better choice. A smaller size and a carrying handle will make it easier to pick up and move around. However, if a larger heater is needed for commercial or industrial applications, there are powerful propane heaters that sit on a set of wheels. The wheels make it easier to move the heater around a space.

Whenever using any type of heating device, it’s critical to be certain that all the necessary precautions are being followed to ensure that no one is at risk. This includes the proper storage of propane tanks and adequate ventilation when the heater is in use. There are other safety features to consider like overheating protection, a tip-over mechanism, and an oxygen-depletion sensor.

The heat output of a propane heater is normally measured in BTUs, with each BTU equal to the heat it would take to increase the temperature of 1 pound of water by 1 degree Fahrenheit. The BTU rating of a propane heater can range widely from as low as 3,000 BTUs to higher than 300,000 BTUs. The best BTU output for a heater will depend on how and where it will be used. For example, outdoor heaters naturally require a higher heat output.

Before deciding on a product, measure the room that needs to be heated. To help figure out which heater is best suited to a particular need, most manufacturers list the BTU output and include the approximate square footage that is appropriate for the heater. For example, a heater with a maximum of 10,000 BTUs may heat a space of approximately 250 square feet, while a unit that has a maximum of 18,000 BTUs will have no problem with 450 square feet.

Size is a factor that can impact where the heater will be used, how it is set up, and whether it’s a portable heater or a stationary unit. A small heater can often be picked up and carried around without a problem. Always check with the manufacturer, but smaller units usually can be used both indoors and outdoors without producing harmful fumes, as these smaller heaters tend to burn fuel at a slower pace.

Large propane heaters can take up a lot of space, which can become a safety hazard if they are too close to flammable objects in the room. Their size also may affect the placement in the room, or it may limit the product to outdoor use. However, a larger propane heater is able to hold an equally large propane tank so it won’t need to be replaced as frequently as the fuel in a small heater.

There are many advantages to owning a propane heater. One of the defining features is that these heaters are typically fueled by a portable container of propane, giving users the freedom to carry them from room to room or even take them out into the middle of the woods when camping. Unless the heater has a built-in fan unit, users won’t have to be tethered to a power outlet with this heater.

There is also the benefit of cost savings with a propane heater. This is because the average cost of electricity is higher than the average cost of propane. With a propane heater, there is a wide range of heat-output options that can increase well beyond the capabilities of an electric or natural gas heater, allowing users to rapidly heat up large outdoor spaces.

Whether you want to supplement heat for a greenhouse or have access to a source of emergency heat when the power goes out, propane could be the answer. If you still have questions about propane heaters, read below to find the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions.

While it’s unlikely, if the propane heater is not designed for indoor use, it could put off some carbon monoxide fumes. If you are using the heater in a larger enclosed space like a garage, make sure that you have a carbon monoxide detector installed to warn you of any danger.

It is generally considered to be a bad idea to have a lit propane heater in your bedroom because it will quickly burn up the oxygen in an enclosed room, which could cause the oxygen levels to drop. Fortunately many of today’s indoor propane heaters, such as those made by Mr. Heater, come with low-oxygen sensors that shut the unit off if the oxygen level in the room drops.

Outdoor propane heaters need proper ventilation to ensure that you don’t get carbon monoxide poisoning. Indoor propane heaters—often called “vent-free” heaters—do not put off carbon monoxide, but ventilation is still necessary to ensure healthy oxygen levels in the room.

While it’s essential to always follow the manufacturer’s directions for safe use, here are the basic steps for how to light a propane heater:1. Turn on the propane tank.2. Adjust the knob on the front or side of the heater to the “start” or “light” position.3. Push the knob in and hold it to send gas to the unit. Continue holding the knob in for 30 seconds to ensure adequate gas flow.4. Press the igniter button firmly until you hear a click. You may need to press it more than once on some heaters.5. Adjust the control knob to the desired temperature.

#7831. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

#7830. Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

My Stanford law school colleagues Nora and David Engstrom, as well as Berkeley law professor Jonah Gelbach and others, have asked the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recommend a new Rule of Civil Procedure (5.3) governing the sealing of court records. I think this is an excellent idea: While there is a good deal of precedent on the question, distilling it into a rule that can easily be consulted by judges, lawyers, law clerks, and pro se litigants would be very helpful.

Just today, Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas (also a former law professor), submitted a letter endorsing the proposed rule, and I thought it was much worth passing along:

Dear Members of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules:

I write to express my strong support for proposed Rule 5.3, a much-needed recapitulation of the procedural standards governing sealing of judicial records.

The public has a presumptive right to access judicial records. This right serves several important societal functions. By exposing the records of private wrongdoing to the public eye, this right deters further wrongdoing. By forcing the government to litigate out in the open, it empowers the public "to keep a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies." Nixon v. Warner Commc'ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 598 (1978). And by enabling the public to dig into the bases for judicial decisions, it enables the public to assure itself of the strength of judicial reasoning, the cornerstone of judicial legitimacy. This right thus not only "diminishes possibilities for injustice, incompetence, perjury, and fraud," but also provides "the public with a more complete understanding of the judicial system and a better perception of its fairness." In re Avandia Mktg., Sales Prac. & Prod. Liab. Litig., 924 F.3d 662, 672 (3d Cir. 2019) (internal quotation marks omitted).

On paper, this right looks strong. In the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where I sit, a district court issuing an order to seal "must articulate the compelling, countervailing interests to be protected" and "make specific findings on the record concerning the effects of disclosure." Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). But that standard is a paper tiger—mighty in appearance, but toothless in practice. Time and again, we see cases on appeal where the parties asked to seal large parts of the record below, and the district court, with little discussion, agreed to do so.

Take one recent motion to seal in a Third Circuit case. The district court had certified a multi-state class action against a car company. On appeal, the company asked us to seal ten volumes of appendices, totaling nearly three thousand pages of material. The company told us that sealing was necessary to prevent competitors from copying its design choices, stealing its engineering solutions, and exploiting its sales strategy.

But it took only a cursory glance at the appendices to see how overbroad the company's request was. Hundreds of pages, for example, covered deposition testimony from one of the plaintiff's lay witnesses, a mechanic who had worked on the defendant's cars and had commented on their alleged defects. Hundreds of other pages dealt with one of the plaintiffs' experts, who had opined on the veracity of the defendant's public comments and sales catalogues. But if the mechanic based his testimony on his day-to-day work on the defendant's cars, and the expert had based his testimony on the company's public statements, how would these materials reveal competitive secrets? So I denied the request without prejudice, asking the company to come back with a narrower request if it so chose. But why had the record below been sealed in the first place?

It should come as little surprise that motions to seal almost always go unopposed. The harm of overbroad sealing falls on future victims of repeat tortfeasors, future litigants in related cases, and the public at large. It does not fall on the parties to the case.

Indeed, the parties generally have an active interest in secrecy. The party who moves to seal records fears that the information produced in the case could lead to bad press coverage, competitive harms, or even follow-on litigation. The other party presumably does not share those same concerns about broad disclosure, but it does not share the public's concerns about overbroad sealing, either.

So in the give-and-take game of litigation, where it can be important to reserve your capital for fighting the fights that matter to your client, opposing a motion to seal is a waste of that capital. At the very least, it is a waste of time and money. For lawyers in an active dispute—so used to viewing themselves as only agents of their clients, and not also officers of the court—submitting an opposition to an overbroad motion to seal might not seem worth the cost of the paper to print it.

This leaves it to district-court judges to police these motions and protect the public's presumptive right of access to judicial records. But what my experience as a judge on the court of appeals has taught me, Professor Engstrom et. al's empirical work now confirms: Most district courts rubber-stamp these requests.

This might come as a surprise to some members of the Judicial Conference. After all, the law of every circuit requires district courts to reject requests to seal that are too broad to be justified by their supposed rationale.

So why do district courts frequently fail to apply that law? One problem might be the lack of developed precedent in this area. Because motions to seal are almost never subject to full treatment in district court opinions, let alone appellate review, there are few decisions applying legal standards to specific facts, teasing out what interests suffice to justify sealing, and how broad is too broad. Without clearly factually analogous precedent to rely on, district courts might be more hesitant to deny a motion to seal as overbroad, even though the operative legal standard compels that result.

Another problem is rooted in the lack of adversarial presentation. With no one on the other side, inflated claims of confidentiality go unchallenged.

Other problems might boil down to the mechanics of busy district court dockets. Perhaps, for example, when a district court grants a protective order, that decision generates an inertial force that skews the outcome of the subsequent motion to seal, even though the two decisions are subject to different legal standards. Or perhaps a motion to seal, because it is unopposed, slips under the radar, resembling an administrative matter to be rubber-stamped rather than a legal decision to be carefully scrutinized.

But whatever the reason, the results are clear: For most motions to seal, "the parties agree, the busy district court accommodates, and nobody is left in the courtroom to question whether the decision satisfied the substantive requirements." Binh Hoa Le v. Exeter Fin. Corp., 990 F.3d 410, 417 (5th Cir. 2021).

This proposed rule will push parties and courts alike to do better. First, this proposed rule will ensure that the parties know what their obligations are when they submit a motion to seal. I often sit by designation on the District of Delaware, where I regularly receive motions to seal with no accompanying explanation or justification, putting the onus on me to push the parties for more. Under Proposed Rule 5.3(c), parties will be reminded that, as our circuit has regularly held, "[b]road allegations of harm, bereft of specific examples or articulated reasoning, are insufficient." In re Avandia Mktg., 924 F.3d at 673 (internal quotation marks omitted).

Second, this proposed rule will act as a process-forcing mechanism for busy district court judges. District courts lack the benefit of adversarial litigation over motions to seal. And without a party opposing a motion, it is easy to think that no reasoning is needed for an order—if no party loses, the thinking goes, no party needs a basis for the court's decision.

Proposed Rule 5.3(h) makes clear that even without an adversarial party, the district court must act as the steward of the public interest in accessing court records, and must reason through its decision. The decision to seal is for the court to make by applying the correct legal standard, not for the parties to make by means of consent. Proposed Rule 5.3(i) provides a checklist that a district court can use in reaching that decision.

Finally, the proposed rule will remind parties and district courts alike that sealing is not an all-or-nothing question. Proposed Rule 5.3(d)(3) and (g) make clear that, where viable, the default approach should be targeted redactions. The choice is not between disclosing a list of social security numbers and sealing an entire document. A happy medium is often readily available.

This proposed rule does not make new law. Sunlight is the best disinfectant for many societal ills, yet sealing "insulates the participants" in the legal process, "masking impropriety, obscuring incompetence, and concealing corruption." Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. F.T.C., 710 F.2d 1165, 1179 (6th Cir. 1983). Judicial reasoning is the basis for judicial legitimacy, yet sealing "withdraws an element of the judicial process from public view," making "the ensuing decision look more like fiat." Matter of Krynicki, 983 F.2d 74, 75 (7th Cir. 1992) (Easterbrook, J.). For these reasons, the courts of appeals have consistently held that the public has a presumptive right to access judicial records, one that should only be abrogated where necessary, and even there only to the extent necessary. This proposed rule simply makes that right harder to neglect.

My then-student Jennifer Welson and I had unsuccessfully proposed a sealing rule to the Rule Committee in 2020, on behalf of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and Electronic Frontier Foundation; but I much hope that the Engstrom et al. proposal, which is backed by considerably more empirical research than mine had been, will be more successful.

#7829. Saudi National Arrested for Installing Surreptitious Audio Recording Device at OpenAI

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.

“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. “I thank Director Patel and our FBI partners for their diligence and swift action. The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”

“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities. Thank you to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and our law enforcement partners for their support — and we will continue working closely with our partners across the U.S. government and private sector to keep American businesses and citizens safe and to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge.”

“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “For us it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.

According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things. The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.

The complaint further alleges that on Oct. 5, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted, as captured below:

Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device (Recording Device 2) similar to Recording Device 1.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker for the Northern District of California is prosecuting the case with valuable assistance from Trial Attorney Kate Tagert of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.

This prosecution is in support of National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11) designed to support American superiority in super intelligence technology.

While many homeowners concentrate on maintaining the ground-level features of their homes, a roof cleaner can help keep the roof looking its best. Often, not until black streaks and patches of moss show up do homeowners realize their roof needs some attention. However, with a good roof washing, even the dirtiest roof can be restored.

While hiring one of the best roof cleaning services is always an option, a roof wash can be a pretty simple DIY job for roofs that are easily accessed. To clean your roof, all you need to do is block out some time, arm yourself with one of the best roof cleaners, and get to work. We evaluated several of the best roof cleaners and even hands-on tested them to provide a list of the products best suited to cut through the dirt, grime, and sludge, revealing your roof’s true colors. After testing, we chose the 30 Seconds Ready-to-Use Outdoor Cleaner as our top pick. We liked it for its versatility, large coverage area, and ease of use.

The cleaners on our list are widely available to order online, so you can have your pick delivered right to your door to save on professional roof cleaning costs. Read on to find out what to look for when shopping so you can choose the best roof cleaners for your needs.

Bottom line: The 30 Seconds Outdoor Cleaner stands out as the best roof cleaner of 2026, offering an effective and user-friendly solution for DIY enthusiasts.

Our Ratings: Ease of Application 5/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Portability 5/5; Ease of Cleanup 5/5; Value 4/5

For a roof wash that really does the job, 30 Seconds Outdoor Cleaner proved to be the best roof cleaner for a variety of reasons. Effective and easy to apply, this product stood out among our group of tested products.

To start with, it actually does live up to its name. Since there’s no mixing of dilution required, all a user has to do is spray it on the surface they want to clean (we tested it on concrete, brick, shingles, and metal roofing), wait 30 seconds (although we found a full minute is even more effective), and then spray it off with a hose. No power-washing is required.

This roof treatment product is also easy to move around with. When you’re climbing on a roof with even a slight pitch, safety is paramount, so it’s important to have a handled container that’s easy to move around with.

The bleach smell is the only thing we didn’t care for with this product; it’s more than faint, but not overpowering. However, wearing a mask or some nose plugs is a small price to pay to get the full effectiveness of 30 Seconds Outdoor Cleaner.

What our tester says: “This was hands-down the most effective cleaner we tested, and wearing a mask for the bleach smell is a small trade-off for how well it works.”—Mike Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the 30 Seconds roof cleaner at Amazon (2-pack) or Do it Best.

There are multiple factors to consider when shopping for an appropriate roof cleaner, from the surface of the roof itself to the specific dirt issues that homeowners are faced with. Our list of recommended products covers the wide array of cleaners available for mold, moss, and mildew to provide the best suggestions for each scenario.

To choose which products to test, we scoured the web for customer reviews, researched all products being considered, and looked for products that we felt could stand up to the rigorous testing we had planned. Since heavy-duty solutions often use bleach and other harsh chemicals, which are not always what shoppers are looking for, we made sure to also include a product that’s more environmentally friendly.

Our testing process included a start-to-finish cleaning session with each product. We applied the roof cleaner by following the instructions on each product, then followed the instructions for cleaning. A typical test had us spraying the product on the affected area of roof, allowing it to sit for an amount of time defined on the product’s instructions (sometimes doing a little scrubbing), and then rinsing the product away.

This section will outline the most important considerations to keep in mind while you’re shopping for the best roof cleaner for your home. It covers aspects including the different types of roofing materials, how much coverage you’ll get, and how easy the products are to use.

Don’t rush out and set up the ladder quite yet. You first need to educate yourself on the different types of roof cleaners available. They all work a little differently, and some are much harsher on the environment than others. It’s important to do a little research before you choose the best roof cleaner for your needs.

For particularly stubborn stains and discolorations, beach-based cleaners might be the way to go. They’re so strong, in fact, that you don’t even need to scrub or rinse down the roof for them to work. Simply apply them to the roof and let them dry. The bleach will eat through the dirt and grime all on its own.

The thing about bleach-based chemicals, though, is that they’re extremely harsh. Breathing in their vapors can cause coughing, lung irritation, and shortness of breath. Any overspray (or runoff when it rains) can wreak havoc on your plants. These cleaners are so strong, in fact, that it’s best to keep your windows closed for a few days to avoid the fumes and odors.

Bleach isn’t the only chemical manufacturers use to restore a roof to its former glory. Some formulas feature ammonia, copper sulfate, and trisodium phosphate, all of which can do a great job of removing the stains, molds, and mosses that grow on roofs.

These formulas can be harsh on your plants as well, though usually to a lesser degree than bleach-based cleaners. They rarely require the user to scrub or apply a second application, and in most cases, there’s no need to keep your windows closed after application. Since they usually come in concentrates, they typically need to be mixed with water unless you have a really stubborn stain.

If you’re looking for a safer, less environmentally detrimental approach to cleaning your roof, check out an eco-friendly cleaner. These formulas break up the dirt, algae, and mold on your roof without the inherent dangers of chemical and bleach compounds.

Eco-friendly cleaners are safe for your kids, plants, and the wildlife that might roam through your property. While it’s entirely possible to have some type of allergic reaction to these products, they’re generally safe to use and less irritating.

Since eco-friendly cleaners tend to use oxygen to break down dirt and roof-loving molds and algae, they work best with a bit of agitation. You’ll likely have to scrub most of your stains and discolorations away, so having a long-handled brush will be incredibly helpful.

If you want to blast your roof clean, you can always set up a pressure washer and get to work. The pump inside your pressure washer boosts the amount of pressure with which the water comes out of the nozzle, knocking dirt and film clear off your roof shingles.

But pressure washers can also blast your roof shingles right off, so take care when you’re doing any kind of roof pressure washing.

To help increase your pressure washer’s effectiveness, there are many products available that can be mixed into the water. If you don’t use a chemical, though, be aware that water alone might not kill any residual moss and algae.

Raw chlorine, also known as sodium hydrochlorite, cleans a roof while also killing mold and mildew spores. This compound is made to sanitize, removing bacteria at the same time it cleans up stains and grime. When diluting, it’s important to ensure that raw chlorine solutions never comprise more than 30 percent of the roof cleaning solution, and it’s important that they’re thoroughly rinsed off after use.

The first thing you’ll want to consider are all the materials that make up your roof to ensure you use the right product.

Less-durable materials like vinyl and rubber membranes found on flat roofs or RVs are particularly susceptible to damage from harsh chemicals. Heavy-duty cleaners can wear down the roofing components faster than if you used an eco-friendly option.

Tougher materials, like asphalt, metal, or slate roofs, can take much stronger chemicals. You’ll be able to use bleach or chemical-based cleaners without worrying about what they’ll do to your roof’s finish.

The best roof cleaners can be broken down into two options: eco-friendly and chemical. Eco-friendly options don’t contain harmful chemicals, so they’re safe to use on roofs above gardens and plants. The composition of chemical-based products, on the other hand, isn’t always so environmentally conscious.

Chemical-based cleaners often use chemicals such as ammonia, copper sulfate, and trisodium phosphate. They can be harsh, but they’re extremely effective at removing the stains as well as the molds, algae, and mosses that cause them. Simply diluting them to the manufacturer’s recommended mixture does reduce some of the risk, so it’s important to read and follow the directions carefully.

Not all roof cleaners can cover the same amount of square footage, so it’s important to understand how much roof a bottle or jug can handle. To do this, you have to know the size of your roof first: Simply multiply each section of your roof’s width by its height. Tally each of those sections. The number you get after you add up all the different planes is your square footage.

Some of the best roof cleaners come in concentrated formulas that you can dilute for maximum coverage. While their bottles might be small, they can often cover thousands of square feet of roof if you dilute them correctly.

Cleaning your roof isn’t all that much fun, so the process should be made as painless as possible. Finding a user-friendly product can make all the difference.

A chemical that you can spray on your roof and leave to do its work is by far the easiest way to clean your roof. Other chemicals might require you to scrub the surface, which can be a challenge if you have a high roof.

Also, consider the application. Although spray bottles are easy to use, covering a large area with a spray bottle is difficult, so they’re ideal for smaller roofs. Concentrate bottles that attach to the end of your hose make applying the chemical to larger roofs extremely easy, but you might not be able to reach high peaks from the ground. Whatever product you choose, be sure to select one that you can apply easily to your particular roof.

Ultimately, how well the product works at removing stains, molds, algae, and discolorations is one of the most important factors to keep in mind. The more effective the product, the fewer coats you’ll have to apply, and the less often you’ll have to apply it.

Less-effective products don’t always kill the root cause of the discoloration, even if the stain disappears. If that root is still present, there’s a good chance that whatever caused the stain will come back. This means you’ll have to apply your product more often to keep up with it.

Harsh chemicals are by far the most effective way to get rid of stains and often require just one application. However, using eco-friendly products might require you to commit to more frequent cleanings or follow-up applications.

For those who have additional questions about choosing or using the best roof cleaner, this section contains answers to some of the most frequently asked questions.

Many of the best roof cleaner manufacturers recommend cleaning your roof every 12 to 24 months to ensure your roof stays clean and free from growths. But whenever you notice discoloration, moss, mold, or mildew, it’s a good idea to give your roof a spray.

It depends on the cleaner. Many of the heaviest-duty cleaners will damage vinyl or fabric awnings, while some biodegradable or lighter-duty cleaners will work quite well. However, it’s important to always refer to the product label before use.

Most roof cleaners are available in concentrated forms, and you can mix them to whatever strength you’d like. If you’re planning to use yours at full strength, it’s a good idea to test it on a smaller space first to see how it affects your surface.

There are a few steps you can take to minimize your roof cleaner’s impact on your plants.1. Cover your plants in tarps or plastic sheeting.2. Use only as much chemical as necessary.3. Ensure your gutters aren’t clogged so any chemical-laden rainwater can flow away from the eaves.4. Water your plants heavily before, during, and after using your cleaner. Diluting the concentration of chemicals is the best way to lessen the risk of damage.

Basic safety items like goggles, a respirator, and gloves are certainly important. You can also wear long sleeves. Using a long-handled brush or roller, or a garden sprayer, can make applying your roof cleaner easier.

#7827. 5 Annual Flowers I Bring Indoors to Brighten Winter

Published Nov 5, 2026 10:34 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

I like to grow exotic species indoors for flowering during the winter months, either under grow lights or on a sunny windowsill. However, I also save a few annuals from my garden, usually container types that don’t require large amounts of light to flourish. After all, annuals are easy to bring into flowering, while some tropicals and other perennials can be challenging to coax into bloom.

Plants like geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) and flowering maples (Abutilon spp.) can be long-blooming indoor annual flowers. In addition, the annuals listed below can often bloom longer indoors, extending the life of your annual flowers and brightening rooms in winter.

Although I bring tuberous begonias indoors over winter, I always let them die back to their tubers, since they require a period of dormancy to bloom well the following summer. However, I’ve found that other begonia species such as the wax begonia (B. semperflorens) will flower cheerfully almost year-round. After all, its species name means “ever-blooming.”

I’ve learned to be careful not to overwater the plants during winter as I have had favorites, including the double-flowered cultivar pictured above, succumb to root rot. But otherwise, wax begonias are easy-care plants that can add indoor winter color.

Common impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) plants flower busily both outdoors and indoors. Because they root easily in water, I often take cuttings of them in late summer to pot up later, but sometimes just prune back a mature plant to bring inside.

The semidouble type of Busy Lizzy is seldom available in my area, so I saved one of my I. walleriana ‘Athena’ plants last autumn, and it continued to perform under the lights over winter and in the container pictured in the banner image this summer. I’ve occasionally also grown more unusual cultivars of impatiens under lights, including Giant Balsam (I. grandis, pictured above) and rare species such as Blue Diamond Impatiens (I. namchabarwensis).

Coleus cuttings also root quickly in water. That’s a good thing because the Big Bad Boys cultivar I grew this summer lived up to its name by eventually growing to 2 feet, even when packed into a container with other shade-loving annuals. So, I will need to take cuttings or prune the plant to restore it to a suitable size for grow lights.

Since coleus annuals, such as the blazingly red type above, are grown for their boldly colored foliage rather than their nondescript blooms, I usually try to pinch out any bud stalks that sprout. Otherwise, these are easy-care indoor annual flowers.

Due to their preference for cool and somewhat humid conditions, fuchsias often do well under my basement grow lights. And, yes, their cuttings, too, will root easily in water should you not want to bring an entire hanging basket indoors.

As with most annuals, fuchsias won’t bloom as heavily in the house as they do outside, but they will make some flowers. I believe those pictured—blooming under lights one late December—are the elegantly elongated Bolivian fuchsia (F. boliviana). But the typical hanging basket type called Lady’s Eardrops (F. magellanica) also will perform as indoor winter plants under the right conditions.

I have a very old Lantana camara plant with a large, gnarled and knotted trunk that looks more like a bonsai specimen than a potted annual. But it proves that lantanas, also called shrub verbenas, can last almost indefinitely if protected during winter. In fact, they can be perennial plants in warm growing zones.(7 to 11).

However, I’ve found that my plant will drop most of its leaves after being brought indoors. It isn’t dying, just adapting to new light levels. It might qualify as one of the fragrant indoor plants since its leaves have a peculiar odor that some people compare to citrus and others to gasoline.

Because my windows are drafty and don’t receive much illumination during winter, I place most of my flowering indoor plants under grow lights, either fluorescent or LED. (I am gradually switching over to the latter, since they make more light while using less energy.)

I use 4-foot fixtures and keep most of the plants in the basement, where conditions are cooler and more humid than in the rest of the house. Since some of my plants require short days to bloom, I keep the lights on timers so they are on for no more than 12 hours per day.

These full-spectrum grow light panels are lightweight and low-heat, making them our top pick for boosting indoor plants during winter.

One problem with having tropical plants and other flowering annuals in the basement is that out of sight often means out of mind. So, I have to remember to trudge down the stairs with a watering can at least once per day. Since it is easy to accidentally overwater plants in winter, I test the surface of their soil with a fingertip first and only water when that surface is dry.

If a plant is blooming, I often bring it upstairs to enjoy before returning it to its original position under the lights. That is my way of feeding my flower addiction during winter.

#7826. Fifth Circuit on Pseudonymity of Libel Defendant (Who Claims She Was Sexually Assaulted)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Doe v. Roe, decided today by Fifth Circuit Judges Jennifer Walker Elrod, Carolyn Dineen King, and Carl Stewart:

After receiving notice of Jane Roe's impending California lawsuit involving allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment, John Doe sued Roe in the Southern District of Mississippi, alleging that Roe was attempting to extort and defame him. Roe moved to proceed pseudonymously in the Mississippi lawsuit. The district court denied her permission to do so. Roe appeals that decision, raising several concerns with the district court's analysis. Because we agree with some of Roe's arguments, we vacate and remand for the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously….

Roe argues that allegations of sexual assault involve matters of the utmost intimacy [and can thus justify pseudonymity]. We agree. There is no doubt that requiring alleged rape and sexual assault victims to proceed "under their real identities would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." It is no surprise, then, that numerous courts have allowed alleged victims of sexual misconduct to proceed under a pseudonym, "including when they are defendants being sued for libel and related torts."

We agree with Roe. To start, we are not persuaded that the proverbial cat is out of the bag here. True, publicly available information cannot be obscured by courts. However, that internet sleuths might speculate that Roe is a particular person because her California complaint "lines up with [her] public profile" is not the same as a public broadcasting of Roe's certain identity. As to the fact that Roe's name was a matter of public record for short periods, that was either because of Doe's actions (which Roe objected to), or Roe's inadvertent disclosures which counsel corrected and constituted no waiver (which we address below)….

Last, Roe argues that she did not waive her right to proceed anonymously. Again, we agree. Roe never waived her ability to request pseudonymity because her conduct does not constitute an "intentional relinquishment" of that position. Roe's opposition to Doe's motion to proceed pseudonymously waived nothing because Roe's position was that she should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously while he should not be. And any confusion about Roe's position based on the precise language in her opposition brief was clarified by her own subsequent motions seeking to seal or redact Doe's amended complaint (which used Roe's real name) and to proceed pseudonymously.

Further, Doe's use of Roe's real name in open court did not constitute waiver on Roe's behalf because, at the time, Doe had already publicly named Roe in his amended complaint, Roe had a pending motion seeking to seal or redact that amended complaint naming her, and Roe objected to the use of her name at the hearing (even if not as fast as a prudent attorney likely should have). Finally, we are not convinced that Roe's inadvertent disclosures of her real name in the California case and on this appeal constitute waiver. The disclosures were unintentional, were made in portions of larger filings, and Roe took steps to correct the errors once becoming aware of them, resulting in the sealing and refiling of the documents. These facts do not demonstrate that Roe intentionally relinquished her request to proceed pseudonymously….

In light of the clarifications provided in this opinion, we find that it is appropriate to allow the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be permitted to proceed under a pseudonym in this case. {We acknowledge Doe's argument that allowing Roe to proceed under a pseudonym would be prejudicial to him. We think that argument is best left for the district court to address in the first instance on remand.}

NEXT: Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7821. Justice Department Announces Coordinated Actions to Combat North Korean Remote IT Worker Schemes Affecting More Than 70 U.S. Companies

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through remote information technology (IT) work for U.S. companies. These actions include an indictment, two arrests, searches of multiple known or suspected “laptop farms” in Texas pursuant to “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used by DPRK IT workers.

“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These schemes threaten the security of the IT systems and data of the deceived U.S. employers and leave countless victims of identity theft. NSD, along with our law enforcement partners, will use every available tool to track down anyone assisting the DPRK and to protect our national security.”

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

“North Korea continues to deploy remote IT workers using stolen identities to infiltrate American companies and generate revenue for the regime and its weapons programs,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “Today, the FBI and DOJ announced a series of coordinated actions against this threat, securing charges against 14 individuals, conducting two arrests, seizing nearly 190 devices, and executing operations at more than 40 suspected ‘laptop farms’ across Texas. Close coordination between the private sector and federal law enforcement was central to this operation. To further combat the threat, the FBI has issued a Public Service Announcement with detailed mitigation guidance for U.S. companies.”

Sun Sheng Ming, et al. Indictment and Arrests – Northern District of Ohio

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced the arrests of U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas pursuant to a four-count wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft indictment. The indictment describes a multi-year fraud scheme by Bostelle, Pena, and their co-conspirators to obtain remote IT work with U.S. companies that generated more than $3 million in revenue. The indictment also charges China-based Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang, Jin Long for their roles in the scheme. The identities of two additional defendants remain under seal.

According to the indictment, from 2019 to in or around July 2025, DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure to appear as though they were U.S. persons working from within the United States. They also relied on U.S.-based facilitators who received and hosted multiple laptop computers — issued by victim U.S. companies — at their residences in the United States (“laptop farms”), housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts.

In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK. Victim employers included companies in the health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio, sixteen additional states, and the District of Columbia.

The FBI Cleveland Field Office is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Duncan T. Brown for the Northern District of Ohio and Trial Attorney Neeraj Gupta of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case.

Operation Lonestar Roundup Disrupts Multiple Known or Suspected Laptop Farms in Texas

Between Sept. 21 and Sept. 25, the FBI conducted searches and other law enforcement action at over 40 residences in Texas known to be, or suspected of operating as, laptop farms for DPRK IT workers. Over the course of the entire operation (Operation Lonestar Roundup), the FBI seized approximately 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices that DPRK IT workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used to commit fraud, obtain remote employment, and generate revenue for the North Korean regime’s sanctioned weapons programs. U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has identified this group of DPRK IT workers and their helpers as “Famous Chollima.”

Investigators discovered that the DPRK operatives allegedly used a network of fraudulent email accounts to facilitate their criminal activity. The following accounts were among those identified as being used in these schemes:

Employers are encouraged to add these accounts to the list of indicators they use to identify and disrupt DPRK IT worker employment.

Today, the FBI published a public service announcement describing the evolving DPRK IT worker threat, including tips on how to detect the threat. Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Additionally, CrowdStrike today published a blog post describing its efforts at monitoring customer networks for DPRK IT worker activity and its successful collaboration with the FBI to disrupt this threat.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, the FBI’s Dallas Field Office, and the FBI’s Cyber Division coordinated Operation Lonestar Roundup. Valuable assistance was provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio.

Today’s announcements represent the Department’s latest actions to combat North Korean IT worker schemes as part of a joint NSD and FBI Cyber and Counterintelligence Divisions effort, the DPRK RevGen: Domestic Enabler Initiative. This effort prioritizes targeting and disrupting the DPRK’s illicit revenue generation schemes and its U.S.-based enablers. The Department previously announced other actions pursuant to the initiative, including in June 2025, November 2025, April 2026, and May 2026.

As described in Public Service Announcements published in May 2024, January 2025, July 2025, and today, North Korean remote IT workers posing as legitimate remote IT workers have committed data extortion and exfiltrated the proprietary and sensitive data from U.S. companies. DPRK IT worker schemes typically involve the use of stolen identities, alias emails, social media, online cross-border payment platforms, and online job site accounts, as well as false websites, proxy computers, and witting and unwitting third parties located in the U.S. and elsewhere. North Korean IT workers leverage these third parties, which include U.S.-based individuals, to gain fraudulent employment and access to U.S. company networks to generate this revenue.

Other public advisories about the threats, red flag indicators, and potential mitigation measures for these schemes include a May 2022 advisory released by the FBI, Department of the Treasury, and Department of State; a July 2023 advisory from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and guidance issued in October 2023 by the United States and the Republic of Korea (South Korea). As described the May 2022 advisory, North Korean IT workers have been known individually to earn up to $300,000 annually, generating hundreds of millions of dollars collectively each year, on behalf of designated entities, such as the North Korean Ministry of Defense and others directly involved in the DPRK’s weapons programs.

The U.S. Department of State has offered potential rewards for up to $5 million in support of international efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s illicit financial activities, including for cybercrimes, money laundering, and sanctions evasion.

The details in the above-described court documents are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
