#7820. The Best Cordless Screwdrivers for Furniture Assembly, Repairs, and Tight Spots

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:47 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The right cordless screwdriver depends on the job. Compact models suit light household tasks, while more powerful ones handle dense wood.

An adjustable clutch helps prevent stripped or overdriven screws, especially on higher-torque models.

Cordless screwdrivers speed up furniture assembly, cabinet adjustments, and other jobs that require driving or removing a lot of screws. We tested 12 top models to see how each one performed.

A good cordless screwdriver should be comfortable to hold, easy to control, and powerful enough for the work you have in mind. Leading our lineup of top-rated screwdrivers is the Milwaukee M12 ¼-Inch Hex Screwdriver Kit. Its 15-position clutch offers precise control, while its 12-volt battery gives it the power to drive screws into tougher wood than the lighter-duty models can manage.

With so many types of cordless screwdrivers to choose from, the right choice also depends on where you’ll use it. For instance, a compact inline driver may be easier to maneuver inside furniture, while a pistol-grip model can provide more power. Ahead, we explain what to look for and how the tested models compare so you can choose the best cordless screwdriver for your projects.

To earn a spot in our lineup, a cordless screwdriver had to be easy to use, durable, and capable of everyday fastening tasks, with a battery that lasted through small projects. We drove screws into drywall, pine, and birch, and tested the new models in prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood to see where each performed best. The picks below offer useful options for projects around your home or workshop.

Right out of the box, the first thing we noticed about the Milwaukee M12 was its weight. At just over 2 pounds with the battery installed, it’s heavier than many cordless screwdrivers, but it fits nicely in the palm and isn’t too cumbersome for installing multiple screws. It made quick work of inserting screws in drywall, and we were able to insert screws in both pine and birch boards as well.

The M12 is less about fancy features and more about getting the job done. This pistol-grip screwdriver uses Milwaukee’s 12-volt lithium-ion batteries to create a mighty peak torque of 175 inch-pounds. It has an RPM range of up to 500, which makes setting fasteners quick work. The 2401-22 model uses a ¼-inch quick-change keyless chuck to swap out bits quickly, and it features a 15-position clutch to help regulate torque. We were also able to switch into drill mode to cancel the clutch feature.

Get the Milwaukee cordless screwdriver at The Home Depot or Ace Hardware.

As soon as we slipped the charged 12-volt battery into the Bosch PS21-2A cordless screwdriver and pulled the trigger, we could tell it offered more torque than most. It has two speed ranges we were able to switch between by sliding a lever on the top of the tool. The screwdriver generates up to 1,300 RPM at top speed, which is quite an accomplishment for an automatic screwdriver.

It also packs some powerful torque, which meant we were able to insert screws with ease into drywall, pine, and birch boards. With that much torque, the 21-adjustment clutch is essential to prevent stripping out the screw heads.

In addition to ample torque and speed, this screwdriver is compact, with a head length of just more than 5.5 inches. It comes with two 12-volt batteries and a charger. Plus, there’s a built-in LED light to help users see in dim locations, but it would be better if it were brighter. If DIYers want a cordless screwdriver to tackle some heavy-duty jobs, the Bosch PS21-2A ought to do the trick. It’s a powerful tool in a small package, weighing just 1.4 pounds.

Get the Bosch cordless screwdriver at Amazon or Lowe’s.

If your goal is to find a budget-friendly, light-duty cordless power screwdriver that won’t crush screws, the Black+Decker 4V MAX cordless screwdriver may fit the bill. We were impressed by its versatile features and even more impressed by its budget-friendly price. While this tool doesn’t generate as much torque as some picks in our lineup, it still drove drywall screws quickly. It wasn’t as successful with wood, but that’s not what this tool is intended to do.

This screwdriver has a three-position handle that swaps easily from a straight screwdriver to a 45-degree or right-angle driver in seconds. It uses ¼-inch driver bits, so users can swap between bits or employ the chuck as a ¼-inch nut driver.

The screwdriver boasts an unusually bright LED flashlight, making it easy to see in dark areas. The 4-volt, battery-operated screwdriver comes with two bits and a charger. Its 4-volt lithium-ion battery held a charge well throughout the testing, and this model features a built-in battery and a simple charger cord that plugs in directly.

Get the Black+Decker cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

For all those little household fastener chores, such as installing outlet and switch plates, tightening cabinet or drawer screws, or hanging pictures on a wall, we think this lightweight Makita cordless screwdriver set is just the ticket. At just 3.6 volts, this cordless screwdriver is designed for light-duty applications, and it excels at that.

Instead of requiring the user to remove a battery, the DF001DW has an internal battery that charges via a USB cord plugged into a computer’s USB port or a standard outlet using the included AC adapter. We tested the DF001DW by inserting and removing screws in drywall and wood. It comes with an ample 81-piece accessory set boasting bits for most types of screw fasteners used today, including Phillips, flathead, and star bit. Plus, the tool has an LED guide light that can be turned on when desired (it doesn’t stay on automatically when the screwdriver is in use).

The DF001DW also converts from a pistol grip to a straight-barrel grip, making it even more versatile. It weighs less than a pound, so it didn’t slow us down—yet it offered ample power for inserting and removing screws, even in wood, without the tool’s motor bogging down.

Get the Makita 3.6V cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

The Kobalt is a compact screwdriver best suited to the small fastening jobs that crop up around the house. We tested it on dozens of screws, including fasteners for prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood. At just 0.49 pounds, it was easy to maneuver while assembling furniture, and the soft-grip handle made it comfortable to hold through a string of screws.

Its 280-RPM motor runs at one speed, so there’s no trigger control for easing a screw into place. It also lacks an adjustable clutch to limit torque. We found it most useful for driving screws into prepared holes, where its 13.5 inch-pounds of maximum torque are better matched to the task. For screws going directly into raw wood, especially as resistance increased, we’d reach for a more powerful driver. The built-in LED helps illuminate the screw head, and the charge indicator lets us check the battery before starting a project.

The kit comes with a range of bits, a magnetic bit holder, a case, and a USB-C charging cable. That makes it convenient to keep together for furniture assembly and quick repairs.

Get the Kobalt cordless screwdriver at Lowe’s.

Having previously believed the power to an outlet was shut off only to suffer painful shocks, we know the value of being able to test an outlet in a pinch. So we were pretty impressed with the Skil cordless screwdriver’s ability to sense if the outlet was still hot, just by depressing a button on the top of the tool. The Skil emitted a sharp warning beep when we tested a hot outlet, and a red light flashed. When we tested a dead outlet, there was neither a light nor a beep. This built-in safety feature is a boon for those who don’t typically carry electrical testers around while doing DIY projects.

This compact cordless screwdriver boasts a dual-LED light, 10 changeable bits, and a micro USB charger. The chuck accepts any ¼-inch drive bit and also functions as a ¼-inch nut driver. It has both forward and reverse, but no adjustable clutch or speed settings. While it inserted screws effortlessly into drywall, it bogged down when driving screws into wood boards. Still, it’s so good at sensing circuits that you could reserve this cordless screwdriver solely for electrical maintenance jobs.

Get the Skil cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Menards, or Acme Tools.

The Amazon Basics (formerly Denali) screwdriver doesn’t boast many bells and whistles, but it lets you choose from three torque settings. We found that handy when inserting screws into materials with different densities—for instance, more torque when inserting screws in wood than in softer drywall. It also features an LED guide light, but we found it to be dim and unlikely to offer much illumination in low-light situations.

The screwdriver charges via a USB-C cord (included). We liked this setup, as it simplifies charging—no need to remove and charge the battery separately. A compact tool measuring about 7 inches long, it was useful in restricted spots, but we would have liked a convertible grip. A barrel grip is excellent in some situations, but a convertible pistol grip would add versatility.

The only real downside we noted was that this model tended to bog down a little when we inserted screws in wood. It did the job, but it took longer than it did on drywall. Still, this is a handy little cordless screwdriver to have around the house or to keep in the trunk of a car for when small jobs arise.

Get the Amazon Basics cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

We tested 12 cordless screwdrivers from 10 brands, considering price, battery design, included accessories, grip, speed, torque control, and features such as work lights and interchangeable heads. We drove dozens of fasteners with each tool, using prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood; earlier tests also included drywall, pine, and birch.

We noted how comfortably each screwdriver fit in the hand, how easily we could change bits and direction, and whether the screwdriver had enough power to seat screws without damaging their heads. After testing, we rated each model on a five-point scale for ease of use, build quality, performance, and value, using those scores and our hands-on notes to select the picks in this guide.

A slim cordless screwdriver can reach spots a drill can’t as easily. A cordless screwdriver drives screws faster than a manual screwdriver and reduces wrist strain by eliminating the need for repeated wrist motions. Its light weight and battery power also make it easy to carry from one task to the next. As you shop, consider where you’ll use it and how much power and control your projects require.

The more power a cordless screwdriver has, the faster it can turn. While cordless screwdrivers don’t require the amount of power that a drill driver or an impact driver might have, they still need enough juice to get the job done. If you’re purchasing a straight barrel-type driver, consider one with a speed between 300 and 500 RPM. This range is ideal for loosening or tightening a screw quickly without being too fast to handle. With pistol-grip models, speeds above 1,000 RPM are easier to control.

The more torque your screwdriver has, the denser the material that it can drive a fastener into. Heavy-duty screwdrivers provide more torque and may be suitable for driving a few drywall screws into wood studs, but this can drain the battery quickly.

Small cordless screwdrivers can reach and manipulate various types of screws into awkward spaces much more easily than a manual tool can. As long as there’s room for the tip of the driver to fit onto the fastener, you’re set—a powered screwdriver will help do the rest.

To fit into such tight places, the best cordless screwdrivers are highly maneuverable. A slim, compact design helps, and many models also have rotating handles that swap from a straight grip to a pistol grip, like those seen on drills and screw guns. Also, a smaller battery size makes cordless screwdrivers easier to tuck between boards and other low-clearance scenarios, such as behind sinks for plumbing tasks.

Many cordless screwdrivers come with rechargeable batteries, and they tend to range between 4 and 8 volts. Since a cordless screwdriver requires much less speed and power than a drill, these lower voltages are adequate. Two benefits of a smaller, lower-voltage battery? It fits in smaller places than full-size options, and it helps make the rechargeable screwdriver as light as possible.

Some lower-end screwdrivers use replaceable batteries. These models are less convenient and more expensive, since you have to replace batteries frequently. They usually have less power and torque as well.

If you have a large project coming up, it helps if a cordless screwdriver has enough power to see it through to the end. Luckily, battery life isn’t much of a concern for most of the best cordless screwdrivers because their small motors don’t use as much battery energy as a large motor does.

However, some cordless screwdrivers have a battery-level indicator that alerts users when the battery is running low. It’s helpful to know the battery status so that you can juice it up while on a lunch or supply-run break. Many models take about an hour to recharge.

Cordless screwdrivers tighten or loosen screws in prethreaded holes. They’re perfect for screws in electrical boxes and fixtures, screws used in automotive interiors and appliances, installing door locks and cabinet hardware, and other mechanical settings with threaded holes.

Except for the most heavy-duty electrical screwdrivers, these tools aren’t typically designed for lag screws and bolts, wood screws, or fasteners in other dense materials. While it’s technically possible to drive a screw through drywall with one of these tools, that’s simply not the type of job they’re made for. For this situation, grab a drill or an impact driver instead.

Cordless screwdrivers use toolless chucks, so swapping between bits is quick and easy. These chucks fit ¼-inch bits—the same bits used in standard multi-bit manual screwdrivers. There are also ¼-inch-drive drill bits, allowing a screwdriver to be used as a drill in light-duty material like thin wood or plastics.

The variety of ¼-inch bits available makes cordless screwdrivers incredibly useful: For instance, you can alternate from driving Phillips head screws to removing Allen or Torx screws in seconds. Most cordless screwdrivers use magnets to hold the bits in place while also providing a bit of magnetism to keep the screw on the end of the bit.

The clutch in fastening tools regulates the amount of torque applied to a fastener. Once the set torque is reached, the clutch will start to “slip,” preventing the tool from driving the fastener or drilling any deeper. Simply adjust the clutch according to the fastener and material type. Since this is situation-specific, the rule of thumb is to set the clutch to a low setting and increase slowly as needed.

Too much torque can break smaller, older, or low-quality fasteners. Fortunately, the best cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutch settings to avoid stripping or breaking these fasteners. The clutch can also avoid overdriving the screw too deeply, which may also cause unwanted results.

Torque settings can make a significant difference when working with old, stubborn fasteners. Instead of tearing the heads off screws or stripping the fastener beyond recognition, the clutch will begin to slip, preventing the driver from continuing to turn and causing damage.

Not all cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutches, though. Some don’t have the power to require one. However, higher-end screwdrivers with more torque usually do.

By the time a project with a lot of assembly is finished, your forearm and hand might be tired from using a manual screwdriver. Lesson learned: To forgo hand and arm fatigue, opt for a cordless screwdriver. This’ll also save you energy and time, allowing you to move on to the next project faster.

Being able to see what you’re doing is key to a quality finished project. If, while using a drill, the tool keeps getting in the way, it may slip off the screw, marring the surface or scratching the workpiece. Cordless screwdrivers let users see what they’re doing since a hand won’t block the view.

Instead of carrying several screwdrivers around in a tool box or tool belt, it can be easier to tote just one cordless model. Since the bits are easy to swap, a complete bit set can reduce the overall weight and free up space in a belt for other tools. It’s much easier to carry one cordless screwdriver with eight tips than eight separate screwdrivers.

A cordless screwdriver is a tool that many reach for again and again for a host of different tasks. Here are a few ways to get the most help from this handy tool.

There’s a lot to consider when choosing a new cordless screwdriver, so you may still have questions. If you’re still wondering about the ins and outs of cordless screwdrivers, check out these answers to some commonly asked questions.

A cordless screwdriver is a battery-powered tool that tightens and loosens screws with a motor and trigger rather than relying on hand power.

Cordless drills for DIYers accept several drill bit sizes with adjustable chucks, while mini cordless screwdrivers only accept ¼-inch bits. Also, cordless drills tend to be more adjustable in terms of speed, letting the user drill into different materials accurately and efficiently.

There are a few slightly different methods for operating a cordless screwdriver, but here is a general usage guideline:1. Choose the right bit and place it in the chuck.2. Adjust the direction you want to drive the screw (tighten or loosen) with the switch on the screwdriver.3. Seat the bit completely into the head of the screw.4. Maintain pressure on the fastener and squeeze the trigger.

Yes, higher voltage tends to be better for cordless tools, but there are some caveats. Cordless tools with higher voltages are certainly more powerful, but that power comes at a cost. They weigh more and are less compact than lower-voltage options. For cordless screwdrivers, 4 to 8 volts is usually sufficient, especially for light-duty tasks.

Yes, but it depends on how often you’ll use them and the tasks you do most often. They can save quite a bit of time and effort and can increase your efficiency, all at a typically affordable price.

#7819. What Does a Green Porch Light Mean? The Tradition, Explained

By Savannah Sher, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 5, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

In November, you may notice your neighbors replacing their white porch light bulbs with green bulbs. While it’s easy to assume that they’re getting a head start on their Christmas decorating, green porch lights have a significance that has nothing to do with the holiday season. Americans use green porch lights to show support for U.S. military veterans. The idea began as part of the “Greenlight a Vet” project. According to the campaign, “The simple action of changing one light to green is intended to spark a national conversation regarding the recognition of veterans, and ‘greenlight’ them forward as valued members of our communities.”

In 2013, Walmart’s Veterans Welcome Home Commitment initiative, which provides jobs to any honorably discharged U.S. veteran, created an ad campaign asking people to turn on a green porch light as a way to recognize and show appreciation for veterans in their community. They encouraged people to share their support on social media by taking a photo of their green light and sharing it with the hashtag #GreenlightAVet.

The Greenlight a Vet initiative is not the only one to shine a light, so to speak, on our country’s veterans. In 2022, The National Association of Counties (NACo) in affiliation with the National Association of County Veterans Services Officers (NACVSO), launched Operation Green Light for Veterans (#OperationGreenLight). In the program’s debut year, over 300 counties participated nationwide, including Fairbanks, Alaska’s North Star Borough and Mohave County, Arizona. Nicole Weissman, NACo’s director of strategic communications, expects the number of participating counties this year to be “significantly larger” than it was last year.

“We must support our veterans and their families—not only during Operation Green Light but all year round,” says NACo President Jo McGuire. “Counties are advocating for legislation to secure appropriate resources at the local level to help veterans access their federal benefits, ease their transition into civilian life, and support their long-term health and well-being.”

The association explains, “By shining a green light, county governments and our residents will let veterans know that they are seen, appreciated, and supported.” NACo’s initiative encourages all U.S. counties and parishes to show support for military veterans by illuminating courthouses, offices, and other municipal buildings in green from November 4 to 11, the week leading up to Veterans Day.

In September 2023, the House of Representatives introduced House Resolution 750, a bipartisan bill recognizing Operation Green Light for Veterans for “supporting veterans and…help[ing] veterans transition to civilian life.”

Illuminate Enbrighten’s waterproof Eternity lights green for Veterans Day and leave them up year round, changing colors and modes via app.

Green is a color that is often associated with the military because of the green uniforms traditionally worn by troops, but there’s a more symbolic meaning as well. According to the Greenlight a Vet campaign, “Green is the color of hope, renewal and well-being.” They add that “‘Greenlight’ is also a term commonly used to activate forward movement.”

Govee’s smart light bulbs support millions of hues and can be controlled by phone app. Read the review.

While Veterans Day on November 11 is the most symbolic time of year to show support for America’s troops, why not follow Operation Green Light for Veterans’ lead and shine the light for the whole week of Veterans Day, or even keep your green light up year-round to show your ongoing appreciation for our military?

In Prattville, Alabama, community advocate Julie Cooley, who is also a military spouse and mother, went a little further. She encouraged “neighbors, municipalities and businesses to show their love and support of our veterans this week. Some choose to put signage on their marquis, some offer discounts, some turn their lights green! What’s important is that our military veterans and their families feel a great big hug from their Prattville community.”

“One of NACo’s goals for Operation Green Light is to equip counties to participate in a way that’s meaningful to veterans in their community, so we’re always looking for ways to do that,” says Weissman. In some counties, she says, this outreach includes “distributing green light bulbs or otherwise encouraging residents to participate” in Operation Green Light for Veterans.  If you’d like to show your support for veterans this month, pick up a green light bulb at your local hardware store—or at one of the following retailers.

#7817. Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

Tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

Both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

They give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, issue an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

“Each office knows the local area and will issue Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”

Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can issue one before snow or ice begins falling.

A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

“Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

Once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

If the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

Residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

Don’t Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise” Federal Emergency Management Agency, “Be Prepared for a Winter Storm”

#7815. No Problem with Recognizing Islamic Talaq Divorce from Dubai, When Wife Didn't Want to Stay Married

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Schultz v. Stevenson, decided today by California Court of Appeal Judges Peter Krause, Shama Hakim Mesiwala, and Stacy Boulware Eurie:

In 2004, [the parties] purchased a residential property in Grass Valley, California, taking title as "husband and wife as joint tenants." In 2020, [husband] Schultz obtained a judgment of divorce from [wife] Stevenson in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE). The Dubai divorce decree addressed marital status and child custody only; it made no findings related to division of property or spousal support.

Years later, Schultz commenced an action … to partition the Grass Valley property [by ordering it sold and the proceeds split -EV]. Stevenson opposed partition, arguing that the Dubai divorce decree is not enforceable in California and therefore the property is community property and not subject to partition [since California law does not allow partition of community property among married parties -EV]. The trial court ultimately … [decided] in favor of Schultz, finding that the parties are divorced and that the property is not community property….

Stevenson … argues that the trial court abused its discretion by extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree because it was based on Islamic (Sharia) laws that violate state public policy and constitutional principles of equal protection and due process…. [S]he argues that the Dubai divorce is not entitled to comity because it is based on a talaq pronouncement of divorce, which violates California's public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment. [Generally, a talaq divorce can only be initiated by a husband. -EV] Stevenson contends therefore that she and Schultz are still married, and that the Nevada County property is community property, which is not subject to partition.

We conclude that Stevenson has failed to show that the trial court erred in extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree.

Under the doctrine of comity, courts of this nation generally will give effect to the judgment of a foreign nation if the foreign court had proper jurisdiction and enforcement of the judgment will not prejudice the rights of United States citizens or violate domestic public policy…. Even if we agree that parts of Sharia law—such as a talaq pronouncement of divorce—are contrary to domestic public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment, the mere fact that some laws of the foreign nation are inconsistent with those of the sovereign does not preclude application of comity.

The basic principle of judicial comity is that "'a court should not assume to disturb another court's disposition of a controversy unless there are good reasons for doing so.'" The standard for refusing to enforce a foreign judgment on public policy grounds is high and infrequently met. The standard "'is not simply that the law is contrary to our public policy, but that it is so offensive to our public policy as to be "'prejudicial to recognized standards of morality and to the general interests of the citizens….'"' [E]ven when a foreign law offends public policy, 'it may still be applied in a limited context where the potential harm is minimal….'" (See In re Dalip Singh Bir's Estate (Cal. App. 1948) [in context of intestate succession, foreign law permitting polygamy may be applied under principles of comity].)

Here, we are not persuaded that extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree impermissibly prejudiced Stevenson's rights or flouted state public policy favoring gender equality. It is important to remember that the Dubai judgment only adjudicated two issues—marital status and child custody—and that the trial court extended comity to the judgment as it related to the status of marriage only. {Stevenson contends that issues related to child custody and support have been rendered moot as the children have reached the age of majority.} Since Stevenson plainly did not wish to remain married to Schultz, we cannot say that it was an abuse of discretion for the trial court to recognize the Dubai judgment as dissolving marital status.

The premise underlying Stevenson's claim of prejudice appears to be that recognizing the foreign divorce precludes her from obtaining spousal support and an equitable division of the marital property. We disagree with this premise…. As noted, the Dubai judgment only adjudicated the issues of marital status and child custody. It did not address, and therefore has no effect upon, spousal support or the division of community property in California….

In reaching this conclusion, we note that the trial court has ordered the partition and sale of property but has not yet determined how the proceeds will be disbursed, reserving jurisdiction "to order the manner in which the sale proceeds are to be disbursed, and to order equitable adjustments that the Court considers just and appropriate." It is therefore premature for us to consider whether the distribution of proceeds amounts to an abuse of discretion….

Robin D. Shofner (Scale LLP) represents Schultz.

#7814. 6 Ways to Stop Chimney Fires Before They Start

Updated Nov 5, 2026 12:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

There are more than 25,000 chimney fires incurring $125 million-plus in property damage every year in the United States. That damage is largely due to flames in the lower chimney migrating upward to crack, warp, melt, or otherwise negatively affect the masonry or metal chimney walls. In the most severe cases, chimney fires can destroy houses and put lives at risk. These tragedies are often preventable: Failure to regularly inspect, repair, and clean a chimney can cause it to malfunction or collect dangerous buildup that puts your family at risk.

If you practice these prevention tips, that hard-working column above your fireplace or wood stove should continue to do its job of ushering smoke and other by-products out of your home, so you and yours can safely cozy up in front of the flames. Ahead, learn what causes chimney fires and steps you can take to prevent them.

The main culprit of chimney fires is creosote. This highly flammable, dark brown substance coats chimney walls when by-products of a fire (smoke, vapor, and unburned wood) condense as they move from the hot fireplace or wood stove into the cooler chimney. If the temperature in the chimney flue (the space inside the chimney) is high enough, and the creosote build-up thick enough, creosote can catch fire—and that fire can spread and move up the flue.

To minimize creosote build-up, only burn seasoned hardwood that has dried for at least six months and contains a moisture content of no more than 20 percent, which you can easily test with a wood moisture meter. And remember to always keep the damper (a metal plate in the flue that regulates the draft) open during a fire to maintain adequate airflow.

And if your chimney’s flue liner (the layer between the flue and chimney walls) is uninsulated, it’s recommended to insulate it by either wrapping a heat-resistant insulation blanket around the liner or pouring an insulation mix like vermiculite into the space between the flue liner and flue. An insulated flue liner will prevent flue temperatures from getting too cool—a condition that could encourage fire by-products to condense and form creosote.

Because many defects that lead to chimney fires, such as a cracked flue liner, aren’t visible to the naked eye, it’s crucial to have a Chimney Safety Institute of America-certified chimney sweep inspect your fireplace or woodstove, chimney, and venting system once a year. This pro will inform you of any damage and, if desired, repair it as well as remove soot, creosote, or obstructions such as bird nests.

There are three levels of chimney inspections:

Consult your chimney sweep company about which inspection level is recommended for your chimney and venting system.

If when you scratch a finger against a chimney wall and uncover one-eighth of an inch of build-up, it’s time for a cleaning. A professional chimney cleaning costs between $100 and $350 and usually includes a sweep of the outside of the chimney along with the firebox, the smoke shelf, the smoke chamber above the firebox, the flue, and the flue liner. However, budget-conscious DIYers willing to get up on a ladder can also clean their chimney without professional help by using a wide chimney brush.

This creosote destroyer coats your chimney liner with protective chemicals while you burn, preventing creosote buildup. Read our full review.

Leaves and animal nests inside a flue can quickly fuel a chimney fire when touched by loose embers from a fire. A chimney cap on the crown around the outside opening of the flue will keep debris and critters out. The cap will also prevent “back puffing,” whereby escaped smoke from a fire re-enters the chimney and then the home. Caps also prevent acidic rainwater from entering and corroding the chimney. Expect to spend anywhere from $50 for galvanized metal caps to $500 or more for decorative models. While some homeowners opt to put in a chimney cap themselves, self-installation may void the warranty—it may be worth it to call a pro.

Always stick to the best fire starters when selecting fuel, kindling, and tinder.

Low-temperature, slow-burning fires, particularly those left to smolder overnight, produce more smoke and leave behind more unburned combustible material. When that hardens into creosote on the chimney walls, there’s an increased risk of chimney fires. Hot, fast-burning fires, on the other hand, leave far less smoke, vapor, and unburned wood behind, so little to no creosote forms.

The best way to burn a clean fire is to use the top-down burn method: Place the large logs vertically at the bottom of the fireplace or wood stove (with the bottoms of the logs facing you), add four to five horizontal layers of kindling, then top with tinder and light.

And, before retiring for the night, always extinguish the fire: Spread out the wood and embers with a fireplace poker, then cover them with the ash lying at the bottom of the fireplace using a fireplace shovel. Then douse the cooled wood and embers with enough baking soda to cover them completely—the sodium bicarbonate will extinguish any remaining embers. After the firebox cools (for a minimum of three hours, but preferably eight), shovel the ashes into a metal container. Fill the metal container with water and store it outside the home away from other flammable materials until you’re ready to discard them.

#7813. Tool Trials: Putting Ridgid’s Cordless Crown Stapler To the Test

Is a cordless stapler a real upgrade, or just a nice-to-have? I put one to the test to find out.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”

Fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

It drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

The short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

There were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

Second, the depth drifted. After every 20 or 30 staples, I’d notice they were no longer seating at the depth I’d set and were starting to sit proud. I don’t know if that was due to denser 2x4s or inconsistencies between strips of staples, but it was something to keep an eye on. When I noticed it, I’d add a few clicks on the depth knob.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The tool alone retails at The Home Depot for $119, but for the last few months, there’s been a special buy that includes the tool, a charger, and a 2.0 Ah Ridgid battery for $104.

Ridgid is owned by Emerson Electric Co., which makes the red Ridgid plumbing and pipe tools directly. The orange Ridgid cordless power tools, including this stapler, are made by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the company behind Milwaukee and Ryobi, under a licensing agreement with Emerson.

No. Staple guns need staples that match the tool’s crown width, leg length, and wire gauge. The Ridgid 18V crown stapler takes 3/8-in. crown staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long, including standard T50 staples. Other staplers may use different types, like narrow-crown or other heavy-duty series, so check the tool or the manual before you buy.

#7812. 14 Types of Blinds Every Homeowner Should Know

Updated Nov 5, 2026 3:38 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you’ve weighed the benefits of curtains, shutters, and blinds in your search for the right window coverings for your home and you’ve settled on blinds, you’re in good company. According to a study by research firm Market Research Future, the size of the window blind market was an estimated $75.48 billion in 2025, and it’s expected to grow to $136.35 billion by 2035. Another research firm, Global Market Insights, found that blinds and shades dominated the window treatment industry in 2025.

With so many different types of blinds on the market, how do you decide which will suit your home best? Whether you’re looking for something sleek and modern or traditional and classic, this guide will help you figure out which ones might be the right pick for your windows.

Blinds are a type of window covering composed of numerous slats, vertical or horizontal, that can be tilted or rotated to adjust the amount of light entering a space. Blinds made of aluminum or vinyl are typically the most cost-efficient types, but there also are blinds crafted of fabric and wood.

They can be installed inside the window frame or above it. Window blinds are typically mounted with specially designed brackets that are sold with the blinds.

Blinds consist of many parts. The headrail, for example, is the top part of the blind that contains the operating mechanisms such as the cords, pulleys, or tilt wands. The headrail provides structural support for the blind. The valance is the decorative cover that hides the headrail and its workings.

Depending on the style of the blinds, there may be a cord that draws the slats up and down. A wand adjusts the tilt of the louvers, which are the collection of narrow horizontal slats that tilt to adjust the amount of light that passes into the space.

The slats are suspended from a track that runs along the top of a window frame. This style of blinds collects less dust than other types of blinds and is easy to clean. The slats just need to be wiped down with a damp cloth.

Best For: Affordability and minimal maintenance

Blinds.com’s vertical blinds are textured, available in a variety of colors, and are guaranteed to fit.

The Home Decorators faux wood Venetian blinds are cordless, making them safe for households with pets or young children.

Mini blinds are like Venetian blinds, with some minor differences. Like Venetian blinds, they are typically made from aluminum or vinyl instead of wood or bamboo. Mini blinds have smaller slats than Venetian blinds, though: Mini-blind slats are usually an inch wide or smaller. While these two types of blinds perform the same way, mini blinds have a sleeker design and thus tend to look more modern and contemporary.

With a minimalist design and cordless operation, the Achim mini blinds are safe and stylish.

Wood blinds are a popular choice for those looking to add an element of luxury to their window treatments since wood blinds offer a natural, timeless look that never goes out of style. Not only do they exude sophistication, but they are also incredibly durable and can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. They can be painted or stained to match any color palette, and different slat sizes are available to accommodate shoppers’ specific needs. Wooden blinds tend to be horizontal—or Venetian—style, though vertical wooden blinds are also available.

Best For: Homeowners who are in it for the long haul—these are built to last

Levolor’s 2-inch wood blinds have cordless lift and wand tilt and come in a variety of wood stains.

Aluminum blinds are one of the most popular types of window blinds because of their affordable price and lightweight yet durable design. A sleek, modern look that can complement many decor styles, they are easy to install and incredibly long-lasting. Aluminum blinds also come in a variety of colors, sizes, and textures, allowing homeowners to customize the look of their windows to suit many different aesthetics. In terms of energy efficiency, aluminum blinds help keep a home’s interior cooler by reflecting the sun’s rays away from the window. This helps reduce air conditioning costs since less energy is required to maintain steady temperatures inside the house.

Best For: Easy installation and durability

Sleek and affordable, Blinds.com’s 8-gauge aluminum blinds are available in a variety of neutral colors.

If you’re looking for blinds to cover sliding doors or large windows, consider panel blinds. These window treatments are composed of several panels affixed to a headrail at the top of the window. Each panel is attached to a carrier that slides along a track in order to open or close the blinds. They offer a unique look that differs from standard vertical blinds, making them a great choice for design-forward shoppers.

Roller blinds are technically a type of window shade, making them different from many of the other types of blinds on our list. An alternative to curtains, these shades are made up of a single piece of fabric material that rolls up and down to control the amount of sunlight that enters the space. Roller shades can be made from a variety of fabrics, ranging from sheer materials to opaque options. While roller blinds might have a reputation for being low quality and not performing well, their design has actually come a long way in recent years.

Chicology’s blackout roller shade has a cordless design and is made from hypoallergenic polyester that won’t attract dust.

UNISHASDES bamboo blinds  partially filter sunlight and come in a variety of sizes and finishes.

Motorized blinds are a modern window covering solution that allows users to open and close their blinds using a remote control, phone app, or voice command. Some models come with sun sensors that automate the opening and closing of your blinds at certain times of the day. Unlike traditional blinds that must be adjusted manually, motorized blinds use either electric or battery-powered motors to raise and lower them. This makes it easier to control the lighting in a room without ever having to leave your seat. Today, many window blind types can be motorized.

Our Recommendation: Custom Home Collection Designer 2-Inch Wood Blinds at The Home Depot, priced from $105.70.Featuring a traditional Venetian aesthetic, these motorized blinds offer both familiarity and convenience.

Our Recommendation: Coolaroo Exterior Roller Shade at Amazon, priced from $35.25.This exterior window treatment is affordable, cordless, protects against UV rays, and comes in a wide range of finishes.

Sometimes called layered or dual shades, zebra blinds consist of two layers of fabric, each with alternating horizontal bands of sheer and opaque fabric. You can adjust, or roll, the fabric to line up the stripes on the two layers of fabric, meaning opaque is lined up with opaque, and sheer with sheer; this allows light to enter. If you roll the shade such that the opaque stripes on one layer are lined up with the sheer strips on the other layer, the effect is that of an opaque shade, and no light comes through.

Our Recommendation: Chicology Zebra Blinds at Amazon starting at $36.58. These cordless, pull-down zebra blinds are available in four colors and numerous sizes.

Also called cellular blinds or cellular shades, honeycomb blinds are constructed of two sheets of fabric that are seamed together horizontally at regular intervals. When looking at these blinds from the side, the resulting pattern somewhat resembles that of a honeycomb. Highly insulating, the design is considered one of the most energy-efficient, and the cellular construction is also good at noise cancellation

Best For: Energy-efficiency; they also offer a modern vibe

Our Recommendation: BlindsAvenue Cellular Honeycomb Cordless Shade at Amazon starting at $32.85.Made of polyester, these cordless, pull-down blinds are available in 10 colors and a wide variety of sizes.

Pleated blinds are made from a single length of woven fabric that is pressed into sharp, horizontal pleats at regular intervals, yielding a zig-zag appearance. The blind is raised or lowered to adjust the amount of light entering the room. While they’re often compared to honeycomb blinds, pleated blinds don’t offer the same insulating properties as cellular blinds. Pleated blinds offer a clean, modern look.

Best For: Decorators in search of an elegant, minimalist  look.

Our Recommendation: Calyx Interiors Pleated Fabric Window Shade at Amazon, priced from $30.97.Semi-sheer and cordless, these pull-down blinds are available in four colors and several sizes.

“Blackout” is a descriptor applied to a number of types of blinds and shades that are designed to block out all light. Not only do they work to block light from entering a room, but they’re also typically made of thick, dark-colored materials that absorb light. Blackout window coverings might be cellular blinds or roller shades.

Best For: Rooms in which someone needs to sleep during the day.

Our Recommendation: Persilux Custom, Cordless Blackout Cellular Blinds at Amazon starting at $63.99. These cordless, pull-down blinds are available in five colors and numerous sizes.

The prices listed here are accurate as of March 31, 2025.

#7811. Your Level Might Be the Wrong Size, and It Could Be Throwing Off Your Work

A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

It depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:

“Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”

Another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.

#7810. 2027 Garden Planning: What the Experts Say Will Be Big Next Year

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:51 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

There’s always something new and exciting on the horizon in the world of gardening. Around this time every year, various organizations release their favorite gardening and landscaping trends for the coming year. From the color of the year to new plants and outdoor décor, the list below represents our favorite 2027 gardening trends for you to consider as you plan or update your outdoor space in the coming months.

Garden Media Group has identified ancient blue as the garden color of the year for 2027. As the first manufactured color in history, blue was created by the Egyptians 5,000 years ago to imitate precious lapis lazuli. While blue is consistently the favorite color around the world, it is the rarest color in the garden, showing up in fewer than 10 percent of flowers. “This makes growing it in the garden feel like victory,” says Katie Dubow, president of Garden Media Group.

Here are some planting and décor tips to seamlessly incorporate this calming color into your garden:

Gardeners prefer more from their edible plants than just fruits and vegetables to harvest, according to Monrovia’s 2027 Garden Design Trends Study. “We’re seeing shoppers be more discerning in their edible choices,” says Katie Tamony, chief marketing officer and trend spotter at Monrovia. “They’re looking for plants that add a design element or feel more exotic than the common choices their neighbors grow. People are also interested in edible plants that look good all season long.”

Adding an edible garden ranks among the highest-interest projects in Monrovia’s survey, with more than 45 percent of respondents saying they are looking for more unique selections. Enhance your edible garden with specialty herbs; berries with year-round interest; and conversation-starting selections like pomegranate, figs, kiwi, and olives.

After years of beige minimalism and tidy rows of shrubs, the “Let’s Go Rococo” theme is all about exuberance over restraint, says Dubow. Emerging in early 18th century France, rococo design was a deliberate rebellion by artists and craftsmen against the stiff grandeur of Baroque and societal wealth inequality. Think flowers, shells, gilded flourishes, ruffles, jewel-tone palettes, and asymmetry. “It’s ornamental, romantic, a little over the top, and joyful,” notes Dubow.

Here are some ways to infuse rococo style into your garden:

Garden Media Group’s OutdooRx trend positions the garden as medicine, says Dubow. “In the United Kingdom, doctors now “socially prescribe” gardening programs to patients, and research continues to show that gardening lowers stress hormones like cortisol while boosting mood-lifting dopamine and serotonin,” she explains. Approaches like the Sunday Garden Trend can provide relaxation.

Fortunately, you don’t need a prescription to benefit. You can create a therapeutic garden in your own backyard with these helpful tips:

This long-handle digging tool allows gardeners to work the soil more comfortably (and for longer periods of time) from a standing position.

National Garden Bureau also tracks garden trends, especially when it comes to which specific plants are the most popular in a given year. “Coming up in 2027, we see an enormous interest in hellebores, and that is our Year of the Crop for Perennials,” says Diane Blazek, executive director for All-America Selections at National Garden Bureau.

Often called the Christmas rose or Lenten rose, the hellebore is a hardy perennial that does well in full shade and brings beauty to winter and early spring gardens when most other flowers have faded. It produces elegant 2- to 3-inch blossoms in a cup shape that resemble roses. Hellebore flowers grow in a variety of colors, so you have plenty of options. It grows in USDA Hardiness Zones 5 to 8, and does best in cottage gardens, winter gardens, or woodland gardens. Take note that this plant is toxic and should be handled with caution.

As another season of the popular show The Gilded Age is released this month, romance and beauty are alive and well in gardens, too. This look maximizes the popularity of European-inspired garden design with an elevated, modern twist, shining a spotlight on classic plants like roses, peonies, hydrangeas, and boxwood. In addition to these timeless plants, this trend showcases artful hedges, chartreuse foliage, and collector statement plants.

“This trend appeals to established gardeners,” says Tamony. “Homeowners who have invested in their interior design are taking that high-end look to the garden.” Their interest in rare, collector plants is increasing, and Monrovia’s research shows their willingness to pay for premium plants and exquisite blooms is up between 5 and 9 percent since 2025.

Another style that is expected to be popular is the Palm Springs outdoor space. This works well for gardeners looking to create an attractive desert oasis through containers as well as the landscape. “The Palm Springs Style trend is all about creating a calming, wellness-focused outdoor space that feels more upscale,” says Tamony. With this aesthetic, gardeners can transform their landscape by choosing structured succulents and lush, tropical colors found with species from Agave, Bougainvillea, Mandevilla, and tropical hibiscus.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7809. Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations.

Law.com reported Thursday that Sullivan & Cromwell and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison are speaking with Weil Gotshal’s associates and trainees, and that other firms—including DLA Piper, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Latham & Watkins—have varying degrees of interest and engagement. According to Law.com, Weil Gotshal is working to find employment for as many people as possible.

Law.com further reported that priorities differ among the suitors. One source said Sullivan & Cromwell is currently favoring associates over partners, while another said Paul Weiss has already brought on several Weil Gotshal partners and is still courting junior lawyers. Meanwhile, another source told Law.com that some firms are offering places to prospective trainees who were due to join Weil Gotshal in September.

The wind-down still needs formal approval, with a partnership vote expected this week. Weil Gotshal’s leaders said the recommendation followed a thorough review of alternatives, and sources said partners have begun telling clients that the firm cannot continue. According to Law.com, the firms named were approached for comment.

#7808. Don't Expect a Lame-Duck Supreme Court Vacancy (But There Are Other Nominations to Consider)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Both the NYT and Bloomberg reports that Justice Alito still intends to finish out the current Supreme Court term.

There has been rampant speculation that one of the older conservative justices (namely Justice Sam Alito or Justice Clarence Thomas) might choose to retire before the end of the year so that President Trump could name a replacement while there is still a Republican majority in the Senate. But that is all it is: Speculation.

I have previously predicted that neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas would retire during this presidential term (let alone this year). I adhere to this view.

Today, the New York Times and Bloomberg each report that Justice Alito has reaffirmed that he is not planning to retire this year, and that this week's election results have not altered his intentions.

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats' commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The 76-year-old Alito, an anchor of the court's conservative wing, has been the subject of speculation that he might abruptly step down to let President Donald Trump fill the vacancy before Republicans relinquish control of the Senate in January. Such a move could extend Trump's imprint on the court by letting him add a younger, conservative jurist to serve for decades.

The chatter has continued even though Alito said in an interview with Bloomberg News in late September that he had decided to remain no matter how the election turned out. "I intend to stick around through this term," he said then, referring to the nine-month court session that runs through June. "I made that decision many months ago."

Alito indicated that stance hasn't changed despite the Democratic takeover in Tuesday's election, said the person, who asked not to be identified discussing a private conversation with the justice on Wednesday.

While there is no equivalent report on Justice Thomas, there is little reason to think he is going anywhere. Justice Thomas is on the verge of becoming the longest serving justice in the nation's history. Moreover, Justice Thomas has previously said he intends to spend at least 43 years on the Court. Were he to stick to that plan, he would have several more years to go.

While there may not be a Supreme Court nomination to keep the Senate busy during the lame-duck period, there are lower court nominations to consider, including nominees for the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Fifth, Eighth, and Tenth Circuits. As Michael Fragoso notes in the Wall Street Journal, the lame duck may be Republicans' last opportunity to confirm conservative constitutionalist judges for some time.

Republican senators can make a difference and send a message by putting the Constitution first and confirming the originalist nominees now pending. Petty or parochial squabbles with Mr. Trump may get favorable headlines today but they will be forgotten in a week. A judicial appointment can last a lifetime.

#7807. "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

#7806. Lawyer, business partner accused of defrauding cannabis investor of $750K

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows. (Image from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows, including the unsuccessful Green Street Festival in 2022.

A Los Angeles County court complaint filed by investor Jamie Chisick alleged that attorney Joshua Shelton of the Winston Wolfe Law Firm and his business partner, Rama Mayo, took $750,000 for a 15% ownership stake in the Green Street Symposium.

According to the Oct. 19 complaint, Shelton and Mayo, cannabis entrepreneurs, promised to organize large trade events that would attract thousands of attendees and generate “millions of dollars in revenue,” according to coverage on Law360.

Chisick obtained documents that he said shows that his money had been used for “personal payments, including but not limited to private jets, health insurance, bar dues (Shelton) and general overhead unrelated to GSS operations.”

The 2022 Green Street Festival brought in about $190,000 with about $178,000 refunded. A 2023 festival with projections of attracting over 10,000 attendees and up to $4.7 million in revenue drew a smaller crowd and did not produce a profit.

Chisick seeks to recover his investment and punitive damages, according to the complaint.
